## Fix cuBLAS DLL failure surviving Whisper's CUDA-to-CPU fallback (this session)

Christer reported a real crash from `bv-generate` on his machine:
"bv-generate: 20260715_143340_N: language detection failed for
20260715_143340_N.aac: Library cublas64_12.dll is not found or cannot
be loaded". This looked at first like task #48's GPU auto-detect/CPU
-fallback work not actually working, but the real cause was narrower:
`_load_whisper_model()`'s existing CUDA-then-CPU fallback only catches
problems that surface while *constructing* the `WhisperModel` object.
CTranslate2 (faster-whisper's backend) lazily initializes its actual
CUDA/cuBLAS runtime on first real inference, not at construction time
- so on a machine with the CUDA driver present but the cuBLAS runtime
DLL missing, the CUDA `WhisperModel` builds successfully (passing the
load-time probe cleanly) and only fails later, on the first real
`.transcribe()` call - which is exactly what "language detection
failed" surfaced, since `detect_language()` was that first call.

Fix, scoped to `speech.py` only: a new `_load_cpu_whisper_model()`
helper (forces a CPU model directly, skipping the CUDA attempt
entirely - unlike calling `_load_whisper_model()` again, which would
uselessly retry CUDA first) and a new `_whisper_transcribe(model_size,
source, **kwargs)` wrapper that calls the cached model's
`.transcribe()`, and on any exception, evicts the cache entry, loads a
forced CPU model in its place, and retries once. Both `detect_language()`
and `transcribe()` now call `_whisper_transcribe()` instead of calling
`_get_whisper_model()` + `.transcribe()` directly - `_get_whisper_model()`
itself, `_load_whisper_model()` itself, and the shared
`_WHISPER_MODEL_CACHE` dict's value shape (a bare model, not a tuple)
are all deliberately left untouched, since `test_speech.py` has direct
call sites and monkeypatches against exactly those functions/that
shape (checked before writing any code, same "check existing test call
sites before changing shared function contracts" discipline as this
session's earlier mirror/map-icon defaults work).

Once the CPU fallback fires for a given `model_size`, the cache holds
the working CPU model from then on - every later call for that size
skips straight to CPU instead of hitting the same DLL failure again,
without needing to remember "this machine has no working CUDA" anywhere
else.

Verified without pytest (still no network access in this sandbox to
install it): re-ran all four of `test_speech.py`'s existing
Whisper-model tests by hand (CUDA-fails-at-load-falls-back-to-CPU,
CUDA-succeeds-no-fallback-attempted, segment-timestamp-clamping via a
monkeypatched `_get_whisper_model`, and the missing-faster-whisper
`MediaToolError` message) - all four still pass unchanged, confirming
the existing load-time behavior and test contracts weren't disturbed.
Then reproduced Christer's exact failure directly: a fake CUDA model
that constructs fine but raises "Library cublas64_12.dll is not found
or cannot be loaded" on `.transcribe()`, seeded straight into the
cache to mirror the real sequence (load-time probe already "succeeded"
before this). `detect_language()` now recovers instead of raising -
returns the real result, evicts the broken model, and leaves a working
CPU model cached for next time (confirmed a second `transcribe()` call
for the same `model_size` used the cached CPU model directly, no
second failure). Also confirmed a genuine, non-recoverable failure (a
fake model that fails identically on both CUDA and the forced CPU
retry) still raises `MediaToolError` with both the "language detection
failed for ..." context and the underlying error text intact - the
fallback doesn't swallow a real problem, only recovers from the CUDA
-runtime-specific one.

Not yet run through the project's own `pytest` suite, and not yet
re-confirmed against Christer's own `20260715_143340_N.aac` file on
his machine - worth both once he can pull this commit.

## Trip detection now only considers recordings with Front video (this session)

Christer reported a real problem from his own archive: a trip's recordings included entries with GPS/3G/thumbnail data but no Front/Rear video for stretches in the middle (he doesn't download every recording's video by default - storage limits on a 256GB card - only specific ranges pulled down later once something nearby turned out to be worth keeping), and "Map videos are not in sync when there is missing footage." He proposed the fix himself: "I think it should only check for front camera video to determine trips."

Traced the mechanism before implementing (his own bv-ls --trips output was the reproduction case: `20260715_141235_E` (video) .. four GPS-only recordings roughly 5 minutes apart .. `20260715_143340_N` (video), all merged into one trip by the old logic). Two real, confirmed problems, both from TripBuilder.build() and export_trip() treating every Recording the same regardless of what it actually contains:

1. TripBuilder's gap rule is evaluated pairwise between consecutive recordings, not video segment to video segment. A run of several video-less GPS pings a few minutes apart each (individually under the 5-minute threshold) chain-bridged what was actually a ~19-21 minute real gap between the two genuine video segments into one trip.
2. Even where trip splitting was otherwise "correct" by the old rule, a video-less recording's own GPS fixes still got merged into the trip's route by trip_export.py. Concatenated Front/Rear video has no representation of missing time at all - it jump-cuts straight from one real segment to the next - while the merged GPS track still spans the real, unrepresented gap in between. render_map_video() has no way to know that gap didn't actually play out on screen, so it kept smoothly interpolating position across it: the map visibly crawling forward while the real video had already jump-cut past that whole stretch. This is the actual root cause of the reported desync, not a rendering bug in map_render.py/map_video.py themselves (those work correctly against whatever fixes/duration they're given - the problem was what was being fed to them).

Fix: `blackvue/trip/trip_builder.py` gained a new public `recordings_with_front_video(recordings)` helper (filters to `recording.has(Asset.FRONT)`) - TripBuilder itself stays completely asset-agnostic, unchanged; the filtering happens upstream, applied at both call sites that feed it real archive recordings: `bv_export.py`'s `bv_export()` (filters `archive.recordings` before building `all_trips`) and `bv_ls.py`'s `print_trips()` (filters before its own `TripBuilder(...).build()` call). A video-less recording is now simply never part of any trip - no export, no `--trips` row - though it still appears in a plain, non-`--trips` `bv-ls` listing, since that path doesn't go through TripBuilder at all. `docs/man/bv-export.md` and `docs/man/bv-ls.md` both gained a short note about this.

Verified directly (no pytest/network in this sandbox, standing limitation): reproduced Christer's exact scenario with a synthetic archive (one Front-video recording, four video-less GPS/g-sensor-only recordings roughly 5 minutes apart each, another Front-video recording ~21 minutes after the first) - confirmed the *old* unfiltered `TripBuilder.build()` call chain-bridged all six into one trip, and the *new* `recordings_with_front_video()`-filtered call correctly splits into two separate trips containing only the two video-having recordings, with all four GPS-only recordings excluded from both. Ran this same scenario through the real `bv_ls()` and `bv_export()` entry points end-to-end (not just the underlying TripBuilder class) - `--trips` output and the exported trip.log's own "Trip membership" section both confirm the same result. Re-ran every existing `--trips`/movement-bridging test from `test_bv_ls.py` and `test_bv_export.py` by hand against the changed code (gap threshold, gap-tolerance, movement-bridge-on, movement-bridge-off-by-default, and the plain trip-folder-creation test) - all pass unchanged, since every one of those tests' recordings already has Front video, none of them exercised the video-less case this fix targets.

Not yet run through the project's own pytest suite, and not yet re-confirmed against Christer's own real archive - worth both once he pulls this commit. Also worth him re-running `bv-export --map` on the specific trip he originally reported, to confirm the map/video desync is actually gone in a real render, not just in trip membership.

## Fix Trip.end_timestamp to include the last recording's own real video span (this session)

Christer noticed right after the front-video trip-detection fix: "notice that trip only count from the start, so trips that are only 1 recording is showing duration as 0" - a real `bv-ls --trips` run showed four legitimate single-recording trips (500+MB videos each) all reading `0:00:00` in the Duration column.

Root cause: `Trip.end_timestamp` was always just `self.last_recording.id.timestamp` - the last recording's own *start* timestamp, never its start plus its real video length. `Trip.duration` (`end_timestamp - start_timestamp`) and `Trip.label` (used for both `bv-ls --trips`'s displayed label and `bv-export`'s actual output folder name) both derive from it. For a single-recording trip this made `end_timestamp == start_timestamp` unconditionally, so `duration` was always exactly zero no matter how long the real video was. It also silently undercounted multi-recording trips by the same amount (the final recording's own span was never added) - just far less visibly, since those already had a real gap between start and end. This became much more visible after the front-video trip-detection fix earlier this session, since that fix produces far more single-recording trips than before.

Asked Christer whether to fix just the bv-ls display or fix `Trip.end_timestamp` itself everywhere (including `Trip.label`, meaning future `bv-export` folder names would change too, though existing exported folders keep their old names) - he chose "fix it everywhere."

`trip.py`: `Trip` gained an optional `recording_duration: RecordingDuration | None = None` field (a new local `RecordingDuration` type alias, defined in `trip.py` itself rather than imported from `trip_builder.py` to avoid a circular import - `trip_builder.py` already imports `Trip` from `trip.py`). Marked `compare=False` so two Trips built from the same recordings still compare equal regardless of whether a duration lookup was threaded through - equality was never about which callable happened to build them. `end_timestamp` now uses `recording_duration(self.last_recording)` when given, adding that many seconds on top of the last recording's own start timestamp; falls back to the exact old behavior (bare start timestamp) when `recording_duration` is `None` or returns `None` for that specific recording (e.g. `.duration.txt` doesn't exist for it yet) - fully backward compatible for any `Trip` built without one, which is how every existing test constructs them.

`trip_builder.py`: `TripBuilder.build()`'s two `Trip(...)` construction points now pass `recording_duration=self.recording_duration` - the exact same callback `TripBuilder` already threads through internally for its own gap calculation (`_end_timestamp()`), just now also handed to the `Trip` objects it returns. No change needed in `bv_ls.py` or `bv_export.py` themselves - both already pass `recording_duration=read_duration_seconds if duration/use_duration else None` into `TripBuilder(...)`, so the fix reaches `--trips` display and `bv-export` folder naming automatically once `TripBuilder` forwards it.

Verified directly (no pytest/network in this sandbox, standing limitation): re-ran every existing `test_trip.py` assertion by hand against a `Trip` built without `recording_duration` - all pass unchanged, confirming full backward compatibility. New checks: a single-recording `Trip` with a fake `recording_duration` returning 341 seconds correctly reports `end_timestamp` = start + 5m41s, `duration` = `0:05:41` (not zero), and `label` reflecting the real end; a `recording_duration` returning `None` for a specific recording falls back to the old bare-timestamp behavior; a multi-recording trip's `end_timestamp` now also includes the last recording's own real span; equality between two `Trip`s with different `recording_duration` values (one `None`, one real) still holds, confirming `compare=False` works as intended. End-to-end: built a real archive with two single-recording trips, each with a genuine `ffmpeg`-generated video and a real `.duration.txt` (341s and 600s) - `bv-ls --trips` now shows `0:05:41`/`0:10:00` instead of `0:00:00`, with the End column and trip label both reflecting the real end time; `bv-export` on the same archive produced folders named with the real end timestamp too. Re-ran every previously-verified `--trips`/`bv-export` regression check (gap threshold, movement bridging, plain trip-folder creation, front-video-only filtering) against archives with no `.duration.txt` present - all still pass exactly as before, confirming the fallback path is unaffected.

Not yet run through the project's own pytest suite, and not yet re-confirmed against Christer's real archive.

## Trip distance/speed/duration + reverse-geocoded start/end address in a new trip_info.txt, plus a letterboxed (not distorted) --stitch-map panel (this session)

From a screenshot Christer sent of a real `--stitch.mp4` render: the map panel at the bottom showed mostly empty background with the real route squeezed into a narrow band. Traced the mechanism in `stitch.py` without needing his real GPS data: `_map_panel_dimensions()` already sizes the panel's free dimension from the trip's own real-world aspect ratio (via `osm_roads.aspect_ratio_of()`), but clamps it to between 20% and 50% of the composite's matching dimension - a near-straight-line or sharply-angled trip routinely lands outside that range. `_render_map_panel()`'s static "map" mode then forced the geographic bounding box itself to match whatever (possibly clamped, mismatched) panel shape resulted, via `bounding_box_for_fixes(fixes, aspect_ratio=width/height)` - when the trip's true shape didn't match the clamped panel shape, this made the map zoom out in whichever direction was too short to make the (distorted) box fit, leaving most of the panel as background with the real route crammed into a fraction of it.

Christer then asked for something bigger picture in the same message: "I am thinking in a bigger picture, it would be interesting to know the distance for the trip, average speed and other useful information should be entered into 1 file for each trip. Can you get a name or an address for the first and last gps position in a trip." Given the size (three separable pieces), proposed a 5-task breakdown and got explicit sign-off via one consolidated question covering all of it: letterbox bars for the map fix (vs. alternatives like re-clamping the panel-sizing range itself, which would still be an approximation, not the trip's true shape); Distance/Average speed/Max speed/Duration for the stats file; automatic reverse geocoding (same as how `--map`'s road/area data already fetches automatically once requested, not a separate opt-in flag); and a new dedicated `trip_info.txt` file rather than appending to the existing `trip.log`.

**Map panel letterboxing.** Rather than re-clamping `_map_panel_dimensions()` (still just a different approximation), `_render_map_panel()`'s static "map" mode was changed to render the map undistorted at its own true geographic shape, sized to the largest fit within the panel's width x height (a new `_contain_fit(aspect_ratio, max_width, max_height)` helper - the same "CSS `object-fit: contain`" computation, even-dimension-rounded the same way `_map_panel_dimensions()` already is), then letterboxed/pillarboxed up to the panel's exact requested size via the existing `_fit_and_pad()` filter-chain helper (already used elsewhere in this file for the analogous camera-composite-into-a-mismatched-`--stitch-resolution` case) and `encode_with_nvenc_fallback()`. When the trip's true shape already exactly matches the panel (or in a 1x1 test placeholder), the extra render+encode pass is skipped entirely - `render_map_video()` writes straight to the final destination as before. "zoom" mode is untouched - it's already well-composed at any panel shape on its own (a fixed real-world radius centered on the vehicle every frame, not derived from the trip's overall shape).

**trip_info.txt.** Three new modules under `src/blackvue/export/`: `trip_stats.py` (`compute_trip_stats(fixes)` - haversine distance summed across consecutive valid/positioned fixes at ~1Hz, average speed as the mean of each fix's own instantaneous `speed_kmh` reading rather than distance/duration - deliberately, so a long stationary stretch correctly pulls the average down the way a real GPS trip computer does - and max speed as the highest single reading; returns `None` if fewer than two positioned fixes exist), `geocoding.py` (`reverse_geocode()`/`load_or_reverse_geocode()` against OpenStreetMap's Nominatim service, following the exact fetch-if-not-cached-then-persist pattern `osm_roads.py` already uses for road/area data - `USER_AGENT` shared with that module, a process-wide 1-request/second throttle per Nominatim's own public usage policy, and a genuine "no result" response cached same as a real address, but a network/parse failure NOT cached so a transient outage gets retried on the next export rather than permanently remembered as "no result"), and `trip_info.py` (`write_trip_info()` - plain text, `Duration:` always present, `Distance:`/`Average speed:`/`Max speed:` present whenever stats exist (speed lines individually omitted if that data isn't available, distance still shown), `Start location:`/`End location:` each independently present depending on whether that lookup succeeded).

`trip_export.py`'s `export_trip()` now computes trip stats and geocodes the first/last positioned GPS fix unconditionally whenever the trip has fixes (not gated behind `--map`/`--stitch-map`), reusing the same `.osm_cache` directory `--map`'s road/area cache already writes to. A geocoding failure for either point is caught independently into its own warning (`trip info: could not geocode start/end location: ...`) and degrades gracefully - the rest of the export, including `trip_info.txt` itself with whatever stats/addresses did succeed, still completes normally. `ExportResult` gained a `trip_info: Path | None` field.

**Verification.** No pytest/real network in this sandbox (standing limitations) - confirmed the sandbox's proxy rejects fast (~0.01s, 403 Forbidden) rather than hanging, so real-network code paths fail quickly here rather than stalling. Direct Python re-implementations of every `trip_stats.py`/`geocoding.py`/`trip_info.py` unit behavior (distance against known geography, avg/max speed, invalid-fix filtering, cache hit/miss/failure-not-cached semantics, throttle timing via mocked `time.monotonic`/`time.sleep`) all confirmed correct by hand.

For the letterbox fix specifically: re-ran `test_stitch.py`'s existing map-panel test suite by hand (default side-picking, `--stitch-map-size` override, zoom mode untouched, rearview_mirror's 30% cap, combining with an explicit `--stitch-resolution`, combining with a g-sensor overlay) - all pass unchanged, since none of them assert on the panel's *internal* composition, only its outer width/height (which the letterbox change deliberately preserves exactly). New check: a sharply east-west trip forced into a square 200x200 panel now renders a genuinely different-shaped (200x136) undistorted inner map, confirmed via real pixel sampling that the top/bottom rows of the final 200x200 output are solid black letterbox bars rather than stretched map content.

For `trip_info.txt`/geocoding, re-running `test_trip_export.py`'s existing test suite surfaced a real problem: `export_trip()` now makes real Nominatim calls for any trip with real GPS fixture data, and several existing tests already build such fixtures (`_trip_with_two_gps_fixes`, `_trip_with_front_rear_and_gps`, `_trip_with_front_rear_and_gps_shape`) without mocking it - in this network-isolated sandbox those calls fail fast and surface as unexpected warnings, breaking `assert result.warnings == ()`-style assertions in roughly 16 existing tests. Along the way, the same investigation also turned up a second, pre-existing gap unrelated to this session's own work: `load_or_fetch_areas()` (the water/green-areas feature from an earlier session) was never mocked in these tests either, for the same reason. Fixed by extending the existing `_fake_roads`-style mocking convention: a new `_fake_geocode`/`_fake_areas` pair, threaded into each of the three shared trip-fixture helper functions (which now take `monkeypatch` and patch `load_or_reverse_geocode` themselves, so every caller gets it for free) and added alongside every existing `_fake_roads` patch site for `load_or_fetch_areas`. `test_export_trip_writes_everything_available` also gained direct assertions on `result.trip_info`'s existence and content (duration/distance/both address lines using the mocked geocode value), since it's the general "writes everything" test and trip_info.txt is now one of those things. All 55 non-`capsys` tests in `test_trip_export.py` re-run by hand afterward - pass. The remaining 4 `capsys`-fixture tests (unsupported by this session's hand-rolled fixture shim) were confirmed by inspection to build only g-sensor fixtures, no GPS data, so they're unaffected by either change.

`docs/man/bv-export.md` gained a `trip_info.txt` row in the OUTPUT table and a DESCRIPTION paragraph explaining it's automatic (not a flag) and what happens on a geocoding failure.

Not yet run through the project's own pytest suite, and not yet confirmed against Christer's real archive - worth checking in particular whether Nominatim's real response shape/timing holds up as expected outside this sandbox, and whether the letterboxed map panel looks right on the real trip whose screenshot started this.

## Four more trip_info.txt fields: start/end clock time, moving/idle time, Parking-mode indicator, total size (this session)

After the trip_info.txt/geocoding/letterbox commit above, Christer asked "any more meta data we can [get] out from this." Rather than guessing, did a factual inventory first (via a research subagent, reading `GpsFix`, `GSensorSample`, `Recording`/`AssetFile`, and `Road`/`Area` directly) of what's actually already parsed and available - notably: no altitude/HDOP (the `.gps` file's `$GGA` sentence is read but its fields are discarded, only `$GRMC` is parsed), no road names (Overpass geometry is kept but tags are dropped after the request), no video resolution/codec (ffprobe is only asked for duration/frame rate), and g-sensor x/y/z values have no confirmed physical unit (the reader's own docstring warns against building calibrated g-force thresholds on them). Reported back four fields genuinely available without new parsing work, Christer picked all four via a multi-select question: start/end clock time, a Parking-mode indicator, total file size, and idle-vs-moving time.

`trip.py`: `Trip` gained two new properties - `total_size` (sums `Recording.size`, itself accumulated per-asset in bytes by `ArchiveReader` as it reads the archive - not a fresh filesystem scan) and `has_parking_footage` (`any(recording.id.is_parking for recording in self.recordings)`, `RecordingId.is_parking` being `kind == "P"`). `start_timestamp`/`end_timestamp` already existed from earlier work, so no changes needed there.

`trip_stats.py`: `TripStats` gained `moving_seconds`/`idle_seconds` (both `float | None`, defaulting to `None` so any existing caller constructing a `TripStats` without them still works). `compute_trip_stats()` now also classifies the time between each pair of consecutive positioned fixes as moving or idle, using `telemetry/movement.py`'s existing `DEFAULT_SPEED_THRESHOLD_KMH` (5.0 km/h) - the same cutoff already used to decide whether GPS evidence shows movement at a trip-gap edge, reused here rather than inventing an unrelated second number. Each segment is classified by the *mean* of its two endpoint speed readings (whichever of the two actually has one - a segment with neither is skipped, counted toward neither bucket, the same "unknown, not zero" handling `average_speed_kmh`/`max_speed_kmh` already use). Both fields are `None` under the same "no speed data anywhere in the trip" condition those two already use.

`trip_info.py`: `write_trip_info()` gained `start_timestamp`/`end_timestamp` (formatted `%Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%S`, matching `bv-ls --trips`'s own timestamp column exactly, so a reader who's seen that table doesn't have to mentally translate a different format for the same value), `has_parking_footage` (only written when `True` - a normal-driving trip is the common case, so this flags the exceptional one rather than restating "no" in every file), and `total_size_bytes` (formatted via a new small local `_format_size()` - deliberately a reimplementation of `cli/bv_ls.py`'s own `format_size()` rather than an import, since that one lives in the CLI layer, which already depends on this export layer and not the other way around, and is tuned for a compact table column ("512.34M") rather than this file's more prose-like style ("512.34 MB")). `Moving time:`/`Idle time:` lines were added right after `Max speed:`, reading straight off `TripStats`.

`trip_export.py`'s `export_trip()` now passes `trip.start_timestamp`, `trip.end_timestamp`, `trip.has_parking_footage`, and `trip.total_size` into the existing `write_trip_info()` call - no new computation needed there, since all four ultimately come from `Trip`/`TripStats`, which already had everything else they needed.

Verified directly (no pytest/network in this sandbox, standing limitation): this time also wrote proper permanent test files rather than only hand-run scripts, since `trip_stats.py`/`trip_info.py` had no dedicated unit tests at all before this (only integration coverage via `test_trip_export.py`, plus this session's own ad-hoc verification scripts for the rest). New `tests/blackvue/trip/test_trip.py` cases for `total_size` (sums correctly across recordings, zero when no sizes recorded) and `has_parking_footage` (true when any recording is Parking-mode, false for an all-normal trip), using real `Recording`/`RecordingId` objects rather than the file's existing `FakeRecording` (which doesn't define `.size`/`.id.is_parking` - same reasoning as the file's own pre-existing `test_trip_works_against_a_real_recording_not_just_the_fake`). New `tests/blackvue/export/test_trip_stats.py` (8 cases) covering the pre-existing distance/speed behavior for the first time as well as the new moving/idle split - including one case that caught a real mistake in a first draft of the moving/idle test itself: because segments are classified by the *mean* of both endpoints, a transition segment between a slow and a fast fix gets pulled toward "moving" by its one fast endpoint, not cleanly split at the fix boundary the way a first intuition suggests - the test was corrected to match the actual (intended) behavior once traced through by hand. New `tests/blackvue/export/test_trip_info.py` (7 cases) covering the full new field set, omission-when-unknown for each, and `_format_size()` across B/KB/MB/GB. All 15 new tests plus the 12 existing `test_trip.py` tests re-run by hand - pass. Also re-ran `test_export_trip_writes_everything_available` (the broadest existing `test_trip_export.py` integration test) end-to-end with a real `Trip` containing a sized recording and a Parking-mode recording - confirmed `trip_info.txt` came out with `Started:`/`Ended:`/`Includes Parking-mode footage`/`Total size: 117.74 MB` all correct.

`docs/man/bv-export.md`'s `trip_info.txt` OUTPUT row and DESCRIPTION paragraph both updated to mention the four new fields.

Not yet run through the project's own pytest suite, and not yet confirmed against Christer's real archive.

## Fixed a real moving/idle-time undercount Christer found by reading a real trip_info.txt/trip.log (this session)

Christer uploaded a real `trip_info.txt` and `trip.log` from his own archive and asked to find the faults. Cross-checked every field against the accompanying `bv-ls --trip`/`bv-ls` output he pasted: Started/Ended/Duration matched `bv-ls` exactly, Total size matched exactly, the Parking-mode indicator was correctly set (the trip's membership section in `trip.log` does include two `_P` recordings), and distance/speed/both geocoded addresses all looked like plausible real values.

The one real fault: `Moving time: 0:10:47` + `Idle time: 0:01:01` = 11:48 total, but the trip's ten `_N` (normal) recordings run continuously from 03:51:49 to about 04:20:21 - roughly 28 real minutes - and `trip.log` confirms `trip.gpx` was written with 1708 fixes, consistent with ~1Hz continuous GPS coverage across that whole span. So the reported moving+idle breakdown accounted for barely 40% of the real, continuously-GPS-tracked driving time, with the other ~60% silently missing and no indication in the output that anything was incomplete.

Root cause, confirmed by reading `compute_trip_stats()`: a segment between two consecutive positioned GPS fixes was only classified as moving or idle if *at least one* of the two fixes had a `speed_kmh` reading of its own; if both were missing (while still having a perfectly valid position), that segment's elapsed time was dropped entirely - counted toward neither bucket. The math only adds up if a large fraction of Christer's real fixes have a valid position but no speed reading, in long-enough runs that entire consecutive pairs land in "neither has one." Reported the finding back to Christer with the evidence and a proposed fix (carry the last known speed forward across gaps, vs. an alternative of surfacing an explicit "unknown time" line) - he picked the carry-forward fix.

Implementation, `trip_stats.py`: `compute_trip_stats()` now does a forward-fill pass over `positioned` first, building `effective_speeds` - each fix's own `speed_kmh` if it has one, otherwise the most recent earlier fix's real reading (`None` only for fixes before the very first real reading anywhere in the trip - unavoidable, nothing to carry from yet). The moving/idle loop then classifies each segment by the mean of `effective_speeds[index]`/`effective_speeds[index + 1]` instead of the two fixes' own raw readings - identical result to before whenever both fixes in a segment already have real readings (the common, dense-data case), but now correctly carries a real reading across any run of speed-less-but-positioned fixes in between, rather than dropping that time. `average_speed_kmh`/`max_speed_kmh` were deliberately left untouched - they still use each fix's own raw reading only, not the carried-forward value, since carrying a value forward into an *average* would bias it in a way carrying it forward into a *time classification* doesn't.

Verified directly (no pytest/network in this sandbox, standing limitation): all 8 pre-existing `test_trip_stats.py` cases re-run unchanged and still pass, confirming the dense-data case (both endpoints have real readings) is bit-for-bit identical to before. Two new regression tests added: one reproducing the exact shape of Christer's bug at a small scale (a real reading, two consecutive fixes with no reading of their own, then a real reading again - confirming the whole span is now classified using the carried-forward value instead of the middle segment being dropped) and one confirming the carried-forward value actually updates when a *newer* real reading appears partway through (not permanently latching onto the first one ever seen). Also re-ran `test_write_trip_info_*` (unaffected, but confirms nothing broke downstream) and `test_export_trip_writes_everything_available` end-to-end.

Not yet run through the project's own pytest suite, and not yet confirmed against Christer's real archive - worth him re-running `bv-export` on the exact trip that surfaced this and checking that Moving time + Idle time now lands close to the real ~28-minute driving span instead of 11:48.

## Fixed a grainy, badly undersized stitch.mp4 Christer found from the same trip (this session)

Christer sent a Windows file-properties screenshot for `stitch.mp4` from the same trip as the moving/idle-time fix above: 3840x2808, 29.58fps, 396MB, 1889kbps data rate, 00:28:31 long - and reported "the video is very grainy," with front+rear inputs totaling 4.7GB (2.6GB + 2.1GB) producing a 396MB output. No `--stitch-bitrate` was passed in the `bv-export` command captured in that trip's own `trip.log` (`--stitch --stitch-layout rearview_mirror ... --map --map-zoom --stitch-map zoom --gsensor --stitch-gsensor --stitch-subtitles`, no `--stitch-bitrate` anywhere in it).

Traced the full ffmpeg command construction end-to-end (`media.py` -> `stitch.py` -> `trip_export.py` -> `bv_export.py`'s CLI) via a research subagent before proposing anything: `_bitrate_args(bitrate)` in `stitch.py` is the *only* thing that ever supplies rate control (`-b:v`/`-maxrate`/`-bufsize`) to the final stitch encode, and it returns `[]` outright whenever `bitrate is None` - i.e. whenever `--stitch-bitrate` isn't passed, which is the common case (Christer's own `--stitch-bitrate` documentation and every prior WORKING_CONTEXT.md entry treat it as an optional cap, not something every export is expected to set). With no rate-control flag at all reaching ffmpeg, the final quality was left entirely to h264_nvenc's own unconfigured internal default.

Before proposing a fix, cross-checked that default's actual real-world behavior against this project's own history rather than assuming a single flat number: an earlier WORKING_CONTEXT.md entry recorded a native-resolution 5422x4320 stitch with no bitrate given landing at roughly 3.5GB over 20 minutes (~23Mbps) - a full order of magnitude higher than this trip's ~1.9Mbps. Both runs had no bitrate requested at all, on the same encoder, same machine class. That inconsistency - not a claim about NVENC's exact internal heuristic, which isn't documented and wasn't worth overclaiming - was the actual justification for a fix: leaving quality entirely to an unconfigured, apparently resolution/composition-sensitive encoder default isn't safe to rely on for every export.

Presented the finding and two `AskUserQuestion` choices to Christer: the quality target (a CQ/CRF around 18-20 - "visually near-lossless" for real camera footage/grain, vs. a fixed target bitrate, which would need to vary by resolution to give consistent results) and the scope (apply the fix inside the shared `encode_with_nvenc_fallback()` so every caller - stitch.mp4, map.mp4, gsensor.mp4 - gets a sane default, vs. only stitch.py's own call site). He picked CQ/CRF 19 applied everywhere.

Implementation, `media.py`: two new module-level constants, `_DEFAULT_NVENC_QUALITY_ARGS = ["-rc", "vbr", "-cq", "19", "-b:v", "0"]` and `_DEFAULT_LIBX264_QUALITY_ARGS = ["-crf", "19"]`, plus `_CALLER_RATE_CONTROL_FLAGS = ("-b:v", "-crf", "-cq", "-qp")` - the set of flags that mean "the caller already asked for their own rate control." `encode_with_nvenc_fallback()` now checks whether any of those flags is already present in the caller's `extra_codec_args` (e.g. stitch.py's own `-b:v`/`-maxrate`/`-bufsize` whenever `--stitch-bitrate` *is* given); if not, the relevant default quality args are prepended ahead of `extra_codec_args` on whichever of the NVENC/libx264 attempts actually runs. An explicit `--stitch-bitrate` therefore still wins outright with no competing `-cq`/`-crf` stacked on top of it - the existing bitrate-cap-vs-intermediate-bitrate logic in `stitch.py`'s `_stack()` is untouched and unaffected, since it only ever runs when `bitrate is not None`. Because the fix lives in the shared function, `map_video.py`/`gsensor_video.py`'s `encode_frame_sequence()` calls (which also previously reached ffmpeg with no rate control at all) get the same default for free, with no changes needed in either of those files.

Verified directly (no pytest/network in this sandbox, standing limitation - ffmpeg/ffprobe/PIL themselves are present and used for real encodes throughout): confirmed `media.py` compiles cleanly. Ran all 15 tests in `test_export_media.py` by hand via a fake-`pytest`-module shim (the file does `import pytest` for `pytest.raises`, but the real `pytest` package isn't installed here) plus the existing `FakeMonkeyPatch` pattern - all pass, including two pre-existing tests updated to expect the new default args (`test_encode_frame_sequence_uses_libx264_directly_when_nvenc_unavailable`, `test_encode_frame_sequence_tries_nvenc_first_when_available`) and four new ones: default quality applied with no `extra_codec_args` at all (NVENC and libx264 paths each), the default skipped outright when the caller supplies `-b:v` (confirming `--stitch-bitrate` still overrides cleanly), and a real (unmocked) libx264 encode with the new `-crf 19` actually producing a non-empty output file, confirming ffmpeg genuinely accepts the flag rather than just satisfying this project's own mocked assertions.

Also checked `test_stitch.py`/`test_trip_export.py`/`test_map_video.py`/`test_gsensor_video.py` for anything that could regress: `test_map_video.py`/`test_gsensor_video.py`/`test_trip_export.py` don't touch `encode_with_nvenc_fallback()`'s internals at all (no matches for codec_args/bitrate/`-crf`/`-cq` in any of them). Every `test_stitch.py` test that inspects codec/bitrate behavior does so by mocking `encode_with_nvenc_fallback()` itself and asserting on the `extra_codec_args` *passed into* it (i.e. what `stitch.py`'s own `_bitrate_args()`/bitrate-cap logic computes) - unchanged by this fix, since that logic lives entirely in `stitch.py`, not in what `encode_with_nvenc_fallback()` does with those args once received. The two `test_stitch.py` tests that run a real, unmocked encode end-to-end (`test_stitch_cameras_falls_back_to_cpu_decode_when_nvdec_fails_for_real`, `test_stitch_cameras_single_camera_falls_back_to_cpu_decode_when_nvdec_fails`) were re-run by hand under the new code path - both still pass, since they only assert on output video dimensions, not bitrate or file size.

Not yet run through the project's own pytest suite, and not yet confirmed against Christer's real archive - worth him re-running `bv-export --stitch` (with no `--stitch-bitrate`) on the same or a similar trip and checking the resulting stitch.mp4 is no longer visibly grainy, and that its file size/bitrate now lands in a more consistent, expected range for its resolution.

## Added --max-parking-duration: a cap on how long a parked stretch can stay part of the same trip (this session)

Christer pasted the `trip.log` membership section for the same trip as the two fixes above and pointed out its last two recordings - `20260724_042022_P` and `20260724_055101_P`, both Parking-mode - aren't actually in stitch.mp4 even though trip.log says they're trip members. He clarified their real length (playback) is about 3 minutes each, but their real elapsed span is around 90 minutes - BlackVue's Parking-mode timelapse: plays back fast, but covers a much longer real stretch of parked time.

That length mismatch traces straight to `recording_duration`'s own fold-in inside `TripBuilder._end_timestamp()` (added in an earlier session specifically so a long-but-genuinely-continuous recording doesn't look like a false gap to the *next* one): it has no ceiling, so a 90-real-minute Parking timelapse gets 90 minutes of "still continuous" credit, reading as zero gap between whatever drive came before it and whatever came after - explaining both why trip.log shows these two `_P` recordings as ordinary continuing trip members (the duration-folded gap between them was computed as 9 seconds, not the real ~89-minute gap), and, separately, why the footage itself doesn't survive `_concatenate_asset()`'s plain `-c copy` stream-copy concatenation cleanly (a time-lapse clip spliced next to normal-speed footage with mismatched real-vs-container timing is exactly the kind of thing that gets silently mangled rather than erroring out) - that second part is a `media.py`/`stitch.py` concatenation problem, not something this fix touches; today's fix is specifically about trip *membership*, i.e. deciding where the trip boundary should be in the first place.

Christer's actual ask, once the mechanism was clear: put a duration limit on Parking-mode footage - "when does a trip end when you have a long pause". Presented the mechanism (cap how much real elapsed Parking-mode time can be credited as "still continuous" before forcing a split) and got two explicit decisions via `AskUserQuestion`: the cap itself (60 minutes - long enough for a normal errand-length stop, short enough that his real ~90-minute case still splits) and whether two chained Parking recordings should be able to split from each other, not just at the point driving resumes (he chose yes - "a long parking session could become multiple parking-only trips").

**Implementation, `trip_builder.py`.** New `DEFAULT_MAX_PARKING_DURATION = timedelta(minutes=60)` constant and a new keyword-only `max_parking_duration: timedelta | None = None` param on `TripBuilder.__init__()` (opt-in, same pattern as `bridge`/`recording_duration` - unset changes nothing for any existing caller). `build()` now tracks a running `trailing_parking_seconds` total across the *trailing, unbroken* run of Parking-mode (`RecordingId.is_parking`) recordings at the end of the trip being built - via a new `_parking_contribution()` helper that returns a recording's own `recording_duration` if it's Parking-mode and a duration is known, otherwise 0 (a non-Parking recording, or a Parking one with no known duration, contributes nothing and - for a non-Parking recording specifically - also resets the running total to 0, since it breaks the continuous-parking run). Before evaluating each recording against the ordinary gap rule, `build()` now also checks whether the *already-accumulated* trailing total exceeds `max_parking_duration`; if so, that alone forces a split, independent of - and evaluated before - the normal `gap > threshold` check, and the would-be-split is never offered to `bridge` (a deliberate policy decision, "a stop this long is a new trip", not ambiguous gap evidence for movement data to weigh in on, so `bridge` is skipped entirely for this kind of split even if it's set). Because the check happens *before* a new recording is added to the total, three or more chained Parking recordings can produce a split between two of them specifically (once their combined span crosses the cap), not just where the next drive resumes - matching what Christer asked for.

`_parking_contribution()` deliberately short-circuits to 0 before ever reading `recording.id.is_parking` whenever `max_parking_duration is None` - important because this project's own test suite has several plain `FakeRecording`/`FakeRecordingId` stand-ins (predating this feature) that don't define `is_parking` at all; without that ordering, every existing test using `recording_duration` alongside a fake lacking `is_parking` would start raising `AttributeError` the moment `_parking_contribution()` ran, even though none of them opt into the new parameter.

**CLI wiring, `bv_export.py`.** New `--max-parking-duration MINUTES` flag (default 60, matching `DEFAULT_MAX_PARKING_DURATION`), threaded through `bv_export()` into the `TripBuilder(...)` construction the same way `--max-gap`/`--gap-tolerance` already are. Depends on real duration data the same way `--max-gap`'s own duration-aware gap calculation does, so `--no-duration` disables it too (with `recording_duration=None`, `_parking_contribution()` always returns 0, so the cap can never fire - a safe no-op, not a separate code path to keep in sync). Deliberately *not* wired into `bv-ls --trips`'s own `TripBuilder(...)` call in `bv_ls.py` in this same change - noted as a known gap in `docs/man/bv-export.md` rather than silently expanded scope, since only the export behavior was asked about.

**Verification.** All 23 pre-existing `test_trip_builder.py` cases re-run unchanged and still pass (confirms nothing regressed for any caller that doesn't opt in). Eight new tests added: reproducing Christer's real case at a small scale (a single 90-minute Parking recording forces a split even though the duration-folded gap to the next recording is a harmless 9 seconds); a shorter 30-minute stop staying under the cap and *not* splitting; three chained Parking recordings where the combined span of the first two (80 minutes) crosses the 60-minute cap, confirming the split lands between the second and third Parking recording specifically, not just at a return to driving; a non-Parking recording between two Parking ones correctly resetting the running total, so two 40-minute Parking spans separated by a drive don't wrongly sum to 80 minutes and split; the feature being a safe no-op with `max_parking_duration` set but no `recording_duration` callback; the explicit `AttributeError` regression guard for `FakeRecording`/`FakeRecordingId` stand-ins lacking `is_parking`; the `reasons` text for a cap-forced split naming both the accumulated time and the limit; and confirming a cap-forced split is never offered to `bridge` even when a bridge that would return `True` is given and the raw gap is also large enough to normally trigger one. All 31 tests in the file (23 existing + 8 new) verified passing by hand. Also compiled `bv_export.py`/`bv_ls.py` cleanly and confirmed `--max-parking-duration` parses correctly end-to-end (`--help` output, a real `--dry-run` invocation) via the CLI itself, not just the library layer.

`docs/man/bv-export.md` gained the new flag in the SYNOPSIS, the Trip detection OPTIONS table, and a DESCRIPTION note flagging that `bv-ls --trips`'s preview doesn't yet apply this cap (unlike the four flags that are genuinely shared between the two commands).

Not yet run through the project's own pytest suite, and not yet confirmed against Christer's real archive - worth him re-running `bv-export` on the exact trip that surfaced this and checking the two Parking-mode recordings now land in separate trips as expected. Also worth a follow-up look at why the Parking footage doesn't survive stream-copy concatenation into stitch.mp4/front.mp4 even when it *is* a trip member - a separate, still-open problem this session didn't touch.

## Fixed trip.gpx silently dropping ~11 minutes of real GPS track at the start of a trip (this session)

Christer uploaded the `trip.gpx` for the same trip as the moving/idle-time and grainy-stitch fixes earlier this session and reported it "doesn't catch any movement before 4:02" - and separately confirmed BlackVue's own official viewer app shows the same gap, so it wasn't obviously a bug in this project's own code alone. The uploaded file's first track point was at 04:03:28, even though the trip's real start (per its own folder name) was 03:51:49 - an ~11.6-minute stretch with zero GPS points, spanning what should have been the trip's first four recordings.

Asked for the raw `.gps` files for those four recordings (`20260724_035149_N` through `20260724_040052_N`) to distinguish two equally-plausible explanations from the merged trip.gpx alone: a genuine GPS cold start (no data to have, not a bug) versus real position data being dropped somewhere in the read/merge/write pipeline (a real bug). The raw files settled it clearly: `035149_N` is 100% NMEA status `V` with the mode indicator (the sentence's last field) also `N` - genuinely no data, a real cold start. But `035450_N` onward, a large and *growing* share of sentences carry status `V` (not yet internally confirmed by the receiver) while the mode indicator already reports `A` (a real position was computed) - 30 such sentences in `035450_N`, 124 in `035751_N`, 142 in `040052_N`, before status itself finally also flips to `A`. `gps_reader.py`'s `_parse_rmc()` parses that mode field into `_mode` but had never actually used it - `GpsFix.valid` was derived from the older `status` field alone, so all of this status-V-but-mode-A data was silently discarded by `write_gpx()`'s existing `if not fix.valid...` filter, along with everything downstream that reuses the same `fix.valid` check (`compute_trip_stats()`, `render_map_video()`, `movement.py`'s edge-movement checks).

Before proposing to change what `valid` means, verified the discarded data was actually trustworthy rather than assuming it: wrote a haversine-based check over the real `status=V`/`mode=A` fixes across `035450_N`→`040353_N`, comparing each consecutive pair's implied speed (distance/time) against the sentence's own reported speed field. Mismatches over 15 km/h occurred on about 4% of pairs - and the same check on the already-trusted `status=A` fixes in the same window showed the *same* ~4% mismatch rate at similar magnitudes, meaning the status-V-but-mode-A data is exactly as noisy as data BlackVue's own viewer already trusts, no worse. No single one-second step exceeded 27.2m (≈98 km/h instantaneous, a plausible brief blip, not a teleport), and the whole track stayed inside one tight ~4.5km x 3km box the entire time - no jump to a wildly distant or nonsensical coordinate. The trajectory itself reads as a real drive: speed climbing smoothly from ~15 to over 70 km/h, then decelerating cleanly to near-zero right at the exact point status finally flips to `A` - consistent with the receiver's stricter internal accuracy/DOP confirmation simply lagging behind having a genuinely usable position, not the position itself being garbage. Reported all of this evidence back to Christer before touching any code; he confirmed to proceed.

**Implementation, `gps_reader.py`.** `_parse_rmc()` now derives `GpsFix.valid` from the sentence's mode indicator (`mode != "N"`) instead of the older status field (`status == "A"`) - the `_mode` local (previously parsed and discarded) is now the actual source of truth, and the old `status` field is parsed into a now-unused `_status` local, kept only because the sentence's fixed 13-field shape still needs unpacking. Both the module-level docstring and `GpsFix`'s own docstring were rewritten to explain the distinction and point to this real-archive finding, so a future reader doesn't wonder why `valid` isn't reading the field literally named "status" in the NMEA spec. No other file needed to change - `gpx_writer.py`, `trip_stats.py`, `map_video.py`, `osm_roads.py`, and `movement.py` all already gate on `fix.valid` (several also redundantly re-checking `latitude is not None`), so every one of them picks up the wider set of usable fixes automatically.

**Verification.** All 7 pre-existing `test_gps_reader.py` cases re-run unchanged and still pass. Three new tests: the real regression case (status `V`, mode `A`, real coordinates -> `valid=True`, position/speed/course all populated); an explicit "no fix mode still means no position" case (renamed from the old "no fix status" test to reflect what's actually being checked now, same assertions); and a deliberately contrived status=`A`/mode=`N` combination (not seen in any real file, purely to prove which field actually drives `valid` - if this ever started passing with `valid=True`, that would mean a future change had regressed back to reading the older status field). All 10 tests in the file pass. Checked every other test file that builds `GpsFix` via real `$GPRMC` text rather than constructing the dataclass directly (`test_movement.py`, `test_trip_export.py`, `test_bv_export.py`, `test_bv_ls.py`) - all of their fixtures use status and mode in agreement (`A`/`A` or `V`/`N`), so `valid` computes identically before and after this change for every one of them; confirmed by grepping each file's `$GPRMC` fixtures for their trailing mode field rather than assuming. Re-ran `test_movement.py` (12/12) and `test_trip_export.py` (56/60, the same 4 pre-existing `capsys`-only gsensor tests skipped as in an earlier session's verification, none involving GPS) by hand - all pass.

Not yet run through the project's own pytest suite, and not yet confirmed against Christer's real archive - worth him re-running `bv-export` on the trip that surfaced this and checking `trip.gpx`/the rendered map now show the drive starting close to its real 03:51:49 start instead of jumping in at 04:03:28, and that BlackVue's own viewer being blind to this same data is no longer something this project's own output inherits.

## Corrected --max-parking-duration to exclude the oversized recording from the trip it would otherwise end, not append it (this session)

Christer reviewed the `--max-parking-duration` feature from earlier this session and was explicit about a boundary problem: "We keep the cap of 60 minutes for P files and end a trip then and I don't want that P file (bigger than 60 minutes) to be a part of the trip at the end." The original implementation checked the *already-accumulated* trailing Parking total when evaluating the recording *after* the oversized one - which meant the over-cap `_P` recording itself was still appended as the last member of the trip it was supposedly ending, and the split only actually landed one recording later. That's backwards from what Christer wants: a Parking recording whose own (or cumulative) real span exceeds 60 minutes should never be part of the trip it would otherwise close out - it should start the next trip instead.

**Implementation, `trip_builder.py`.** Reworked the cap check in `build()` from retrospective to prospective: before appending `recording` to `current_trip`, compute what the trailing Parking-mode total *would become* if it were included (`trailing_parking_seconds + self._parking_contribution(recording)`). If that prospective total exceeds `max_parking_duration`, `recording` is excluded from `current_trip` (which closes as-is) and instead becomes the first recording of a new trip - rather than being let in and only excluding whatever comes after it. This also naturally covers combined spans: two or more consecutive Parking recordings, each individually under the cap, whose running total crosses it partway through still split from each other at the recording that pushes the total over, not just at the point driving resumes.

A subtlety found while redesigning this: naively carrying the old trip's full accumulated `trailing_parking_seconds` forward into the newly-started trip (the one beginning with the excluded recording) would cascade - every recording after it would also look over-cap forever, permanently locking out the trip from ever accepting another recording. Fixed by resetting `trailing_parking_seconds` to just the excluded recording's own contribution when starting the new trip, not the old cumulative total, so the effect is self-limiting: it costs exactly the one recording that triggered it, and normal trip-building resumes cleanly from whatever comes after. A trip can still legitimately *start* with a recording whose own span alone exceeds the cap (nothing earlier to exclude it from) - the recording immediately following it will also get excluded, since the new trip's own trailing total already exceeds the cap regardless of what's added next, but that costs only that one follow-on recording before things resume normally too. A cap-forced exclusion is still never offered to `bridge`, unchanged from before - a deliberate policy decision, not ambiguous gap evidence.

**Tests, `test_trip_builder.py`.** Renamed and re-asserted the single-oversized-recording test (`..._keeps_an_oversized_recording_out_of_the_ending_trip`) to check the oversized `_P` recording lands alone in its own middle trip, sandwiched between the trip before and the trip after, rather than at the end of the first. Updated the chained-Parking-recordings test to reflect the corrected split point. Added a new test confirming the self-limiting cascade fix - driving resumes normally and multiple recordings join back into one trip after the one-recording isolation cost, not lingering broken. Updated the split-reason text assertion (the reasons dict entry that used to name the *next* recording now correctly names the excluded recording itself) and the never-offered-to-bridge test's trip count. All 32 tests in the file (up from 31) verified passing by hand via the project's `FakeMonkeyPatch`/fake-pytest-module harness (no real pytest in this sandbox).

**Docs.** Updated the `--max-parking-duration` argparse help text and `bv_export()`'s own docstring paragraph in `bv_export.py`, and the OPTIONS table row in `docs/man/bv-export.md`, all to describe the corrected behavior ("kept out of the trip it would otherwise end and starts the next trip instead" rather than "the drive that follows it counts as a new trip").

Not yet run through the project's own pytest suite, and not yet confirmed against Christer's real archive - worth a re-run of `bv-export` on the trip with the two real `_P` recordings (`20260724_042022_P`, `20260724_055101_P`) to confirm the oversized one now starts its own trip rather than closing out the previous one.

## Added a live-GPS satellite badge to map.mp4/map_zoom_METERSm.mp4 (this session)

Christer asked for "some marking on the map like a symbol of a satellite or something to show you have valid coordinates." This follows directly from the trip.gpx leading-gap fix earlier this session: render_map_video() already clamps the position marker to the nearest known fix whenever a frame's timestamp falls before the first (or after the last) real fix - e.g. across a leading GPS-cold-start gap like the one that surfaced that bug - but nothing on screen distinguished a frozen, clamped position from a real, live one. Both look identical: the same arrow, sitting still.

Presented four mockup options via the visualize tool (a corner badge, a signal-bars pill with a "GPS" label, a glow ring around the marker itself, and the same corner badge in the opposite corner) and confirmed two decisions before writing any code: the badge shows only when GPS is live (not as a stale/no-signal warning), and it's a Tabler-style satellite icon in a small dot badge, top-right corner - Christer picked this directly from the mockup.

**Implementation, `map_render.py`.** New `_draw_gps_badge()` draws a small RGBA image (a translucent dark circle with a hand-drawn green satellite glyph - a body square, two solar-panel rectangles, and a short antenna with a signal dot) and pastes it onto the frame using itself as the alpha mask - the same compositing approach `_paste_marker_image()` already uses for a custom `--map-icon`, chosen over a bundled PNG asset since it needs no new image file and stays trivially recolorable. `render_frame()` gained a new `show_gps_badge: bool = False` parameter; when true, the badge is drawn last, after the route/marker/text, in the fixed top-right corner (`GPS_BADGE_MARGIN_PX`/`GPS_BADGE_RADIUS_PX`), independent of wherever the position marker itself lands.

**Implementation, `map_video.py`.** `render_map_video()`'s per-frame loop computes `live_fix = positioned[0].timestamp <= timestamp <= positioned[-1].timestamp` - true whenever the frame's timestamp is bracketed by real fixes (so `_interpolate_position_from_index()` actually interpolated between two of them), false when it was clamped to the first or last fix because the timestamp falls outside that range. This is passed straight through as `show_gps_badge=live_fix` on every `render_frame()` call. Deliberately scoped to leading/trailing gaps only for now - a long gap *between* two real fixes mid-trip (e.g. a tunnel) isn't detected separately; both bracketing fixes are real, so `live_fix` reads true across the whole interpolated span between them. Noted as a scope boundary in both the code comments and `docs/man/bv-export.md`, not silently expanded past what was asked for.

**Verification.** Added `test_render_frame_draws_a_gps_badge_when_requested`, `test_render_frame_omits_the_gps_badge_by_default`, and `test_render_frame_draws_the_gps_badge_in_the_top_right_corner` (pixel-diff checks against the badge's own center vs. the opposite corner, same style as the file's existing marker tests) to `test_map_render.py` - 16/16 pass. Added `test_render_map_video_omits_the_gps_badge_during_the_leading_gap` (reusing the existing leading-gap fixture from the video_start/video_duration_seconds tests, confirming frame 0 is off and a later frame is on) and `test_render_map_video_shows_the_gps_badge_for_every_frame_without_a_gap` to `test_map_video.py` - 35/35 pass. Also rendered a real 10-fix synthetic trip end-to-end with a 5-second leading gap and pulled two frames out with ffmpeg to look at directly: the gap frame shows the plain arrow marker with no badge, the live frame shows the same arrow with the satellite badge in the corner, exactly as intended.

Not yet run through the project's own pytest suite, and not yet confirmed against Christer's real archive - worth him re-running `bv-export --map` (or `--map-zoom`) on a real trip and checking the badge disappears during the same leading GPS gap the trip.gpx fix surfaced, and stays on for the rest of the drive.

## Extended the satellite badge to also detect a mid-trip signal-loss gap (this session)

Follow-up to the badge above: I'd deliberately scoped the first pass to leading/trailing gaps only and flagged a gap *between* two real fixes mid-trip (e.g. a tunnel) as undetected, since both fixes bracketing such a gap are individually real - `live_fix`'s old definition (timestamp within the fixes' own range) read that whole interpolated stretch as live even though the straight line between two fixes 10 minutes apart across a tunnel is a guess, not a tracked position. Christer confirmed he wanted this closed too, and picked a 10-second gap threshold (offered 30s/60s/matching `--max-gap`'s own tolerance as starting points; he chose a tighter custom value instead).

**Implementation, `map_video.py`.** New `MAX_LIVE_FIX_GAP_SECONDS = 10.0` constant and a new `_is_live_fix(positioned, timestamp, index)` helper, extracted out of the inline `live_fix` expression so the logic is unit-testable on its own (same pattern as `_advance_fix_index()`/`_interpolate_position_from_index()` already being separately tested rather than only exercised indirectly through `render_map_video()`). Returns `False` for the existing leading/trailing-clamp case (timestamp outside the fixes' own range), `True` unconditionally at the exact instant of a real fix regardless of how wide the gap ahead is (that reading is real no matter what silence follows it), `True` when the bracketing pair of fixes is `MAX_LIVE_FIX_GAP_SECONDS` apart or less, and `False` when that bracketing pair is wider than the threshold - the render loop's own `live_fix = _is_live_fix(positioned, timestamp, position_index)` reuses the same `position_index` `_advance_fix_index()` already tracks, so this costs nothing extra per frame beyond one subtraction and a comparison.

**Verification.** Six new direct `_is_live_fix()` tests in `test_map_video.py` covering: false before the first fix, false after the last, true between two closely-spaced fixes, false at the midpoint of a signal-loss gap wider than the threshold, true right at a real fix even with a wide gap ahead (this one caught a real bug in the first draft - the initial implementation checked the forward span unconditionally and returned `False` for this case, which is wrong; fixed by special-casing an exact match against the current fix's own timestamp before ever looking at the span ahead), and true at exactly the threshold value itself (boundary inclusive). Also added `test_render_map_video_omits_the_gps_badge_during_a_mid_trip_signal_loss_gap`, an end-to-end `render_map_video()` case with a real 40-second gap between two fixes: confirms the badge is on for the frame right at the start, off for frames landing inside the gap, and back on once real fixes resume. All 42 tests in `test_map_video.py` (up from 35) and all 16 in `test_map_render.py` pass.

`docs/man/bv-export.md`'s badge paragraph updated to describe both gap types (leading/trailing and mid-trip) instead of flagging the mid-trip case as future work.

Not yet run through the project's own pytest suite, and not yet confirmed against Christer's real archive - worth him checking a real trip that actually drove through a tunnel or other real dead zone, if one exists in his archive, to see the badge drop out and recover around it.

## Self-healing .duration.txt cache: bv-export computes a missing duration instead of just skipping it (this session)

Earlier this session Christer had asked "does that mean you will create missing duration files?" about a previously-discussed idea, and confirmed later with "do it and the self healing of duration." Before this, `read_duration_seconds()` (used by `TripBuilder`'s `recording_duration` callback for the duration-aware trip-gap calculation and `--max-parking-duration`'s prospective check) only ever *read* an existing `.duration.txt` - if `bv-generate --get-duration` hadn't been run for a recording yet, it silently returned `None` and that recording's real span just wasn't available to trip detection, with no separate warning that anything was missing.

**Implementation, `media.py`.** New `load_or_compute_duration(recording)`, added right after `read_duration_seconds()`: on a cache hit it behaves identically (reads and returns the existing value), but on a cache miss it computes the span itself via the existing `select_source()` + `get_span()` (the same ffprobe/MP4-box-reader machinery `bv-generate --get-duration` already uses) and writes the result back out to `<recording_id>.duration.txt` before returning it - the same load-if-cached-else-fetch-and-write pattern `osm_roads.py`'s `load_or_fetch_roads()`/`load_or_fetch_areas()` already use for OSM data, rather than inventing a new caching convention. Returns `None` without writing anything if the recording has no front/rear video to probe, or if `get_span()` raises `MediaToolError`; still returns the freshly computed value even if the write-back itself fails (read-only archive, full disk) - the same "never worth failing over" convention every other cache-adjacent function in this module already follows. `read_duration_seconds()` itself is untouched and still exists as the ffmpeg-free read-only option for callers that can't carry a hard ffmpeg dependency.

**Wiring, `bv_export.py`.** `bv-export`'s own `recording_duration` callback switched from `read_duration_seconds` to `load_or_compute_duration` (the only line that changed the actual behavior). `bv-ls --trips` deliberately left untouched - it still uses `read_duration_seconds`, keeping that command a cheap, ffmpeg-free preview, consistent with the existing precedent that `--max-parking-duration` is also `bv-export`-only and never applied to `bv-ls --trips`. Updated the `--timestamp`/`--from`/`--until` docstring paragraph and the `--no-duration` argparse help text to describe the new self-healing behavior: a fresh archive with no `.duration.txt` files yet pays a one-time ffprobe cost per recording across the whole archive on its first `bv-export` run (same "trip detection scans the entire archive regardless of the requested range" cost that already existed for reading the cache), and every run after that is exactly as cheap as reading the files back in, same as before this existed. `--no-duration` still skips all of it - no ffprobe calls, no files written, falls back to plain start-to-start timestamps.

**Tests, `test_media.py`.** Six new tests for `load_or_compute_duration()`: cache hit returns the value without calling `get_span()` at all (asserted via a `get_span()` mock that raises if called); a missing file with only a `FRONT` asset gets computed and written; `REAR` is probed when there's no `FRONT` (confirming `select_source()`'s own front-preferred fallback is what's actually used); no video at all returns `None` without calling `get_span()`; `get_span()` raising `MediaToolError` returns `None` and leaves no file behind; and a write failure (`Path.write_text` mocked to raise `OSError` only for `.duration.txt` names) still returns the freshly computed value. All 6 new tests plus all 13 pre-existing tests in the file pass by hand via the project's `FakeMonkeyPatch`/fake-pytest harness (19/20 total - the 1 failure, `test_get_span_falls_back_to_box_reader_when_probe_fails`, is a pre-existing harness limitation unrelated to this change: it uses pytest's string-target `monkeypatch.setattr("module.path.attr", value)` form, which the hand-rolled shim's two-positional-plus-value `setattr(target, name, value)` signature doesn't support - confirmed by reading the test that it doesn't touch `load_or_compute_duration`/`read_duration_seconds` at all).

**Verification against `test_bv_export.py`.** The real risk with this wiring change: nearly every test in that 86-test file builds real (if tiny) video files via `_make_video()` with no pre-existing `.duration.txt`, so switching the default `recording_duration` callback to a self-healing one means trip detection during those tests now genuinely calls `ffprobe` and writes real `.duration.txt` files into each test's temp archive - something that never happened before this change. Ran the whole file by hand in three batches (86/86 accounted for): 83 pass, 3 skipped (`capsys`-only, the project's usual hand-run-harness skip), and 3 genuine failures - all three (`test_main_uses_the_default_stitch_mirror_size_when_not_given`, `..._zoom_when_not_given`, `..._pan_when_not_given`) confirmed **pre-existing and unrelated**: verified by `git stash`-ing this session's changes and re-running the same three tests against the untouched `c0c3a51` commit, where they fail identically. Root cause (not fixed, out of scope for this task): the tests assert the CLI default equals `stitch.py`'s own `DEFAULT_MIRROR_SIZE_PERCENT`/`DEFAULT_MIRROR_ZOOM_PERCENT`/`DEFAULT_MIRROR_PAN_Y_PERCENT`, but `bv_export.py` deliberately overrides those with its own, different `_DEFAULT_CLI_MIRROR_*_PERCENT` opinionated CLI defaults (documented in `bv_export.py`'s own comment block right above where they're defined) - the tests were never updated to match when that CLI-level override was introduced. ## stitch.mp4's default quality now matches the front(+rear) source, not a flat CQ 19 (this session)

Christer: "I think the default should match the front video, what do you think." Discussed before touching anything - most of the plumbing already existed: `_stack()` already had `_video_bitrate()` and a "cap a requested `--stitch-bitrate` to the source's own bitrate" ceiling, just only applied to an *explicit* request, never as the default itself. Flagged one nuance before implementing: the existing ceiling measured `front_decoded`/`rear_decoded` (the intermediates `_stack()` itself produces on the way to the final combine, already re-encoded through this same pass's own CQ 19 default) rather than the true original camera files - measuring off those would just feed CQ19's own output back in as a "target", not the camera's real captured quality. Christer's answers once that was laid out: both cameras summed for `side_by_side`/`top_down`; his call for `rearview_mirror` ("up to you") - front alone, since rear only ever contributes a small inset there, not full-frame pixels; leave `map.mp4`/`gsensor.mp4` on the flat CQ/CRF 19 default (synthetic renders, no camera footage to match); and loosen the existing cap on an explicit `--stitch-bitrate` request from the source's own bitrate to twice that, so someone deliberately asking for more than the source has (overlays add visual complexity beyond the plain camera feed) gets some headroom rather than a hard wall at exactly the source's own number.

**Implementation, `stitch.py`.** The `effective_bitrate` block inside `_stack()` (previously only active when `bitrate is not None`) now always computes a `reference_bps`: `_video_bitrate(front)` alone for `rearview_mirror` (`is_mirror`, already computed earlier in the function), or `_video_bitrate(front) + _video_bitrate(rear)` otherwise - measured off the original `front`/`rear` source `Path`s passed into `_stack()`, not the decoded intermediates. When `bitrate is None`, `effective_bitrate` now defaults to `str(reference_bps)` instead of staying `None` (which used to fall all the way through to `encode_with_nvenc_fallback()`'s own flat CQ/CRF 19). When `bitrate` is given, the cap changed from `reference_bps` to `reference_bps * 2`. Either way, if `reference_bps` can't be determined (ffprobe fails - same "never worth failing the export over" convention as the original cap), `effective_bitrate` stays whatever it already was, so an explicit request still flows through untouched and the no-bitrate case still falls back to CQ/CRF 19 exactly as before this change.

**Tests, `test_stitch.py`.** Renamed/updated the two existing cap tests for the new 2x multiplier and updated wording (`..._caps_an_explicit_bitrate_to_twice_the_source_bitrate`, `..._does_not_cap_bitrate_when_already_below_the_cap`, `..._skips_the_bitrate_cap_when_source_bitrate_unknown`). Added three new tests: side_by_side/top_down defaults to the summed source bitrate with no `--stitch-bitrate` given at all; `rearview_mirror` defaults to front's own bitrate alone, confirming rear's is never even probed for that layout; and falling back to the flat CQ 19 default (empty `extra_codec_args`, no `-b:v` at all) when the source bitrate can't be determined. Replaced `test_stack_skips_bitrate_probing_when_no_bitrate_requested` (asserted `_video_bitrate` was never called with no bitrate requested - no longer true, probing is what computes the default now) with `test_stack_probes_source_bitrate_even_when_no_bitrate_requested`, confirming it's called exactly twice (front and rear) for a two-camera layout.

Two pre-existing tests broke as an expected, understood side effect rather than a real regression: `test_stitch_cameras_passes_bitrate_through_to_the_encoder` and `test_stack_applies_bitrate_only_to_the_final_combine_call` both request `"256k"` against real (unmocked) tiny synthetic `testsrc` clips `_make_video()` produces - those clips' own real bitrate (~61kbps, confirmed by hand with a real ffprobe call) is low enough that the new default cap now legitimately kicks in and reduces "256k" to something smaller, which isn't what either test is actually about (encoder plumbing, not cap correctness - already covered by the dedicated cap tests above). Fixed by mocking `_video_bitrate` to `None` in both, isolating them from real probing.

A third, less expected failure surfaced during verification: `test_stitch_cameras_subtitles_are_confined_to_the_camera_region_not_the_map_panel` uses a flat solid-color fixture (`_make_solid_video`), which genuinely compresses to a near-zero real bitrate (~15kbps, confirmed by hand) - the new default target matched that near-zero figure for a final frame that, once the map panel and subtitle text are actually burned in, is no longer low-complexity at all, starving the encode enough to visibly darken the map panel's supposed-to-stay-white background below the test's own brightness threshold. Fixed the same way (mocked `_video_bitrate` to `None`), but flagging this as a real, not just test-fixture, edge case worth keeping in mind: a genuinely low-complexity source scene (a very dark tunnel, a blank wall, heavy motion blur) composited with map/gsensor/subtitle overlays could plausibly hit the same starvation in a real export. Not fixed as part of this change since it wasn't asked about and no floor value was agreed - noted here as a candidate follow-up if it ever shows up on a real trip.

**Docs.** Updated the `--stitch-bitrate` argparse help text in `bv_export.py` and its OPTIONS table row in `docs/man/bv-export.md` to describe the new default-matches-source behavior and the 2x cap, and to explicitly note `map.mp4`/`gsensor.mp4` are unaffected.

**Verification.** All 12 bitrate-focused tests pass. Ran the rest of `test_stitch.py` (117 tests total) in batches by hand: 111 of the remaining 105 non-bitrate tests pass (after fixing the harness's own `pytest.raises(...) as exc_info` support, needed for 3 unrelated `parse_gsensor_position` tests that predate this session and had nothing to do with this change), 4 skipped (`capsys`, the same pre-existing skip this project's whole hand-run harness always has), and 2 (`test_stitch_cameras_scale_shrinks_the_map_panels_own_render_size`, `..._scale_shrinks_the_output_preserving_aspect_ratio`) not run to completion in this sandbox's per-call time budget - both do two full real `map.mp4` renders each (real PIL frame-by-frame drawing plus real ffmpeg encodes), the heaviest tests in the file, and were already the slowest tests before this change; confirmed by code review that this diff doesn't touch map-panel rendering at all, only adds two fast `ffprobe` calls to `_stack()`'s own bitrate computation.

Not yet run through the project's own pytest suite, and not yet confirmed against Christer's real archive - worth him re-running `bv-export --stitch` on a real trip (both `side_by_side`/`top_down` and `rearview_mirror`) and comparing `stitch.mp4`'s resulting file size/visual quality against the previous flat-CQ19 behavior, and specifically checking the two map-rendering tests this sandbox couldn't finish actually still pass under a real pytest run.
