Christer uploaded `dr900s-2ch-v1.015-eng.zip` (the current latest DR900S-2CH firmware, dated Nov 2021 per its own build strings, versus the Dec 2018 `v1.009` already analyzed for `bv-live`) and asked for it to be checked before he updates his camera: "I know they have locked it in a little, beyond video wouldn't work with it like it is today. please analyze it, i think it retains the same .cgi but maybe needs username password." Extracted it the same way as `v1.009` (SD-card layout -> gunzip `patch_DR900S.bin` -> tar -> rootfs) and diffed every part of the web stack against the already-extracted `v1.009` rootfs still on disk from that earlier session.

**Result: no lockdown found.** `res/System/boa`'s own `strings` output is functionally identical between the two builds (only the build-date banner and toolchain patch version differ - `Hisilicon_v600_20170104` -> `Hisilicon_v600_20170615`, both GCC 4.9.4 - plus a handful of reordered/renamed low-level ELF symbols, nothing behavioral). The `boa.conf` text block `main_app` writes to `/tmp/boa.conf` at runtime is **byte-identical** in both firmware versions, hardcoded straight into `main_app`'s own binary as a string constant - still `Port 80`, `DocumentRoot /res/System/www`, and critically **`AuthType None`**, exactly as in `v1.009`. Since this is a literal hardcoded string `main_app` writes out (not something built from a runtime setting), there's no config toggle that could switch it on either - it would take an actual code change to `main_app`, which didn't happen between these two builds. All four CGI binaries (`blackvue_live.cgi`, `blackvue_livedata.cgi`, `blackvue_vod.cgi`, `upload.cgi`) diff to functionally identical `strings` output too (a handful of blank-line differences only) - same `QUERY_STRING`/`direction=R` handling, same `v:1.00`/`n:%s/%s,s:%u` VOD listing format, same multipart JSON livedata stream. `do_ap.sh` (the WiFi-AP-mode + `boa` launch script) is **byte-for-byte identical**, including the camera's own IP `10.99.77.1`.

The shipped default `Config/config.ini` did pick up some new keys in `v1.015` (`UseGpsInfo`, `AccelEvent`/`HarshEvent`/`SharpEvent` and their matching voice-alert toggles) and dropped some old `[Cloud]` per-endpoint alarm keys (`sta_garage`, `AlarmManual`, etc., collapsed down to a single `CloudSettingVersion`) - all in-app feature settings, nothing related to local web access. `main_app` itself grew substantially (9,411 -> 14,867 `strings` lines) - three years of BlackVue Cloud feature work - but none of that growth touched the boa/CGI code paths this project depends on.

**Conclusion reported to Christer:** the specific concern (CGI endpoints now requiring a username/password) doesn't match what the firmware itself shows - `bv-download`/`bv-live`/`bv-config`'s endpoint-based connection should keep working unchanged on `v1.015`. Caveat given honestly: this is still a static diff of two firmware images, not a live test against a real camera actually running `v1.015` - if something does break in practice after he updates, it'd be a genuinely new finding this analysis couldn't have caught (e.g. any purely runtime-only behavior with no footprint in the binaries themselves).

## Analyze v1.012 firmware - the version Christer recalled actually breaking a script (this session, no code change)

Christer then uploaded a third firmware, `dr900s-2ch-v1.012-eng.zip` (built Jun 2019, chronologically between `v1.009` and `v1.015`), recalling: "I once installed this firmware and then my bash script didnt work." Extracted and `md5sum`-compared it against `v1.009`'s already-extracted rootfs, file by file: `blackvue_live.cgi`, `blackvue_livedata.cgi`, `blackvue_vod.cgi`, `upload.cgi`, and `do_ap.sh` are all **byte-for-byte identical** to `v1.009` - not just functionally equivalent this time, literally the same bytes, same md5. `boa` and `main_app` differ (expected, different firmware build), but the `boa.conf` text block `main_app` writes is - again - identical: same `AuthType None`. So `v1.012` doesn't change the web/CGI layer relative to `v1.009` either; whatever broke Christer's script wasn't a change to the HTTP API.

Diffing `main_app`'s full `strings` output between `v1.009` and `v1.012` turned up one genuinely new, relevant string: **`WiFiPwReset`** (alongside a related `WiFiPwRemove`), present in `v1.012` and still present in `v1.015`, absent entirely from `v1.009`. These read as internal log-tag/function-name strings for a WiFi-password reset/removal capability that didn't exist in `v1.009` and was introduced in `v1.012`. This lines up with BlackVue's own general history around this period - dashcams in this generation shipped with default/predictable WiFi AP passwords that drew security criticism, and firmware updates around 2019 are understood to have moved toward camera-specific randomized passwords. A WiFi AP password changing out from under a script that had it saved/hardcoded would produce exactly the symptom described - the script can no longer connect to the camera's WiFi at all - without any change to the CGI/web layer itself, which the byte-identical comparison rules out as the cause.

Reported to Christer as the most likely explanation given the evidence, with an honest caveat: this is inferred from a log-tag string appearing in the binary, not confirmed by tracing exactly when/how `WiFiPwReset` fires (e.g. automatically during the firmware update itself, vs. only via a later manual trigger) - that would need disassembly of `main_app` (stripped, no debug info) to nail down precisely, which wasn't done here.

**Correction, same message thread:** the `WiFiPwReset` write-up above assumed Christer's setup was AP direct-connect (PC joins the camera's own hotspot at `10.99.77.1`, the only mode analyzed for `bv-live`/`bv-download` so far). He corrected this: his camera instead connects *out* to his own Netgear router's WiFi. Re-reading `main_app`'s strings confirmed the camera runs two WiFi interfaces concurrently - `wlan0` for its own AP (`do_ap.sh`, `hostapd`, `10.99.77.1`, and critically `boa` itself) and a separate `wlan1` running `wpa_supplicant` to join a home network as a client, using the `sta_ssid`/`sta_pw` credentials in `config.ini`'s `[Cloud]` section - and that this station-mode capability already existed in `v1.009` too (not new to `v1.012`). `boa`'s own config only has `Port 80` with no bind-address restriction, so once launched (via `do_ap.sh`, string-adjacent to the `wlan1` bring-up code, suggesting both interfaces come up together at boot rather than being mutually exclusive) it's reachable on any interface with an IP - `wlan1`'s Netgear-assigned address included, which is how `bv-download`/`bv-live` reach the camera in Christer's actual setup today (his `bv-config` endpoint is that LAN IP, not `10.99.77.1`).

This reframes which credential `WiFiPwReset` most plausibly resets: there are two separate saved-password slots (`ap_pw` for the camera's own AP, `sta_pw` for rejoining the home network) and the strings alone don't say which one the reset targets. Given Christer wasn't using AP mode, `sta_pw` is the more relevant candidate - a cleared/reset home-WiFi credential would make the camera fail to rejoin his Netgear router after the `v1.012` update, going invisible on his LAN with no CGI/API involvement at all, needing the SSID/password re-entered in the BlackVue app afterward. Still unconfirmed without disassembling `main_app`'s actual reset trigger.

**Resolved by a primary source: the `WiFiPwReset` theory was wrong.** Christer found and shared his actual September 2019 BlackVue support ticket about this exact incident. His own message to support at the time: he'd been using `blackvue_vod.cgi` (downloads) and `blackvue_live.cgi` (live view) successfully, then updated to `v1.012` and it stopped working, and he asked for the functionality back (ideally over HTTPS with a username/password) rather than being forced to downgrade. BlackVue's second-level support replied directly: **"we have recently blocked the access to browser using dashcam's wifi due to various privacy concerns from users. In [a] scenario where the network is open, anyone on the same network could access your live view if they know the IP address."** - an intentional, deliberate access block, not a side effect of a WiFi password reset.

This doesn't fully reconcile with the static binary analysis above, though, which is worth recording honestly rather than glossing over: the `v1.012` firmware zip Christer uploaded and had analyzed in this same session shows no such block - `blackvue_live.cgi`/`blackvue_vod.cgi`/`boa.conf` are byte-identical to `v1.009`, same as documented above. Two explanations seem most plausible, neither confirmable from the firmware images alone: (1) BlackVue may have walked the block back in a later build carrying the same `v1.012` version number, before the file now distributed as the public "v1.012" download was packaged - support tickets like Christer's, filed right when the change shipped, are exactly the kind of user pushback that would prompt a quick reversal; or (2) the block specifically targeted AP mode ("the dashcam's wifi," matching support's own "open network" framing, where an arbitrary nearby stranger could join) rather than a station-mode setup joining a private, password-protected home network like Christer's actual current setup - a materially different privacy scenario that a targeted fix might not have touched at all.

What actually matters practically is settled by better evidence than any firmware diff: `bv-download` and `bv-live` both work against Christer's real camera today, on firmware newer than this incident. Whatever was blocked in September 2019 either got reverted or doesn't apply to his current setup - live, working evidence outranks static analysis here.

**Correction: Christer never went back up.** He clarified he's still running `v1.009` today - the exact version his own 2019 support ticket says he downgraded to at the time, never updated since. So "his camera works with beyond-video today" isn't evidence the September 2019 block got fixed or doesn't apply anymore - it's simply that he's never been back on a firmware version new enough to test that. The real state of things: `v1.009` is confirmed solid (it's the version this whole firmware analysis has used as its baseline throughout - `bv-live`/`bv-download` built and tested against exactly this version's CGI behavior). `v1.012` and `v1.015`, as officially published today, show no lockdown in static analysis either - but that directly contradicts what Christer's own support ticket says actually happened to him on a `v1.012` install in 2019, so those two clean results shouldn't be taken as confirmation it's safe to upgrade. The likeliest reconciliation remains that whatever blocked him in 2019 shipped through a different channel than these exact downloadable zips - possibly Cloud FOTA (the over-the-air auto-update path referenced throughout `main_app`'s strings), possibly a since-reverted point build - something outside what a static diff of these three specific files can see.

**Practical guidance going forward:** stay on `v1.009` (or verify any future firmware the same way before installing it) rather than treating the clean `v1.012`/`v1.015` analysis as a green light to upgrade - the one real, lived data point (his own 2019 support ticket) says upgrading broke this exact functionality once already, and static analysis of the public download alone wasn't able to explain why.

## Find the CGI API in a different, newer BlackVue model's firmware: Elite 10 (this session, no code change)

Christer uploaded `ELITE10_FASTBOOT_p1.0_b1.008_tF1.3_R1.3.zip` - firmware for the BlackVue **Elite 10**, a materially different and much newer camera than the DR900S-2CH this whole investigation has otherwise been about. Confirmed from the unpacked platform details: aarch64 (ARM64, `ld-linux-aarch64.so.1`), `GCC: (Buildroot 2022.08.3-9-g4ba9647) 10.4.0` - a 2022-era Buildroot/glibc build, versus the DR900S-2CH's 2018-2021 Hisilicon/Hi3559 toolchain - and Novatek-branded binaries (`nvtrtspd`/`nvtrtspd_ipc`, an RTSP daemon) rather than Hisilicon's `HI_MAPI`/`HI_SNAP` capture stack. Different SoC vendor, different Linux distribution approach, same overall BlackVue product-family conventions underneath.

**Container format was new and had to be worked out from scratch.** The firmware zip's `BlackVue/System/upgrade/` folder has many more image files than the DR900S-2CH (`atf_*`/`fdt_*`/`fdt_app_*`/`fdt_fast*`/`rtos_*`/`uboot_*` in addition to a kernel and rootfs) - ARM Trusted Firmware + device-tree-based boot, not a simple u-boot `uImage`. `rootfs_ELITE10_FASTBOOT` and `uImage_ELITE10_FASTBOOT` both start with a custom 16-byte `BCL1` header (magic + what look like a CRC and size fields) directly followed by a raw zlib stream (`78 da`); stripping the 16-byte header and `zlib.decompress()`-ing the rest of `rootfs_ELITE10_FASTBOOT` (1.68MB compressed) produced a clean 3.4MB `cpio` archive (SVR4 format) - a standard Linux initramfs, extractable with plain `cpio -idm`. `rootfs_rw_ELITE10_FASTBOOT` and `pta_ELITE10_FASTBOOT` (the ones that matter most for finding the CGI content) are raw UBI images (`UBI#` magic) instead - no `ubireader`/`binwalk`/UBIFS tooling was available in this sandbox and none could be installed (same no-PyPI-network limitation documented earlier this session), so these weren't formally demounted. Pragmatically, running plain `strings` directly against the raw 58MB `pta_ELITE10_FASTBOOT` blob worked well enough anyway - UBIFS apparently doesn't compress these particular files, so ELF `.rodata` string constants (CGI names, format strings, HTML fragments) came through cleanly without a real filesystem parse.

**Where the pieces live, from the extracted cpio rootfs's own init scripts.** `etc/init.d/S13_PTA` finds the `pta` MTD partition via `/proc/mtd`, runs `ubiattach`, and mounts it read-only at `/mnt/pta` via `mount -t ubifs`, additionally bind-mounting `/mnt/pta/usr/local` onto `/usr/local` - so the real application content (equivalent of the DR900S-2CH's `patch_DR900S.bin`-supplied `res/System/`) lives entirely in this separate `pta_ELITE10_FASTBOOT` image, not in the cpio-based rootfs at all. `app/bootapp` (the actual boot script, found in the cpio rootfs) confirms the exact same `res/System/www` path convention as the DR900S-2CH has carried forward: `ln -sf /app/sd/Blackvue/Config /mnt/pta/res/System/www/`, `ln -sf /app/sd/Blackvue/Record /mnt/pta/res/System/www/`, then `/mnt/pta/bin/main_app &` - same `main_app` name, same general architecture, just relocated onto this new UBI partition layout.

**CGI endpoints found (via `strings` on the raw `pta_ELITE10_FASTBOOT` blob) - eight now, not four:** the four DR900S-2CH ones are all still present (`blackvue_live.cgi`, `blackvue_livedata.cgi`, `blackvue_vod.cgi`, `upload.cgi`), plus four new ones - `blackvue_gps.cgi`, `blackvue_hss_live.cgi`, `blackvue_log.cgi`, `blackvue_snap.cgi`. Each is its own separate ELF binary (same pattern as before, not a monolithic CGI dispatcher), still all built with debug info intact. Notable behavioral upgrades visible directly in the strings: `blackvue_vod.cgi` gained a `del=` query parameter (remote file deletion, not present at all on the DR900S-2CH) alongside its existing `path=d:...` browsing parameter (confirmed identical syntax to what the community `hackvue`/`HTTPGET_URLs` notes described for older models); the VOD-style listing protocol version banners have moved up to `v:1.00`/`v:2.00`/`v:3.00` across the different listing-capable endpoints (`vod.cgi`, `log.cgi`, `hss_live.cgi` respectively) rather than the DR900S-2CH's single `v:1.00`; `blackvue_livedata.cgi`'s GPS JSON changed its format specifier from `%lf` to `%f` but otherwise looks like the same `{"GPS":{"LATITUDE":.., "LONGITUDE":..}}`-shaped payload; `blackvue_snap.cgi` is a plain single-image snapshot endpoint (separate from the continuous MJPEG `blackvue_live.cgi` stream); `blackvue_log.cgi` supports browsing plus a `DELETED file %s` log-line, suggesting it also handles deletion; `blackvue_hss_live.cgi`'s name (HSS - most likely HTTP Smooth Streaming, an adaptive-bitrate protocol) suggests a second, more modern live-view mechanism alongside the older plain-MJPEG `blackvue_live.cgi`, not otherwise investigated further (no time spent tracing its exact request/response shape beyond confirming it exists and takes `path=`/`QUERY_STRING` input like the listing endpoints).

**No authentication found here either.** No `boa` binary and no `boa.conf`-style config block exist anywhere in this firmware at all (unlike the DR900S-2CH) - this camera's local web server is something else entirely, most likely built directly into `main_app` itself rather than a separate process, though that wasn't confirmed by disassembly. Searched broadly for `AuthType`/`AuthUserFile`/`WWW-Authenticate`/`Authorization:`/HTTPS/TLS strings anywhere near the CGI binaries specifically - found plenty of unrelated OpenSSL/TLS strings from a bundled third-party cloud/relay SDK (`thirdparty/.../openssl`, `PINGd`/`ProcessLoop` naming suggesting a P2P/cloud-relay client library), but nothing suggesting the *local* CGI API itself is behind any authentication or HTTPS. The AP-mode IP address is unchanged too - `10.99.77.1`, confirmed both in `strings` output and directly in `etc/udhcpd_wlan0.conf`/`udhcpd_wlan1.conf` (`option router 10.99.77.1`, DHCP range `.20`-`.40`) in the extracted cpio rootfs.

**One genuinely new, potentially very useful discovery: real FTP access.** `etc/inetd.conf` (found directly in the cpio-extracted rootfs, not needing any UBI digging) has two active, uncommented entries: `21 stream tcp nowait root ftpd ftpd -w /mnt/sd` (a real FTP server, serving `/mnt/sd` - the SD card / recordings storage - directly) and `69 dgram udp nowait root tftpd tftpd -l -c /home`. Neither was investigated further (no time spent checking `ftpd`'s own auth requirements, e.g. whether it needs a login or allows anonymous access) but this is a meaningfully different, and possibly simpler, download mechanism than the CGI-based `blackvue_vod.cgi` dance beyond-video currently uses - worth investigating if Elite 10 support is ever built, since a plain FTP client (or Python's stdlib `ftplib`) could replace `BlackVueClient`'s whole HTTP-based download path for this model.

Reported to Christer as a straight factual answer to "can you find the cgi" - not yet wired into beyond-video (no camera-model detection, no Elite-10-specific client code exists; `BlackVueClient`/`core/camera.py` are still DR900S-2CH-only, matching the only camera Christer actually owns and has been testing against all session).

## Build bv-live: a live browser dashboard (this session)

The parked "bv-watch" idea from earlier this session (see this file's own "Analyze DR900S-2CH firmware..." entry) came back with a concrete spec from Christer: "Lets call that bv-live instead of bv-watch. It should by default show he front camera stream with gsensor line at the bottom and a scrolling map to the left with default zoom of 100m. We should also be able to switch between front and rear camera and back by a button... Since the live stream is pretty small we can have the map be a little bigger than usual and the gsensor line too." `bv-live` was free to reuse as a command name, having just been renamed to `bv-gps` earlier this session (see that entry) - Christer named the new feature this himself rather than being asked via `AskUserQuestion`, so no design-choice confirmation was needed for the name this time.

**Architecture.** A new top-level package, `src/blackvue/live/`, separate from `blackvue.web` (bv-web, the archive browser) on purpose - the two solve genuinely different problems (bv-web reads finished trip folders with login/roles and no live camera connection at all; bv-live is nothing but a live camera connection, no archive/login concept). `bv-live ID` follows the exact same connect-and-serve shape as `bv-gps`/`bv-web serve`: loads the camera config, `connect()`s to the first reachable endpoint (same `core/connection.py` used everywhere else), then hands the connected `BlackVueClient` to a new FastAPI app and calls `uvicorn.run()`. No login (unlike bv-web) - a personal, run-when-you-want-it tool, `--host` defaults to `127.0.0.1`; `--port` defaults to 8100 (not bv-web's 8000, so both can run at once).

**New primitive: `BlackVueClient.open_stream(path)`.** Returns the raw `urlopen()` response for the caller to `.read()`/`.close()` itself, unlike every other client method (which reads a response fully, or a bounded slice for `live_gps()`). Both of bv-live's continuous consumers need this: the camera MJPEG passthrough (relays raw bytes for as long as a browser tab has a `<img>` pointed at it) and the telemetry pump (reads `blackvue_livedata.cgi` forever, not just until the first match like `live_gps()` does).

**New parser primitives: `parse_gsensor_reading()`, `find_next_gps()`, `find_next_gsensor_reading()`** in `parser/livedata.py`, alongside the existing `parse_gps_fix()` (left unchanged). `blackvue_livedata.cgi`'s g-sensor object is `{"3G":{"FrontRear":..,"LeftRight":..,"UpperLower":..}}` (confirmed field names/casing from the original firmware `strings` analysis, not guessed) - these three names are used directly as the live g-sensor strip's own trace labels throughout, deliberately *not* relabeled to the offline `.3gf` format's X/Y/Z convention, since there's no independently confirmed mapping between the two (the `.3gf` axis mapping itself isn't confirmed either - see `telemetry/gsensor_reader.py`'s own docstring). `find_next_gps()`/`find_next_gsensor_reading()` return `(value, start, end)` instead of just `value` - a continuous scanner needs to know both where a match starts (to correctly pick whichever of GPS/g-sensor comes first in a buffer holding both, since truncating `buffer[end:]` after consuming a match discards everything before it too - picking the wrong one first would silently lose the other) and where it ends (how much to discard). Caught this exact bug via the hand-rolled test harness: an initial version that always preferred GPS whenever both patterns matched anywhere in the buffer silently dropped a g-sensor reading whenever it happened to sit *before* a GPS reading in the same read chunk - fixed by comparing `.start()` and always consuming whichever object begins earliest.

**`live/telemetry.py`.** `TelemetryState`: a thread-safe, time-bounded (600s) rolling buffer of `GpsSample`/`GSensorSample` readings, each timestamped on receipt via `time.monotonic()` - `blackvue_livedata.cgi`'s own JSON carries no timestamp field of its own, unlike the offline `.gps` files' NMEA-derived ones. `LiveTelemetryPump`: a background `daemon=True` thread reading `blackvue_livedata.cgi` via `open_stream()` forever, auto-reconnecting after a 2s delay on any `OSError` (a WiFi blip shouldn't need restarting `bv-live` to recover from). Started once at server startup and run for the whole process's lifetime rather than lazily per-viewer - the connection is cheap to hold open (small JSON, no video), and it means the map/g-sensor panels have real history the instant a browser tab opens instead of starting empty. `_drain_livedata_buffer()` (the actual buffer-scanning logic) is a pure function of `(buffer, state)`, not a method - trivial to unit test with no thread/socket involved.

**`live/map_stream.py`.** Reuses `export/map_render.py`'s `render_frame()` completely unchanged for the actual per-frame drawing, and `export/osm_roads.py`'s fetch/cache/bbox-filter machinery for road/water/green-area geometry - none of that cares whether the position data came from a finished trip or a live feed. What's new: `LiveMapRegion` decides when the live view has scrolled far enough to need a fresh Overpass fetch (fetches/caches a region `8x` the `--map-zoom` radius around the current position, re-fetching only once the live view's own frame bbox is no longer fully contained within it - a plain rectangle-containment check, no distance math needed), and `render_live_map_frame()` computes what a finished-trip render gets handed already-known: the live position/route trail from `TelemetryState`, and - since `blackvue_livedata.cgi`'s GPS object carries no course-over-ground field at all, unlike the offline `.gps` files' NMEA-derived one - a heading computed locally from the last two *distinct* live positions (skipping stationary GPS-jitter duplicates by searching backward), so the position marker can still be a rotated arrow instead of always falling back to a plain dot. Panel default 720x720 (map_render.py's own export default is 640x640) - "a little bigger than usual", per Christer, since the live camera feed itself is small.

**`live/gsensor_stream.py`.** Deliberately a brand new, simpler renderer rather than reusing `export/gsensor_graph_render.py` directly: that module's precompute-once-then-playhead-overlay split and its `window_start`/`window_end` bookkeeping are both built around a trip with a known, finite length - a live view has no fixed end at all, and there's no "static part" to precompute anyway, since the *entire* visible window changes every frame as it slides forward. Same overall visual language (light background, thin 1px lines, small legend) for continuity, but genuinely fresh code: one shared auto-scale across all three traces (not gsensor_graph_render.py's later-added independent per-axis scaling), no lane-split for a "cluttered" axis, no legend-reserve machinery - a first pass, expected to get the same kind of iterative polish once Christer's actually seen it live, the same as every other visual piece of this project has. Panel default 1600x260, a short wide strip spanning the full dashboard width at the bottom, per Christer's own "gsensor line at the bottom" + "bigger than usual" instructions.

**`live/mjpeg.py`.** Shared plumbing for both kinds of MJPEG stream this feature serves: `rendered_frame_stream()` (calls a zero-arg render callable at a target fps, wraps each frame as one `multipart/x-mixed-replace` part - used for the two synthetic streams) and `relay_raw_stream()` (forwards an already-open camera connection's bytes through completely unmodified - used for the camera passthrough, since there's nothing to change about the camera's own existing multipart framing).

**`live/app.py`.** FastAPI app: `/` (a plain hand-written HTML string, not a Jinja2 template - one page, one dynamic value (the camera's display name), not worth a `templates/` dir + package-data entry for that), `/stream/camera?direction=F|R` (opens a fresh camera connection per request, closed when the browser switches direction or the tab closes - so switching Front/Rear doesn't leave the old direction's connection dangling), `/stream/map`, `/stream/gsensor`. Layout: map panel left, camera feed + Front/Rear toggle button top right, g-sensor strip spanning the full width along the bottom - exactly Christer's own described layout. Map renders at 2fps (roads/areas projection is the more expensive of the two, and changes slowly at driving speed within a close 100m view), g-sensor at 5fps.

**Verification note.** Same sandbox limitation as `bv-gps`'s own entry: no PyPI network access, so fastapi/uvicorn aren't installed here, and Python is 3.10 (no `tomllib`). Everything that doesn't import fastapi at module level - `parser/livedata.py`'s new functions, `core/blackvue_client.py`'s `open_stream()`, and all of `live/telemetry.py`/`live/map_stream.py`/`live/gsensor_stream.py`/`live/mjpeg.py` - was verified two ways: a plain `python3 -c "import ..."` sanity check (confirms the modules load cleanly with real PIL, no stubbing needed there), and the same hand-rolled pytest-stub harness used all session, run against 58 tests across the new/updated test files (parser, client, telemetry, map_stream, gsensor_stream, mjpeg, and the CLI's arg-parsing/error-path tests) - all 58 pass, including a caught-and-fixed real bug (the buffer-scanning ordering issue described above). `live/app.py` and `cli/bv_live.py`'s own `_run()` success path (the actual `create_live_app()`/`uvicorn.run()` call) could only be syntax-checked (`ast.parse`), not imported or run - no fastapi/uvicorn available, same as `bv-web`'s own CLI tests handle this (the `test_main_serve_reports_missing_uvicorn_cleanly`-style pattern, reused verbatim for `bv-live`'s own "missing uvicorn" test). None of this has been run against Christer's actual camera yet - the MJPEG passthrough, the live map's OSM fetching, and the overall dashboard layout are all unverified against a real browser/camera and should be expected to need the same kind of iterative tuning every other visual feature in this project has gone through.

## bv-live follow-up: auto-open a browser window, keep the camera feed visible longest (this session, direct follow-up)

Christer tried the real thing and reported two problems: "I would like for it to show up in a new empty browser window. When i resize the window and make it smaller, the map and gsensor are still there but the stream vanish. The stream should be there as long as possible since it is the star."

**Auto-open a browser window.** `cli/bv_live.py` now calls a new `_open_browser_soon(url)` right before `uvicorn.run()`, which schedules `webbrowser.open_new(url)` on a `threading.Timer` (1 second delay, `BROWSER_OPEN_DELAY_SECONDS`) rather than calling it inline - `uvicorn.run()` blocks the main thread until the server stops, so opening the browser has to happen out-of-line, and the short delay gives uvicorn a moment to actually finish binding the port first (if the browser still somehow beats it on a slow machine, it just shows an ordinary "can't connect" page to refresh - not worth polling the socket instead). New `--no-browser` flag opts out, for anyone who'd rather just get the printed URL (e.g. running this on a headless NAS). If `--host` is a wildcard bind address (`0.0.0.0`/`::`, meaningless to actually browse to), the browser opens `127.0.0.1` instead while uvicorn itself still binds to whatever was asked for.

**Camera panel stays visible longest when the window shrinks.** Root cause, diagnosed from the CSS rather than a live repro (no camera/browser available in this sandbox - see this feature's own verification note): flex items refuse to shrink below their own content's natural size by default (`min-width: auto`), and the camera feed's native resolution is very likely larger than the map/g-sensor panels' own fixed render sizes (720x720/1600x260) - without an explicit override, that kept the whole row from shrinking below the camera's own width at all, rather than letting it scale down, and once the row ran out of room it likely wrapped/overflowed in a way that pushed the camera panel out of the visible area while the map (small enough to still fit) stayed put. Fixed with three CSS changes together in `live/app.py`'s `_PAGE_HTML`: `min-width: 0` on every `.panel` (lets flex items actually shrink below their image's native size); the camera panel gets `flex: 3 1 320px` against the map's `flex: 1 1 220px` (three times the grow-share, so it's the last to give up space as the row narrows); `order: -1` on the camera panel (renders it first both in the flex row and, below a new `@media (max-width: 700px)` breakpoint that stacks everything into a single column instead of squeezing side-by-side panels into illegibility, first in that stacked order too) - so on a small window the camera feed is the one panel guaranteed to still be on screen without scrolling. `.panel img` switched from `max-width: 100%` to `width: 100%; height: auto` so every panel's image predictably fills and scales with its own panel's box rather than depending on the image's own intrinsic size for layout.

**Verification note.** Same sandbox limitation as the rest of this feature - no real browser or camera to actually resize a window against. The flex/min-width diagnosis is a well-established CSS pattern (a very common "flex item won't shrink below an image's intrinsic size" issue), not confirmed against Christer's own real repro beyond his description matching it, so this may need another round of tuning once he's tried it again. `_open_browser_soon()` and its `--no-browser`/wildcard-host-rewrite logic were verified with the same hand-rolled test harness (webbrowser.open_new/threading.Timer call recorded via monkeypatching, plus `_run()`-level tests stubbing sys.modules for uvicorn/blackvue.live.app the same way the CLI's own "missing uvicorn" test already had to) - all passing, `webbrowser.open_new` itself was never actually invoked against a real browser.

## bv-live follow-up #2: a real new window, and fix an ordering bug that swapped map/camera sides (this session, direct follow-up)

Christer tried the previous follow-up and reported two more things: "It doesnt get its own window, it became a tab in the web browser. The map was place to the right of the stream instead of the left."

**Real new window, not a tab.** `webbrowser.open_new()` on Windows goes through `os.startfile()`, which just hands the URL to the OS's default-app association - the browser's own already-running instance almost always reuses itself and opens a tab, regardless of what was actually asked for. There's no portable way around this through the `webbrowser` module alone. Fixed by launching the browser's own executable directly instead, with a flag it actually respects for "open a real new window": `--new-window` for Chromium browsers (Edge, Chrome), `-new-window` for Firefox. New `_open_new_window(url)` in `cli/bv_live.py` tries a short list of typical Windows/macOS install paths plus a PATH lookup (`_find_browser()`, `_CHROMIUM_PATHS`/`_CHROMIUM_COMMANDS`/`_FIREFOX_PATHS`/`_FIREFOX_COMMANDS`) for Edge/Chrome first (Edge ships by default on every Windows install, Christer's own platform), then Firefox, launching whichever is found via `subprocess.Popen`. Falls back to the plain `webbrowser.open_new()` behavior (still opens *something*, just possibly a tab again) if no known browser executable can be found at all, or if launching one raises `OSError`. `_open_browser_soon()`'s timer now schedules this instead of calling `webbrowser.open_new` directly.

**Map/camera ordering bug.** The previous follow-up's CSS gave `#camera-panel` a blanket `order: -1` to make sure it rendered first once panels stack vertically on a narrow window - but `order` isn't scoped to the media query it was reasoned about, so it applied at every width, dragging the camera panel in front of the map even in the normal, wide layout where Christer explicitly wants the map on the left. Fixed by moving `order: -1` entirely inside the `@media (max-width: 700px)` block, so it only takes effect once things actually stack - the wide layout now uses the markup's own natural map-then-camera order again, unchanged from the original design.

**Verification note.** Same limitation as this feature's other entries - no real browser/camera to test the actual window-vs-tab behavior or resize the window against. `_open_new_window()`/`_find_browser()` were verified via the hand-rolled test harness (monkeypatching `subprocess.Popen`/`shutil.which`/`Path.exists` and `webbrowser.open_new` to confirm the right command gets built and the fallback chain behaves correctly) - the actual `--new-window`/`-new-window` flags' effect on a real Edge/Chrome/Firefox install is unconfirmed, going on published browser command-line documentation rather than a live test. The CSS ordering fix is a plain, easily-inspectable change (moving one declaration inside a media query) rather than something needing new test coverage.

## Investigate the BlackVue app's two-way-talk/push-to-talk feature (this session, no code change)

Christer described the mobile app's talk feature ("I first says something so the people in the car now they are being listened on, then you have a push to talk button") and asked whether anything found in the firmware would let beyond-video use it too. Re-searched the still-present firmware extractions from earlier sessions (`/tmp/fw`, `/tmp/fw12`, `/tmp/fw15` for the DR900S-2CH at v1.009/v1.012/v1.015, `/tmp/elite10` plus its own earlier `pta_strings.txt` dump for the Elite 10) rather than answering from memory alone.

**The feature is real in the firmware, but it isn't a local CGI endpoint.** The DR900S-2CH's `main_app` binary has a complete two-way-audio subsystem - `TwoWayAudio_Open`/`TwoWayAudio_Close_phase1`/`TwoWayAudio_Close_phase2`, a dedicated `twowayaudio_thread`, and `TWOWAY_START`/`TWOWAY_NONE` state constants (source path embedded in the v1.015 binary's debug info: `.../pittaBB_app/pitta/src/TWOWAY_AUDIO.c`) - but it's wired entirely into the camera's own persistent RTMP connection to BlackVue's cloud (`pitta.blackvuecloud.com`, `api.blackvuecloud.com`, both hardcoded as strings), the same connection used for `RTMP_EVT_DO_PUBLISH`/`RTMP_EVT_GET_GPS_DATA`/`RTMP_EVT_UPLOAD_FILE` and friends. `TWOWAY_START` is almost certainly one more event delivered over that RTMP session, not something requestable via a plain HTTP CGI call the way `blackvue_live.cgi`/`blackvue_livedata.cgi` are. None of the four confirmed local CGI endpoints (`blackvue_live.cgi`, `blackvue_livedata.cgi`, `blackvue_vod.cgi`, `upload.cgi`) reference anything talk/audio/mic-related.

**Elite 10 has the same feature on different plumbing.** Its firmware (searched via the earlier session's own `pta_strings.txt` dump, since its `main_app`-equivalent binary wasn't separately extracted this session) has `TwoWayStart`/`TwoWayStop`/`TWOWAY_STOP`/`twoway_spk_voldb` strings, plus `subscribe_iot_twoway_start` and `KVS_TWOWAY` - tied into AWS IoT/MQTT (`aceoyq4kn0fxp-ats.iot.ap-...`, `x-amzn-iot-th...`, `mqtt_config`) and Kinesis Video Streams (`KvsWebRtc`, `KvsRtcConfig`) rather than RTMP. Same conclusion as the DR900S-2CH: cloud-relay-mediated (MQTT/KVS-WebRTC this time, a newer stack than the DR900S-2CH's RTMP one), not exposed on the local, unauthenticated LAN CGI API either camera's own 4/8 endpoints already cover.

**Conclusion given to Christer.** Nothing in the local CGI surface of either camera model gives beyond-video a hook into this - it would require speaking BlackVue's own cloud protocol (registering as a legitimate RTMP client with custom events for the DR900S-2CH, or MQTT/KVS-WebRTC for the Elite 10), a materially bigger reverse-engineering effort than anything built so far, or capturing the real app's traffic during an actual PTT session and replicating it - the latter lines up with the already-parked task #261 (packet-capture + phone-app analysis) rather than being a new standalone task. Not opened as its own task; flagged as a natural extension of #261 if Christer wants to pursue it later.

## bv-live follow-up #3: match the map's height to the camera feed, answer a stream-quality question (this session, direct follow-up)

Two more things from Christer after trying the real-window/ordering fix: "The map should have the same height as the video" (design request, acted on directly), and "Could anything be done to enhance the quality of the stream (i have a good graphics card)" (question, answered from the firmware - no code change for this one).

**Map height now matches the camera feed's height.** Previously the map and camera panels split the row's *width* via flex-grow shares (map `1`, camera `3`), each panel's own height following independently from its own image's aspect ratio at that width - the map's fixed 720x720 square render and the camera's native (likely 16:9-ish) aspect ended up different heights as a result, which is what Christer noticed. Switched both `#camera-panel img` and `#map-panel img` to `width: auto; height: 55vh` instead - both images now render at the same height by construction, and each panel's own *width* just follows from its image's own aspect ratio at that shared height (the map's square render ends up exactly as wide as it is tall; the camera feed's native aspect is untouched, still relayed unmodified - see `stream_camera()`'s own docstring). `#camera-panel`/`#map-panel` themselves switched from flex-grow shares (`3 1 320px`/`1 1 220px`) to `flex: 0 0 auto` - they now just take exactly the width their (now height-locked) image content needs, rather than negotiating a share of the row. `.dashboard`'s existing `flex-wrap: wrap` (unchanged, was already there) is what keeps this safe if the two panels together don't fit the row's width at 55vh - the map panel simply wraps to its own line instead of overflowing or squeezing either image out of its own aspect ratio. The existing `@media (max-width: 700px)` stacked-layout breakpoint gets its own override back to `width: 100%; height: auto` for both images, since height-matching two side-by-side panels makes no sense once they're stacked full-width instead. 55vh is a starting guess, not measured against Christer's own screen - flagged in the CSS comment itself as something to nudge if it's too tall or short in practice. Also updated `docs/man/bv-live.md`'s panel descriptions to mention the height-matching and to note the g-sensor strip may sit below the fold now (Christer: "I need to scroll down to see the gsensor line, but thats ok for now" - not acted on, explicitly deferred by him).

**Stream quality: nothing to enhance on beyond-video's side.** Checked directly in the firmware rather than guessing: the `blackvue_live.cgi` binary itself (a separate small ARM ELF under `res/System/www/`, not part of `main_app`) only ever reads its `QUERY_STRING` for a `direction=R` parameter - no resolution/quality/size/fps/bitrate parameter exists anywhere in its strings. It reads already-encoded JPEG frames out of a `shmget`/`shmat` shared-memory segment written by some other process (almost certainly `main_app`'s own live-view encoder pipeline) and streams them out completely unmodified - the resolution and quality are fixed at the source, on the camera itself, with no way to request anything different over HTTP. `bv-live`'s own `stream_camera()` route (`live/app.py`) already just relays those bytes unchanged (`relay_raw_stream()`, confirmed by re-reading the code, not just the firmware) - no resizing, no re-encoding, nothing a GPU could accelerate even if it wanted to. Told Christer his graphics card can't help here: the bottleneck (if there is one) is the camera's own fixed live-view output, not anything beyond-video or his PC does to it, and a browser decoding MJPEG frames isn't GPU-bound work in the first place.

**Verification note.** The CSS change was checked two ways beyond visual review: `ast.parse()` on `live/app.py` (confirms the file is still valid Python), and a direct `.format(camera_name=...)` call against the extracted `_PAGE_HTML` string body (confirms no stray single-brace/double-brace mismatch was introduced by the new CSS, since `.format()` treats unescaped `{...}` as a substitution placeholder and would raise `KeyError`/`ValueError` on any mistake here). Re-ran the full 70-test hand-rolled harness across every `bv-live` test file - all still pass, expected since this was a pure CSS change touching no Python logic the tests actually exercise. Not verified against a real browser - same standing limitation as every other visual tweak to this feature this session; the 55vh figure and the flex-wrap fallback behavior should both be expected to need another look once Christer's actually resized a real window against it.

It's not a sign anything is broken - `bv-live` never claimed to serve a favicon, and nothing about the dashboard's actual function (camera/map/g-sensor streams) depends on it. ## bv-live follow-up #5: fix the Ctrl-C hang after closing the browser (this session, direct follow-up, real bug)

Christer: "When i first shut down the browser and then use ctrl-c to stop the bv-live it hangs at `INFO: Shutting down` / `INFO: Waiting for connections to close. (CTRL+C to force quit)`. The only way to take it down is to use task manager." Unlike the earlier CSS-only follow-ups, this is a real logic bug, not a visual tweak - and one that was actually findable and fixable from the code alone, not just diagnosable from a description.

**Root cause.** `live/mjpeg.py`'s `rendered_frame_stream()` and `relay_raw_stream()` - the generators behind all three of `bv-live`'s streaming routes (map, g-sensor, camera) - both looped with a bare `while True` and, per their own original docstrings, deliberately had "no separate stop signal", relying entirely on "the caller stops iterating" to end them. That's fine while a browser tab is actually pulling frames, but once uvicorn starts a graceful shutdown (Ctrl-C), it waits for every in-flight request's handler to actually finish before the process can exit - and these generators have no way to notice a shutdown is happening and never return on their own, so that wait never ends. Closing the browser first doesn't reliably help either: a closed browser tab is why the wait *should* be quick (no client left to serve), but without something actively telling the generator to stop, it just keeps rendering/reading and yielding into a response nobody's consuming, structurally unable to end itself.

**Fix.** Both generators gained an optional `stop_event: threading.Event | None = None` parameter, checked once per loop iteration (`while stop_event is None or not stop_event.is_set()`) - a plain, cheap check that doesn't touch the existing behavior when no event is passed (kept `None`-safe for any other caller/test that doesn't care about this). `create_live_app()` (`live/app.py`) now creates one `threading.Event()` per app instance, passes it as `stop_event=` into all three route handlers' `rendered_frame_stream()`/`relay_raw_stream()` calls, and sets it in `_lifespan`'s existing `finally:` block right alongside the telemetry pump's own `pump.stop()` - so the moment uvicorn's shutdown sequence runs, every currently-looping stream generator notices on its very next iteration and returns, letting the request handler finish and uvicorn's "waiting for connections to close" resolve instead of hanging forever. For the two synthetic streams (map, g-sensor) this is checked between fast, bounded iterations (a render call plus a sub-second sleep), so it should take effect near-instantly; for the camera relay it's checked once per chunk read from the camera's own continuous MJPEG stream, which under normal operation (camera still sending frames) should also resolve within about one frame's worth of delay, though there's no hard guarantee if the camera itself were to stop sending data mid-stream.

**Tests.** Added four new tests to `test_mjpeg.py`: `rendered_frame_stream`/`relay_raw_stream` both get one test confirming they stop as soon as the event is set mid-iteration (from inside a fake `render()`/by inspecting yielded chunks) and one confirming they yield nothing at all if the event is already set before the first iteration. `create_live_app()`'s own wiring (the `threading.Event()` creation, passing it into the three routes, setting it in the lifespan) is *not* separately unit tested - consistent with this whole file's established pattern of only syntax-checking `app.py` (no fastapi in this sandbox to actually build and run the app against), so this part of the fix is verified by direct code inspection rather than a test asserting it.

**Verification note.** `ast.parse()` on both changed files, plus a direct `.format(camera_name=...)` call against `_PAGE_HTML` (unchanged by this fix, but re-checked since `create_live_app()`'s body changed) - both clean. Re-ran the full hand-rolled harness: 74 tests now (70 previous + 4 new), all passing. This is the one bv-live fix this session that's an actual logic bug rather than a CSS/UX tweak, and it's also the one most worth flagging as still fundamentally unverified against Christer's real hang - there's no live uvicorn server, real browser, or real camera anywhere in this sandbox to reproduce the original hang or confirm the fix resolves it end to end. The diagnosis (infinite generator + no shutdown signal = graceful shutdown waits forever) is a well-understood, common category of bug for exactly this shape of streaming ASGI endpoint, and the fix directly addresses the mechanism described, but Christer should expect to need to confirm a single Ctrl-C now works cleanly the next time he runs it, and report back if it still hangs (in which case the camera-relay's per-chunk-only check, or a leaked background thread from Starlette's own sync-generator-in-a-threadpool machinery, would be the next things to look at).

**Confirmed working.** Christer, next session: "It worked well with ctrl-c." No further action needed on this one.

## bv-live: zero-offset calibration + a growing g-sensor scale watermark (this session)

Christer, parked: "the sensor on the bv-line that doesn't work. The car is parked right now, but the lines shows an offset from zero. So I think we need some type of ero calibration, then when data comes in we put it at maximum and then when newer data comes in and are greater than the previous max value, we scale down the lines to math the new max value. Is that something that could be done?" Yes - and there was already precedent for exactly this class of fix in this codebase: `export/gsensor_render.py`'s `baseline_for_samples()` already centers the *offline* gsensor.mp4 gauge on a finished trip's own median reading rather than raw (0, 0), for the identical underlying reason (task #45, much earlier this session's history) - "a dashcam mounted at even a slight angle - or a plain sensor bias - means 'level, driving straight' rarely reads exactly raw (0, 0)". The live strip never had an equivalent, since it was built as a genuinely new, simpler renderer (see this feature's own original entry) rather than reusing that module. This entry brings the same idea to the live version, adapted for an open-ended stream instead of a whole trip known upfront.

**Two separate, related pieces, both living in `live/telemetry.py`'s `TelemetryState` rather than in `gsensor_stream.py`'s renderer** - they have to persist for the *whole session*, not just whatever's inside the display's own rolling `--gsensor-window` (60s default): recomputing either fresh from the currently-visible window every frame, as the renderer used to do, would mean an old peak "forgets itself" and the scale shrinks back down the moment it scrolls out of view - the opposite of what Christer asked for.

1. **Zero-offset calibration.** New `GSENSOR_CALIBRATION_SECONDS = 3.0` - the first three seconds of g-sensor readings after the pump starts producing data get buffered, then frozen (once) into a per-axis baseline: the *median* (not mean) of FrontRear/LeftRight/UpperLower across that window, mirroring `baseline_for_samples()`'s own median choice and its own stated reason (robust to one jostle - a door closing, someone bumping the car - skewing an average far more than a median). `TelemetryState.gsensor_baseline()` returns `None` until calibration finishes, then a frozen `(front_rear, left_right, upper_lower)` tuple for the rest of the session - a one-time calibration, deliberately not a continuously updating one, since actual driving afterward would otherwise slowly drag "zero" toward wherever the car spent the most time.
2. **A growing-only scale watermark.** Once calibrated, every new reading updates `TelemetryState._gsensor_max_deviation` to `max(current, |reading - baseline|)` across all three axes - `gsensor_max_deviation()` exposes this raw watermark, which `gsensor_stream.py` then applies its own existing `SCALE_PADDING`/`MINIMUM_SCALE` on top of, same as before. This is Christer's own proposed algorithm almost verbatim: "when data comes in we put it at maximum and then when newer data comes in and are greater than the previous max value, we scale down the lines to match the new max value" - "scale down the lines" here meaning the *displayed* amplitude of any given raw deviation shrinks (visually) as the watermark itself grows, since the same raw value now divides by a bigger number.

**`gsensor_stream.py` changes.** `render_live_gsensor_frame()` gained `baseline: tuple[float, float, float] | None = None` and `max_deviation: float = 0.0` params, replacing its old on-the-fly `peak = max(...)` computed fresh from `samples` each call. `baseline=None` (calibration not finished yet) now suppresses the trace entirely - reusing the same "insufficient data" fallback shape the `len(samples) < 2` case already had, rather than plotting anything meaningful against a baseline that hasn't been decided. Every plotted value is `sample.<axis> - baseline[<axis>]` rather than the raw reading. `live_gsensor_frames()`'s factory closure now reads `state.gsensor_baseline()`/`state.gsensor_max_deviation()` on every frame render, alongside the existing `state.gsensor_history(window_seconds)` call, and passes both through.

**Tests.** `test_telemetry.py`: four new tests - baseline stays `None` short of `GSENSOR_CALIBRATION_SECONDS`; baseline becomes the correct per-axis median once the window elapses (including a deliberately planted mid-window outlier, confirming the median - 25.0 - barely moves for it where a mean of the same four readings would have landed at 265.0); `max_deviation` only ever grows, confirmed by feeding a big deviation, then a much smaller one (watermark unchanged), then a bigger one on a *different* axis (watermark grows again); calibration doesn't drift once frozen, confirmed by driving big post-calibration readings through and checking the baseline itself never moves. `test_gsensor_stream.py`: `render_live_gsensor_frame`'s existing tests updated to pass an explicit `baseline`/`max_deviation` now that these actually gate the trace-drawing branch; new tests confirm `baseline=None` draws no trace at all (image differs from the calibrated version given identical samples), a flat trace exactly on the baseline draws perfectly flat at the strip's own zero_y row (checked at a single pixel column deliberately chosen to sit left of `_draw_legend()`'s own drawing so the legend can't contaminate the assertion), and that `max_deviation` - not the window's own local peak - is what actually drives the scale (same samples, two very different `max_deviation` values, visibly different output). `live_gsensor_frames()` gained a test confirming a full state -> render round trip produces a real baseline and a real image once enough time has passed. 82 tests total now (74 previous + 8 new), all passing via the same hand-rolled harness this whole feature has used all session.

**What's a first-guess, not a measured choice.** `GSENSOR_CALIBRATION_SECONDS = 3.0` is exactly that - flagged directly in its own code comment as assuming the car is roughly stationary right after `bv-live` starts (true of Christer's own test just now, and the natural way anyone would first try this feature), easy to widen if a startup jolt (a door closing, the engine starting) ever ends up baked into the baseline in practice. The scale watermark is genuinely permanent for the life of one `bv-live` process - there's no way to manually "re-zero" or reset the watermark mid-session if, say, the mount gets bumped and genuinely changes the sensor's own resting angle; not asked for, but worth knowing about if it comes up.

**Verification note.** Same standing limitation as the rest of this feature - no live camera or browser in this sandbox to confirm the parked-car strip actually sits flat now. Verified via `ast.parse()` on both changed files and the 82-test harness run above; the calibration timing (3 seconds), the median-based baseline, and the never-shrinking watermark are all real, tested behavior, not just described - but whether 3 seconds is the right amount of time, and whether the resulting live strip actually looks right to Christer once he tries it again with the car parked, are both unconfirmed.

## bv-live g-sensor: confirmed calibration fix works in the field; jaggedness left as-is (this session, no code change)

Two follow-ups on the calibration fix directly above, both resolved without touching code:

Christer asked whether saving the zero calibration to disk (to skip the ~3-second recalibration each `bv-live` start) was a good idea, or whether the sensor's own zero-point drifts over time. Checked the firmware's own strings for any gsensor calibration/offset/temperature-compensation evidence - found none either way (doesn't rule out compensation happening inside the accelerometer chip's own silicon, which wouldn't show up as strings). Answered from general MEMS-accelerometer knowledge instead, flagged as such rather than device-specific fact: consumer-grade accelerometers are known to have a temperature-dependent zero-g bias, and a camera mount getting bumped between sessions is a real, separate risk too - both would make a saved calibration silently stale in a way that's harder to notice than the original offset bug (it would look calibrated). Recommended keeping the current fresh-per-session calibration (self-correcting, ~3 seconds, trivial for a run-when-you-want tool) rather than persisting it - Christer didn't ask for the change to be made either way, this was purely a discussion.

## Determine `--stitch-gsensor`'s real axis convention from a test recording, remap the dot gauge (this session, task #283/#284)

Long-standing unknown, flagged in `gsensor_render.py`'s own docstring since it was first written: "which physical direction each axis corresponds to isn't confirmed" for the raw `.3gf` X/Y/Z fields. Christer asked earlier this session whether the dot gauge's raw X/Y meant left/right and acceleration/deceleration, guessing "if you turn left it should show increased x, and if you brake it should show increased y." Rather than accept that as a guess (or substitute a different unverified guess), agreed a real test recording with known, timestamped maneuvers was the only way to actually answer this - Christer recorded one and uploaded the raw `trip.3gf` sidecar (362.5s), then gave exact timing: a right turn at 91s, another right turn at 120s, and a left U-turn at 164s.

**Empirical findings, from the raw samples themselves** (read via the project's own `read_gsensor()`, whole-trip median as baseline, ±8s window around each named event): raw X showed no sustained response to any of the three events - just the same tight, noisy band the whole trip through, turning or not. Raw Y showed a clear, repeatable pattern: sustained positive deviation (+20 to +34) during both right turns, and a sustained negative deviation (-20 to -38, roughly double the magnitude - consistent with a U-turn being sharper) during the left U-turn - i.e. **Y is the lateral/left-right axis**, not X. Asked Christer for a braking-specific test to pin down the third axis; he predicted a small slowdown right before the U-turn instead of a separate recording, and that call was correct - raw Z showed a sustained negative dip (-8 to -24) for about 4 seconds right before the U-turn began, distinct from Z's normal noise elsewhere, while X again showed nothing during that same window. **Z is the longitudinal/forward-back axis** (braking reads negative), and **X is left unexplained by any of the three tested events** - presumed to be the vertical/mounting axis, picking up road vibration rather than a directional force, though that's an inference by elimination rather than something independently confirmed the way Y and Z now are.

This contradicts what `gsensor_graph_render.py`'s own strip-chart legend currently says ("X - Left/right", "Y - Forward/back") - that wording was Christer's own best-effort guess from earlier this session, explicitly flagged there as unconfirmed. **Not changed as part of this entry** - that legend belongs to a separate visualization (`--gsensor-graph-video`/`--stitch-graph`, the static strip chart) from the one this task was scoped to (`--stitch-gsensor`, the dot gauge); flagged to Christer as a likely-needed follow-up rather than changed unasked.

**Design question, asked via `AskUserQuestion`:** engineer vs. "what the car is doing" display conventions differ on at least one axis (raw negative G during braking vs. an intuitive "slowing down" feel) - Christer, an engineer himself, said raw G is right for him but most people would want the opposite; landed on fixing the confirmed axis swap now and holding off on a dual-mode toggle until braking's sign convention was independently nailed down. The braking sample above answered that in the same exchange, but the display-mode question (raw G vs. "intuitive" sign flips) was intentionally left for a later request rather than assumed.

**Change - `gsensor_render.py`.** `baseline_for_samples()` and `scale_for_samples()` now read the raw Y (lateral) and Z (longitudinal) fields instead of X and Y - same median-based, deviation-from-baseline logic as before (see the original task #45 entry for why median), just pointed at the two fields the real data actually confirmed. Module docstring rewritten to describe the confirmed Y/Z mapping and the evidence behind it, replacing the old "not confirmed either" disclaimer.

**Change - `gsensor_video.py`.** `render_gsensor_video()`'s per-frame position calculation changed from `(x - baseline_x, y - baseline_y)` to `(y - baseline_lateral, z - baseline_longitudinal)` - the interpolation helpers themselves (`interpolate_sample()`, `_advance_search_index()`/`_interpolate_from_index()`) are unchanged, since they already returned all three raw fields; only which two fields get turned into gauge coordinates changed. Variable names renamed throughout (`baseline_x`/`baseline_y` -> `baseline_lateral`/`baseline_longitudinal`) for clarity. Docstrings updated to match.

**Docs.** `docs/man/bv-export.md`'s `--gsensor-video` row rewritten to describe the lateral/longitudinal mapping and note it was confirmed against a real recording, rather than the old bare "(x, y) readings."

## Fix `gsensor_graph_render.py`'s stale legend to match the confirmed Y/Z axis mapping (this session, direct follow-up)

Direct follow-up to the axis-remap entry above, which deliberately left this file untouched and flagged it as a likely-needed follow-up. Christer, on being told the legend was still stale: "I hope we didnt fool ourself. A brake will usually lower the height in front side of the car. Yes fix the legends."

**Sanity-checked the physical mechanism before touching anything.** Christer's point - that braking pitches a car's nose down, a rotational/weight-transfer effect, not a pure fore-aft force - is a fair challenge to "Z = forward/back." Answered directly rather than just proceeding: a MEMS accelerometer with no independent tilt/gyro correction can't distinguish pure translational deceleration from the gravity vector's own re-projection as the car's body pitches forward under braking, and since this camera's mount is already known to be off-level (the whole reason `baseline_for_samples()` exists), a nose-dip event bleeding into "Z" alongside genuine deceleration is expected behavior for this class of sensor, not a sign the axis was misidentified. The empirical result stands regardless of which exact physical mechanism is at play: Z dipped in a sustained, repeatable way specifically during the braking window Christer predicted, X did nothing, both times checked. Whatever the precise cause, Z is the axis that reliably responds to braking on this camera's own mount - which is what a working gauge or legend needs, mechanism aside.

**Change - `gsensor_graph_render.py`.** `LEGEND_LABELS` (the strip chart's own color-key, used by both orientations) changed from `(("X", "Left/right"), ("Y", "Forward/back"), ("Z", "Up/down"))` to `(("X", "Up/down"), ("Y", "Left/right"), ("Z", "Forward/back"))` - tuple order (X, Y, Z) deliberately left unchanged, since `_draw_legend()` zips it against a fixed `(X_COLOR, Y_COLOR, Z_COLOR)` tuple by position, not by matching the "axis" string; only the wording changed. Module docstring and the constant's own preceding comment rewritten to state Y/Z were confirmed against a real recording (pointing at `gsensor_render.py`'s own docstring for the underlying evidence) and that X's "Up/down" label is an inference by elimination, not independently confirmed the same way - carrying the same honesty about what's actually verified into this file that the dot-gauge fix already had. Two internal docstring examples that named "Y — Forward/back" as the legend's longest row (used to explain the vertical-mode centering math) updated to "Z — Forward/back," now the actual longest row.

**Tests - `test_gsensor_graph_render.py`.** `test_legend_labels_spell_out_what_each_axis_physically_means`'s assertion updated to the new tuple; two comments referencing the old "Y — Forward/back"/"Z — Up/down" wording updated to match. One test broke and needed a real fix, not just a comment update: `test_render_base_frame_vertical_centers_the_legend_block` computed its own expected legend width by measuring the widest label across all of `LEGEND_LABELS` (all three axes), but `render_base_frame()` in that test is called without `show_z`, so only the X/Y rows are actually drawn (see `_legend_rows()`). This was a latent test bug that happened not to matter under the old wording - Y's "Forward/back" was already the widest of X/Y *and* the widest of all three, so measuring against all three coincidentally gave the right answer. Under the new wording Z's "Forward/back" is the widest of all three, but Z isn't drawn in this test - measuring against all three overstated the block's width and threw the centering math off by exactly one swatch length in the actual pixel check. Fixed by measuring against `LEGEND_LABELS[:2]` (X/Y only, matching what's actually on screen), with a comment explaining why. Full harness re-run: 51/51 passing (was 50/51 immediately after the label change, confirming this catch was real and not a false alarm).

**Not touched.** `docs/man/bv-export.md`'s `--gsensor-graph-video`/`--stitch-graph` rows reference "X/Y" only to describe *which two raw fields are plotted by default* (still true - the field selection itself didn't change, only what each field is labeled as meaning), so they didn't need editing. `gsensor_graph_video.py` and the stitch-panel tests were grepped for the same stale wording and came back clean - the legend text lives only in `gsensor_graph_render.py`. The slower ffmpeg-backed test files (`test_gsensor_graph_video.py`, stitch's own graph-panel tests) weren't re-run end to end this round (timed out in the sandbox on real encoding, unrelated to this change) - confirmed by grep that neither references legend wording, so nothing in them could have been affected by this specific edit.

**Verification.** `ast.parse()` on both changed files, plus the full 51-test `run_test_gsensor_graph_render.py` harness run (51/51, including the one test that needed a real fix, not just a relabel). Not verified against a real `--stitch-graph`/`--gsensor-graph-video` export - same standing caveat as the dot-gauge fix above.

**3. Confidence in the axis mapping - answered honestly, no code change.** Christer: "I am not a 100% we got it right." Agreed that's a reasonable place to be: the whole finding rests on one recording with three maneuvers (two turns, one incidental braking event), not a dedicated multi-sample validation. What's solid: the pattern reproduced twice in the same direction (both right turns gave positive Y) and flipped consistently for the opposite direction (the left U-turn), and the braking dip landed exactly where Christer predicted it before being told what the data showed - that's a real, blind prediction confirmed, not a post-hoc rationalization. With `scale_for_samples()`'s scale computed as `peak_deviation * padding`, and `_project()` dividing every plotted value by that same scale before multiplying by the gauge's radius, `padding=1.0` means the trip's single largest recorded deviation maps to exactly `radius` (the outermost of the three concentric rings), by construction - nothing in a normal trip can land past it, since the scale is defined as that trip's own peak. Docstring and the constant's own comment rewritten to state this directly rather than the old "leaves headroom" framing, including a note that a caller wanting headroom (e.g. a scale meant to be reused across multiple trips) can still pass `padding > 1.0` explicitly. This only touches `gsensor_render.py`/`gsensor_video.py` (the dot gauge, `--stitch-gsensor`) - `gsensor_graph_render.py`'s own separate `DEFAULT_SCALE_PADDING` (the strip chart's per-axis amplitude scaling) is untouched, since "outer ring" only describes the dot gauge's own concentric-ring geometry.

## bv-live: remove the g-sensor strip's zero-offset calibration, keep the growing-only scale (this session)

Christer: "remove the zero calibration on graph from bv-live." Two pieces made up the earlier calibration feature (see the "zero calibration + growing max scale" entry above): a per-axis zero-offset baseline, frozen from the first `GSENSOR_CALIBRATION_SECONDS` (3.0) of readings, subtracted from every plotted value; and a growing-only scale watermark (`gsensor_max_deviation()`), independent of the baseline. Asked via `AskUserQuestion` which part(s) should go, since the request named only "zero calibration" but the two pieces are related. Christer: keep the growing-only scale, remove just the zero-offset baseline.

**Change - `telemetry.py`.** Removed `GSENSOR_CALIBRATION_SECONDS`, `TelemetryState._gsensor_calibration_start`, `_gsensor_calibration_buffer`, `_gsensor_baseline`, and the `gsensor_baseline()` accessor entirely - no more startup buffering window, no more frozen per-axis median. `_update_gsensor_calibration()` renamed to `_update_gsensor_scale()` and simplified to a single `max()` update per sample; deviation is now `abs(sample.<axis>)` (raw magnitude from zero) rather than `abs(sample.<axis> - baseline.<axis>)`. `gsensor_max_deviation()`'s own docstring rewritten to describe the current raw-zero behavior and note the removed calibration step for context, rather than silently going stale. The `statistics` import (only used for the removed median calculation) was dropped as unused.

The trace-drawing gate changed from `if baseline is not None and len(samples) >= 2` to `if len(samples) >= 2` - a trace now draws the moment there are two samples, with no startup delay. Every plotted value changed from `sample.<axis> - baseline_<axis>` to plain `sample.<axis>` - traces plot raw readings against the strip's own raw zero line now. `live_gsensor_frames()`'s factory closure no longer calls `state.gsensor_baseline()`. Module docstring and `render_live_gsensor_frame()`'s own docstring rewritten to describe the current behavior, with a note that zero-offset calibration was tried and then explicitly removed again, rather than erasing that history.

**Tests.** `test_telemetry.py`: removed the three calibration-specific tests (`test_gsensor_baseline_is_none_before_calibration_finishes`, `test_gsensor_baseline_becomes_the_median_of_the_calibration_window`, `test_gsensor_calibration_does_not_drift_once_frozen` - none of what they exercised exists anymore) and the now-unused `_fake_clock()` helper they shared. `test_gsensor_max_deviation_only_ever_grows` rewritten to not touch calibration/baseline at all - just feeds raw readings and confirms the watermark only grows, including a new case confirming negative readings count by magnitude. New `test_gsensor_max_deviation_starts_at_zero_with_no_readings` replaces the old "before calibration" zero-value check. `test_gsensor_stream.py`: every `baseline=` argument removed from `render_live_gsensor_frame()` calls; `test_render_live_gsensor_frame_draws_no_trace_before_calibration_finishes` replaced with `test_render_live_gsensor_frame_draws_a_trace_with_no_startup_delay` (confirms two samples renders differently from one, with no calibration gate involved); `test_render_live_gsensor_frame_subtracts_the_baseline_before_plotting` replaced with `test_render_live_gsensor_frame_plots_raw_readings_against_raw_zero` (same flat-trace-at-zero_y pixel check, now using raw-zero samples instead of baseline-relative ones); `test_live_gsensor_frames_draws_a_trace_once_calibration_finishes` replaced with `test_live_gsensor_frames_draws_a_trace_immediately_with_no_calibration_delay` (no `time.monotonic()` monkeypatching needed anymore, since there's no calibration window to wait out). ## bv-live: don't let an Overpass fetch failure take down the whole live map stream (this session)

Christer, hitting a real Overpass timeout: "If bv-live gets the error blackvue.generate.media.MediaToolError: could not reach the Overpass API for map data: HTTP Error 504: Gateway Timeout It shouldnt go totally black, it should wait a little and then try again."

**Root cause.** `osm_roads.py`'s `_fetch_overpass_payload()` wraps any network failure (a timeout, a 504, DNS trouble) in `MediaToolError` - a well-established convention for this codebase's external-tool calls. `live/map_stream.py`'s `LiveMapRegion.ensure_covers()` calls `load_or_fetch_roads()`/`load_or_fetch_areas()` with no try/except around them, so that error propagated straight up through `render_live_map_frame()`, into `live_map_frames()`'s `_render()` closure, and out of `live/mjpeg.py`'s `rendered_frame_stream()` generator - which terminates the entire multipart HTTP response the instant it's raised. From the browser's side, the `<img>` tag that was mid-stream simply stops receiving new parts and shows whatever it had (or nothing) - that's the "totally black" Christer saw, and there was no retry of any kind; the stream stayed dead until bv-live was restarted.

**Change - `map_stream.py`.** New `RETRY_DELAY_SECONDS = 30.0` (a first guess, not measured - long enough not to hammer a public, rate-limited, possibly-already-overloaded Overpass instance every single rendered frame; short enough that a transient outage recovers within a session). `LiveMapRegion` gained `self._last_fetch_error_at: float | None`, set whenever a fetch fails and cleared on the next success. `ensure_covers()` now: (1) skips attempting a fetch at all if the last failure was less than `RETRY_DELAY_SECONDS` ago, even if the view has scrolled somewhere the cache doesn't cover; (2) wraps the actual `load_or_fetch_roads()`/`load_or_fetch_areas()` calls in `try/except MediaToolError`, recording the failure time and returning without touching `self._bbox`/`_indexed_roads`/`_indexed_areas` on failure - whatever was already cached (a real region from an earlier successful fetch, or nothing at all if this is the very first fetch of the session) stays exactly as it was. Either way `ensure_covers()` never raises. `render_frame()` itself already handles empty `roads`/`areas` tuples fine (a plain background + route trail + marker, not a crash) - so a session that fails its very first Overpass fetch still gets a real, live-updating map frame, just without road/water/park geometry on it yet, rather than nothing at all. Both `ensure_covers()`'s and `render_live_map_frame()`'s docstrings rewritten to describe this directly.
