## bv-live: detect the real OS-level default browser instead of a hardcoded Edge-first list (this session)

Christer asked why `bv-live` opened Edge instead of Chrome. Answer: `_open_new_window()`'s browser search was never reading the OS's actual default-browser setting - it walked a fixed `_CHROMIUM_PATHS` list and launched the first executable that existed on disk, with Edge's path listed before Chrome's "because Edge ships by default on every Windows install," not because it reflected Christer's real choice. The reason it didn't just ask Windows for the real default in the first place: `webbrowser.open_new()` (which does respect it) goes through `os.startfile()` on Windows, which tends to reuse an already-running browser instance and open a new *tab* instead of a new *window* - a real problem Christer had already reported and this hardcoded-list approach was built specifically to work around.

Christer's follow-up: "I want it to detect my OS-level default browser and use that, unless there is something that breaks the function." "The function" being `_open_new_window()`'s own actual job - a genuinely new window, not a tab - so detection had to be tried first but fail safe into the existing working behavior, not replace it outright.

**Change - `cli/bv_live.py`.** Three new functions, in order of use: `_windows_default_browser_command()` reads the same per-user registry key Windows itself consults (`HKCU\...\UrlAssociations\http\UserChoice`'s `ProgId`), then resolves that `ProgId` to its real launch command via `HKEY_CLASSES_ROOT\<ProgId>\shell\open\command` - wrapped in `try/except OSError` and a `try/except ImportError` around `import winreg` itself (which doesn't exist outside Windows at all, so it can't be imported unconditionally at module level without breaking bv-live on Linux/macOS), returning `None` on any failure. Kept as its own function (rather than inlined) specifically so this project's own Linux test environment can monkeypatch it directly instead of needing a real `winreg` module to test against. `_exe_from_command()` is a small, pure parser pulling the executable path out of that raw command string (handles both the common quoted form and a bare unquoted one). `_default_browser_launch()` ties them together: bails immediately on non-Windows (`sys.platform != "win32"`), then classifies the resolved executable's filename stem against two known sets - `_CHROMIUM_EXE_STEMS` (`chrome`, `msedge`, `brave`, `opera`, `vivaldi`, `chromium` - all take the same `--new-window` flag) and `_FIREFOX_EXE_STEMS` (`firefox` - takes `-new-window` instead) - returning `None` for anything unrecognized (Internet Explorer, some other browser) rather than guessing at a flag that might not exist. Also returns `None` if the resolved exe doesn't actually exist on disk (a stale/dangling registry entry pointing at something uninstalled) - the "unless something breaks the function" case Christer named directly.

`_open_new_window()` now tries `_default_browser_launch()` first; if it finds something, launches it with `subprocess.Popen`, same as before. Any failure at any point - detection returns `None`, or the `Popen` call itself raises `OSError` - falls straight through to the exact fixed Edge/Chrome/Firefox priority list this module already had, which itself still falls back to plain `webbrowser.open_new()` as the very last resort. Nothing about the existing fallback chain changed; detection is purely an earlier, preferred rung added on top of it. The big comment above `_CHROMIUM_PATHS` was reworded to describe that list as the *fallback*, not the primary path, now that it isn't the first thing tried anymore.

**Tests.** New: `_exe_from_command()` (quoted, unquoted, empty, unterminated-quote); `_windows_default_browser_command()` (a real, unmocked assertion that it returns `None` on this project's own Linux test environment, since `winreg` genuinely doesn't exist there - not a stand-in for the Windows behavior, an actual exercise of the `ImportError` branch); `_default_browser_launch()` (non-Windows short-circuit, registry-lookup failure, a quoted Chromium command, an unquoted command, the Firefox flag, an unrecognized browser, and a resolved-but-nonexistent exe - the last two both regression guards for "unless something breaks the function"); `_open_new_window()` gained three new tests (prefers the detected default when available and asserts the fixed priority list is never even consulted in that case; falls back to the priority list when detection finds nothing; falls back to the priority list when the detected browser's own `Popen` call raises) and the four pre-existing `_open_new_window()` tests were updated to explicitly monkeypatch `_default_browser_launch()` to `None` so they keep testing only the fallback chain they always did, rather than relying on the Linux test environment's own `sys.platform` to make that implicit. Full `run_bv_live_tests.py` harness: 103/103 passing (was 88, +15 new).

**Docs.** `docs/man/bv-live.md`'s auto-open sentence updated to mention the OS-default-browser detection and its fallback, since this was a real point of user confusion worth documenting rather than leaving silent.

**Verification.** `ast.parse()` on both changed files, full 103-test harness run, all passing. Not verified against a real Windows machine/registry in this sandbox (winreg isn't available here at all) - the registry-reading function itself (`_windows_default_browser_command()`) is exercised only for its non-Windows `ImportError` path; its actual Windows registry calls are untested beyond what monkeypatching `_windows_default_browser_command()`'s own return value covers for the rest of the logic. Christer should confirm on his own machine that bv-live now opens whichever browser he's actually set as default.

## bv-live: add a `--browser` override, since Windows' own default kept losing to Edge (this session, direct follow-up)

The OS-default-browser detection from the previous entry turned out to work exactly as designed, but didn't fix Christer's actual problem. Diagnostic sequence, entirely empirical rather than guessed: (1) had Christer run `_windows_default_browser_command()`/`_default_browser_launch()` directly - both correctly resolved to `msedge.exe --new-window`, proving the code was reading the registry faithfully; (2) Christer said Chrome was his default, so had him compare the `http` and `https` `UserChoice` `ProgId` values separately via a saved `check_browser.py` script (in case Windows was tracking them independently and only one had actually been updated) - both came back `MSEdgeHTM`; (3) Christer then went into Windows Settings and explicitly changed the per-protocol association, and even rebooted - still got Edge. At that point this stopped being a code bug to chase and became "Windows' own default-browser association is unreliable enough on this machine that depending on it isn't a good design," so rather than keep round-tripping on Windows Settings, added a CLI escape hatch instead.

**Change - `cli/bv_live.py`.** New `--browser {default,chrome,edge,firefox}` argument (default `default` - unchanged auto-detect-then-fallback behavior). Split the existing combined `_CHROMIUM_PATHS`/`_CHROMIUM_COMMANDS` into per-browser `_EDGE_PATHS`/`_EDGE_COMMANDS` and `_CHROME_PATHS`/`_CHROME_COMMANDS` (with `_CHROMIUM_PATHS`/`_CHROMIUM_COMMANDS` now just their concatenation, so the existing generic fallback list is unchanged); added a `_BROWSER_OVERRIDES` dict mapping each explicit choice to `(paths, commands, new-window flag)`. `_open_new_window(url, browser="default")` now takes the browser choice as a second parameter: when it isn't `"default"`, it tries `_find_browser()` against that specific browser's paths/commands first, launching it directly if found - bypassing OS-default detection entirely. If the requested browser isn't found on disk/PATH, or its `Popen` call itself fails, this falls straight through to the same detection-then-fixed-list-then-`webbrowser.open_new()` chain as if `--browser` had never been given, rather than giving up - same fail-safe philosophy as the OS-detection feature itself. `_open_browser_soon()` and the `_run()` call site were threaded to pass `args.browser` through.

**Tests.** New: `test_open_new_window_uses_an_explicit_browser_override_when_given` (asserts `_default_browser_launch` is never even called when an override is given), `test_open_new_window_falls_back_when_explicit_browser_not_found`, `test_open_new_window_falls_back_when_explicit_browser_popen_fails`, `test_open_browser_soon_passes_an_explicit_browser_choice_through`, `test_parse_args_rejects_an_unknown_browser_choice`. Updated: `test_parse_args_defaults`/`test_parse_args_overrides` now check `args.browser`; `test_open_browser_soon_schedules_a_timer_that_opens_the_url` and the three `_run()` browser-opening tests updated for `_open_browser_soon`'s new two-argument signature. Full `run_bv_live_tests.py` harness: 108/108 passing (was 103, +5 new; 2 pre-existing `_run()` tests needed updating for the signature change, not new failures).

**Docs.** `docs/man/bv-live.md`: synopsis line, auto-open paragraph, and the OPTIONS table all updated to document `--browser`.

**Verification.** `ast.parse()` on both changed files, full 108-test harness run, all passing (rebuilt the sandbox's `python -m tomllib` stub and re-derived the hand-rolled `run_bv_live_tests.py` harness fresh this session since neither pytest nor tomllib is available in this particular sandbox - same standing limitation noted in earlier bv-live entries). Not verified on Christer's own machine yet - next step for him is to try `bv-live kirby --browser chrome` and confirm Chrome actually opens.

## bv-export: one corrupted recording no longer takes down an entire trip's front/rear/audio (this session)

Christer, pasting a real export's tail: `ffmpeg concat failed for rear.mp4 ... moov atom not found ... 20260731_173318_NR.mp4`, then "can you fix add the missing atom?" - the moov atom itself can't be recovered (that recording's data really is gone, most likely the camera lost power or was unplugged mid-write), but the actual bug worth fixing was upstream of that: `_concatenate_asset()` handed *every* recording's file for a given asset to `concatenate_media()` in one single ffmpeg concat-demuxer call, so one unreadable file among several good ones failed the whole call and discarded that trip's entire rear.mp4 (or front.mp4/audio.aac) - not just the one bad recording's footage.

**Change - `export/media.py`.** New `check_readable(path)`: a lightweight ffprobe call (`-show_entries format=duration`, no stream selection) that raises `MediaToolError` if ffprobe can't even open/parse the file, otherwise returns cleanly. Deliberately doesn't reuse `generate/media.py`'s `probe()` - that function hardcodes `-select_streams v:0` because it only ever cares about a video stream's own duration/frame rate, which would make it fail *every* audio-only source (this project's own `test_export_media.py` already had a comment flagging this exact trap, from when it built its own duration helper for audio fixtures for the same reason).

**Change - `export/trip_export.py`.** `_concatenate_asset()` now probes every source with `check_readable()` before handing any of them to `concatenate_media()`. A source that fails is left out with a warning ("`{filename}`: `{name}` could not be read and was left out (...) - likely an incomplete recording"), logged the same way as every other per-recording warning this function already produces - the same "just leave it out" treatment already used for excluded Parking recordings, since the corrupted footage is genuinely gone either way; the fix only stops it from taking healthy footage down with it. If literally every source for an asset turns out unreadable, the behavior is unchanged from before (that asset is skipped entirely, same as if there were no sources at all).

**Tests.** New in `test_export_media.py`: `check_readable()` against a valid video file, a valid *audio-only* file (the case `probe()` gets wrong), a real truncated-moov-atom file (built by actually cutting a valid MP4 down programmatically, not just writing garbage bytes - reproduces Christer's exact failure), and a nonexistent path. New in `test_trip_export.py`: `_concatenate_asset()` with one good + one corrupted source (keeps the good one, warns about the corrupted one, output duration reflects only the survivor) and with every source corrupted (returns `None`, one warning, no file written). Also had to fix an existing test, `test_export_trip_concatenates_front_rear_audio_independently` - it fed `_concatenate_asset()` literal garbage bytes (`b"x"`) as front/rear/audio "files" while monkeypatching `concatenate_media()` itself to simulate a front-only failure; with the new `check_readable()` gate running *before* that monkeypatch is ever reached, the garbage bytes would now get dropped as unreadable before the test's own simulated failure logic ever ran, so its fixtures were switched to real (tiny) video/audio files. Full `run_export_media_and_trip_tests.py` harness (this sandbox's usual pytest-free runner, network access for `pip install pytest` unavailable here): 99/99 passing.

**Docs.** `docs/man/bv-export.md`'s DESCRIPTION gained a paragraph explaining this resilience directly, since it changes what a trip actually ends up with when a recording is corrupted (partial output instead of one asset vanishing outright).

**Verification.** `ast.parse()` on all four changed files, full 99-test harness run (real ffmpeg/ffprobe available in this sandbox, so both the new `check_readable()` tests and the corrupted-source `_concatenate_asset()` tests exercise the genuine ffmpeg failure path - a real MP4 built with `ffmpeg`, then truncated to strip its trailing moov atom - not a mocked one). Not verified against Christer's own original failing export; he should confirm on his next `bv-export --stitch ...` run against that same trip (or archive) that rear.mp4 now comes through using the surviving recordings, with a warning about the one that's actually corrupted, instead of rear.mp4 disappearing entirely.

## scripts/check_mp4_recoverability.py: diagnose whether a "moov atom not found" file is worth recovering (this session, direct follow-up)

Christer initially asked "can you fix add the missing atom?" about the same corrupted `20260731_173318_NR.mp4` - I'd misread this as a request to change how bv-export *handles* a corrupted file (the fix above), when he actually meant the file itself. Once clarified: I don't have access to `x:\files\` at all (only `C:\My_git\beyond-video` is a connected folder), so any repair attempt has to be something Christer runs himself. Before recommending a heavyweight tool like untrunc, built a small diagnostic first to check whether there's actually anything worth recovering.

**What it does.** A dependency-free script (stdlib only - no ffmpeg/ffprobe/venv needed) that walks an MP4's raw top-level box structure directly (the same size-prefixed layout ffprobe itself reads) and reports what's actually there: whether `ftyp`/`moov`/`mdat` are present, `mdat`'s declared size vs. how many bytes actually exist in the file, and a plain-language verdict - complete `mdat` with `moov` simply missing (real recovery candidate), `mdat` cut off partway through (partial recovery, camera lost power mid-write), no `mdat` at all (nothing to recover), or `mdat` present but under 100 KB (not worth the effort).

**Real result.** Run against Christer's actual file: `mdat` declared 237,000,313 bytes but only 19,809,723 bytes actually exist - about 8.8% of the intended recording made it to disk before the camera cut out. Told him plainly: this is the partial-recovery case, likely only a handful of seconds recoverable, and untrunc requires a build (no simple pip install) plus a healthy reference file from the same camera/settings - a lot of setup for a small payoff. Gave him an `ffprobe`-based one-liner to check the paired front video's own duration if he wants an exact recoverable-seconds estimate before deciding. He decided to wait until the camera has power again rather than pursue recovery now.

**Verified against synthetic cases first**, not just trusted the logic: built a real MP4 with ffmpeg, then three variants - untouched (has `moov`, correctly flagged as unexpected), truncated mid-`mdat` (correctly flagged as partial/cut-off), and truncated exactly at the `mdat`/`moov` boundary (correctly flagged as `moov`-missing-but-`mdat`-complete, just too small in this synthetic case to clear the 100 KB "worth it" threshold) - before running it against the real file.

**Where it ended up.** First saved into the outputs scratchpad by mistake - Christer tried to run it from `C:\My_git\beyond-video` (where he was already `cd`'d) and got a file-not-found, since scratchpad files aren't visible on his machine. Rewritten directly into the connected folder's root so the path he was already trying would work. Asked afterward whether to keep it, and if so where - Christer chose to keep it as a real, documented project utility rather than a one-off scratch file, so it's been moved to `scripts/check_mp4_recoverability.py` (matching the existing `scripts/` folder) and committed. Note: I don't have a file-delete capability for the connected folder, so the original root-level copy (`C:\My_git\beyond-video\check_mp4_recoverability.py`, untracked in git) is still sitting there - Christer should delete that stray duplicate himself; only `scripts/check_mp4_recoverability.py` is the real, committed copy going forward.

**Verification.** Manually re-ran the script (three synthetic fixtures plus a nonexistent-path case) after the scripts/ move to confirm the relocated copy still works identically - no logic changed, just its saved location.

## CONTRIBUTING.md, scripts/scan_blackvue_endpoints.py, and a GitHub issue template: invite BlackVue owners to help find endpoints for camera models this project hasn't tested (this session)

Christer, after I'd flagged the g-sensor axis mapping as still not settled and the README as the one stale doc that hadn't gotten the same "aspirational, corrected" treatment `docs/CLI.md`/`docs/ARCHITECTURE.md` already got: "I was thinking about asking other developers (if any) for doing network scans for their blackvue (primarily) cameras and help out with finding endpoints and how to call them." Confirmed first that this is actually viable right now - `git remote -v` plus a GitHub API check showed the repo is already public (`sssreh/beyond-video`, GPL-3.0, issues enabled, zero stars/forks/watchers) - the only real gap was that nothing on the repo actually invited or explained the ask: no description, an 8-line README, a genuinely empty `CONTRIBUTING.md`, no Discussions.

I'd tried to ask Christer two clarifying questions (script vs. manual instructions; GitHub issues vs. Discussions vs. something else) via `AskUserQuestion`, but the tool call itself failed (permission stream closed before a response came back) - asked the same two questions as plain text instead, and Christer said "you hang on asking question, please continue," so proceeded on my own judgment: a script (matches this project's existing precedent - `check_mp4_recoverability.py`, the earlier `check_browser.py` - of handing over a runnable diagnostic rather than instructions to follow by hand) reporting into GitHub issues (already enabled, just needed a template; Discussions would've needed enabling from scratch for no clear benefit over issues here).

**Grounding the candidate endpoint list in what's actually known**, not guessed: had a research subagent pull every CGI path this project's own client code calls (`blackvue_vod.cgi`, `blackvue_live.cgi`, `blackvue_livedata.cgi`, `/Config/config.ini`, `/Record/<filename>`) plus everything found only in firmware analysis and never wired into the client (`blackvue_snap.cgi`, `blackvue_hss_live.cgi`, `blackvue_gps.cgi`, `blackvue_log.cgi`, `upload.cgi`, FTP/TFTP) from `WORKING_CONTEXT.md`'s existing DR900S-2CH/Elite 10 firmware-analysis entries (tasks #251/#258/#259/#260) - confirmed `firmware/README.md` itself is empty, so that history only lives in `WORKING_CONTEXT.md` prose, not in any committed firmware artifacts.

**`scripts/scan_blackvue_endpoints.py`.** Stdlib-only (matches `check_mp4_recoverability.py`'s "no dependencies to install" precedent). Safety was the main design constraint, since this runs against a stranger's own camera: only GET, never `upload.cgi` or any delete-capable query param; the continuous-stream endpoints (`blackvue_live.cgi`, `blackvue_livedata.cgi`, `blackvue_hss_live.cgi`, `blackvue_gps.cgi`) never close on their own once they start responding, so every read is bounded to a fixed byte count (`resp.read(2048)`, never a bare `.read()`) rather than waiting for a response that will never finish; every body preview is truncated and, after a first pass showed raw JPEG bytes rendering as a wall of unreadable `�` replacement characters, binary responses are now detected (by how much of the decoded text is actually `�` - `isprintable()` alone doesn't catch this, since Python treats the replacement character itself as "printable") and summarized as `[binary data, N bytes, starts with <hex>]` instead of dumped raw. Also does a plain TCP-connect check on FTP (port 21); TFTP (port 69, UDP) is explicitly *not* probed - a plain connect can't test a UDP service meaningfully - and the output says so rather than silently skipping it.

**Verified against a real (fake) server, not just read for correctness**: wrote a throwaway `http.server`-based mock camera with endpoints that genuinely never stop streaming (a background thread writing MJPEG-style chunks forever) to prove the bounded-read logic doesn't hang - confirmed a full 9-endpoint scan against it completes in ~3 seconds, not indefinitely. Also exercised a closed-port case (connection refused, handled cleanly) and a normal-file case (`/Config/config.ini`, `/blackvue_vod.cgi`) for the plain-text path.

States plainly this is a personal, single-maintainer project, not run with a community roadmap - then gives the one concrete ask: run the scan script, open an issue with the template, include model/firmware. Also covers code contributions briefly (open an issue first before a PR; matches Christer's own instinct to keep changes to his own working setup deliberate) and the GPL-3.0 licensing note.

**`.github/ISSUE_TEMPLATE/camera-endpoint-scan.yml`** (new - no `.github/` directory existed before this). A structured GitHub issue form (not a plain markdown template) with required fields for camera model, firmware version, and the scan script's pasted output, plus an optional free-text notes field - includes the same recording-filename privacy note `CONTRIBUTING.md` and the script's own docstring both already carry.

## Purging the real camera IP from git history entirely (this session, direct follow-up)

Christer asked to also rewrite history so the real IP isn't recoverable from past commits on GitHub, then asked how much that would cost - answered it's trivial for a repo this size (214 commits, 58MB `.git`) and offered to run it here if he'd force-push the result; he said yes.

**Tooling problems, in order:** `git-filter-repo` isn't installed and this sandbox has no network access to `pip install` it. `git filter-branch` (built-in, no install needed) worked in a throwaway test repo, but on the real repo it hit two walls: (1) the sandbox's bash tool hard-kills any command after 45 seconds with no way to extend that, and (2) backgrounded processes (`nohup ... & disown`) don't survive past the end of the bash call that launched them - confirmed directly with a `sleep 20 && touch marker` test that never left a marker file after the launching call ended. `--state-branch` (filter-branch's built-in checkpoint/resume feature) doesn't help either, since a hard SIGKILL from the timeout doesn't give it a chance to save state.

**Switched to a direct plumbing-level rewrite** (`scripts` weren't kept for this one - one-off, written to the outputs scratchpad): since only a single blob at `examples/config.py` ever needed to change, walked `git log --all --topo-order --reverse --format='%H %T %P'` once, and for each commit only rewrote the tree path down to `examples/config.py` (reusing every other tree object unchanged) before calling `commit-tree` with the original author/committer identity and message preserved. First version accidentally recursed into *every* subtree for *every* commit (not just the path to `examples/config.py`), turning it into an accidental full-repo-tree-walk per commit - fixed by making the tree rewrite path-aware (only follow `examples` -> `config.py`, copy every sibling entry through untouched and unread). Also replaced a per-commit `git rev-parse <sha>^{tree}}` with getting the tree hash straight out of the `git log --format` output. Finished in one shot: rewrote 194 of 214 commits (the other 20 predate the leak), `refs/heads/main` moved from `e26cee5` to `c92365f`, tree of the new tip verified identical to the old tip's tree (`eb6e647...` both), working directory stayed clean, commit count and full log preserved.

**Verification, and a second leak caught in the process:** wrote every blob reachable from the rewritten `refs/heads/main` to a file and grepped it for the real IP (first attempt used `git rev-list --objects | git cat-file --batch-check` directly, which silently mis-parsed since `--objects` appends a pathname to each line and `cat-file --batch-check` needs a bare object id - fixed by stripping to the first field before piping in). One blob still matched: **this WORKING_CONTEXT.md file itself** - the entry directly above this one quoted the real IP in prose while documenting the leak, which is its own instance of the same secret, introduced fresh in the tip commit rather than inherited from `1573528`. Since it was only ever in the tip commit (nothing had been pushed or built on top of it yet), fixed by redacting the two occurrences in the file directly and amending the tip commit rather than needing another history rewrite. Re-ran the full reachable-blob scan afterward with zero matches.

**Not yet done:** the force-push. Christer needs to run it himself (`git push origin main --force`) - I don't have push access. Worth flagging to him plainly: this only helps if nobody else has cloned the repo or has a fork - his own local clone (this one) will match automatically since it's the same working directory the rewrite ran against, but any other machine or NAS copy would need a fresh clone afterward, and existing forks (if any) would keep the old history regardless.

## Recognize "A" recording kind and "I" (interior camera) direction (this session)

Christer, following up on the /Config/version.bin note: "notes. I have found that the camera F/R also can have I, i guess for internal camera. There is also a new mode 'A' i dont know what that stands for" - two separate, real gaps in the code, both confirmed by checking the actual parsing logic rather than guessing.

**"A" recording kind.** `RecordingId.kind`/`Recording.kind` just read a single character (`value[16]` / `id.rsplit("_",1)[1]`), so "A" was already handled fine structurally wherever those are used - no crash risk. The actual blocker was `cli/bv_download.py`'s `--mode` flag, which hardcoded `ALL_KINDS = frozenset({"N","E","M","P"})` and rejected anything else, so `bv-download --mode A` would have errored outright, and `--mode all` silently excluded "A" recordings. Fixed: added "A" to `ALL_KINDS`, updated the `argparse.ArgumentTypeError` message and `--mode` metavar/help. Added matching `is_a` properties to both `RecordingId` (`archive/recording_id.py`) and `Recording` (`domain/recording.py`) alongside the existing `is_normal`/`is_event`/`is_manual`/`is_parking`, each with a docstring noting the meaning is unconfirmed - Christer doesn't know what it stands for either, so it's documented as observed-but-unidentified rather than guessed at (Auto? Alert? - deliberately not speculating in the docs).

**"I" interior camera direction.** This one was a real correctness bug, not just a missing option. `domain/vod_entry.py`'s `VodEntry.recording` property only stripped a trailing `F` or `R` off the filename stem to compute the shared recording-grouping ID (`stem.endswith(("F", "R"))`) - an interior file (`..._NI.mp4`) fell through unstripped, so instead of grouping under the same recording as its front/rear siblings, it formed its own bogus, disconnected "recording" entry with a garbled kind (`"NI"` instead of `"N"`). Fixed by adding `"I"` to that endswith check, and added a matching `is_interior` property (mirroring `is_front`/`is_rear`) plus `Recording.interior` (mirroring `.front`/`.rear`). Checked whether this bug also existed on the archive/downloaded-file side (`archive/recording_id.py`'s `RecordingId.parse()`) - it doesn't, since that parser only ever takes a fixed 17-character slice ending at the kind letter and was never looking at the direction suffix at all, so downloaded-archive grouping was unaffected; only the camera-VOD-listing side (used before download) had the bug.

Also added `Asset.INTERIOR`/`Asset.INTERIOR_THUMBNAIL` (`archive/asset.py`) and `("I.mp4", Asset.INTERIOR)`/`("I.thm", Asset.INTERIOR_THUMBNAIL)` entries to `ArchiveReader.ASSETS` (`archive/archive_reader.py`), so a downloaded interior file gets correctly classified and shows up as its own column in `bv-ls` automatically (via `Asset.display_order()`, no separate wiring needed) instead of going undetected. The `.thm` interior-thumbnail suffix is inferred from the F/R pattern, not confirmed - flagged as such in a code comment.

**Deliberately out of scope:** actually processing interior video anywhere downstream - `bv-export`'s trip building, concatenation, and `--stitch` layouts all still only look at `Asset.FRONT`/`Asset.REAR` and are untouched. This was a recognition/correctness fix (get grouped and classified right), not a new "third camera" feature (download-by-default already happened before this fix too, since `bv-download` doesn't filter by direction at all - only the *grouping* was broken). Building real interior-camera export support would be a much larger, separate feature.

**Tests.** New `tests/blackvue/domain/test_vod_entry.py` (front/rear/interior suffix detection, recording-id grouping across all three plus a non-direction-suffixed `.gps` file) and `tests/blackvue/domain/test_recording.py` (`.interior`, `.is_a`) - neither module had any tests before this. New `tests/blackvue/archive/test_recording_id.py` (kind letters including `is_a`, mutual exclusivity) - also previously untested directly. Extended `tests/blackvue/archive/test_archive_reader.py` with an interior video+thumbnail detection case. Fixed `tests/blackvue/cli/test_bv_download.py`'s `test_parse_mode_all`, which hardcoded the old 4-kind set and would have broken the moment "A" was added; added `test_parse_mode_accepts_a`.

**Verification.** `ast.parse()` on all changed/new files. No pytest available in this sandbox (Python 3.10, no network) - verified every changed code path directly instead: stubbed `tomllib` to import `cli/bv_download.py`, then manually exercised `VodEntry`/`Recording`/`RecordingId` front/rear/interior/kind behavior, `ArchiveReader` against real temp-directory fixtures (front+interior video+thumbnail), and `parse_mode`/`ALL_KINDS` including the rejection-message wording - all matched what the new tests assert. Not run against a real camera or real pytest; the interior `.thm` suffix and "A"'s actual meaning remain unconfirmed pending real hardware.

## Official BlackVue filename spec found - corrects/extends the A-kind and I-direction work above (this session, no code change)

Christer linked BlackVue Australia's support article on video file naming: https://support.blackvue.com.au/hc/en-us/articles/13301776266895-Video-File-Naming - read it and it both confirms and complicates what was just built. Recorded here for reference; explicitly **not acting on any of this yet** - Christer's call: "just remember this in a file. We handle it when it comes up in the video listing."

**Real format:** `YYYYMMDD_HHMMSS_[Recording Type][Recording Direction][Other].mp4` - three positional letters, not two. Example: `20250722_110221_NF.mp4` = Normal type, Front direction, blank/original-resolution Other.

**"A" confirmed:** Recording Type `A` = **Acceleration** (event when hard acceleration is detected). The code and the WORKING_CONTEXT entry above currently document this as "unknown meaning" - that's now known to be wrong, just not corrected yet.

**"I" is confirmed but overloaded by position:**
- As a **direction** letter (2nd position): `I` = **IR Camera**. This matches what was just built (`VodEntry.is_interior`, `Recording.interior`, `Asset.INTERIOR`) and Christer's own guess.
- As a **Recording Type** letter (1st position): `I` = **Parking Impact** (an event recorded in parking mode) - a completely different thing, distinguished only by which position it's in. Nothing recognizes `I` as a recording *type* right now - `ALL_KINDS` in `cli/bv_download.py` only has `{N,E,M,P,A}`.

**Full official Recording Type table**, for when any of these actually show up: `N`=Normal, `P`=Parking Motion/Time-lapse, `M`=Manual, `E`=Driving Impact, `I`=Parking Impact, `O`=Overspeed, `A`=Acceleration, `T`=Hard Cornering, `B`=Hard Braking, `R`=Geofence-Enter (Fleet only), `X`=Geofence-Exit (Fleet only), `G`=Geofence-Pass (Fleet only), `D`=Drowsiness (DMS only), `L`=Distraction (DMS only), `Y`=Seatbelt (DMS only), `F`=Undetected (DMS only). Most of the Fleet/DMS ones almost certainly don't apply to Christer's DR900S-2CH.

**A real bug this surfaces, not yet fixed:** the format's third, optional `[Other]` character - `S` (low-resolution file) or blank (original resolution) - isn't handled anywhere. `VodEntry.is_front`/`is_rear`/`is_interior`/`recording` (`domain/vod_entry.py`) all do a bare `stem.endswith("F"/"R"/"I")` check, so a low-res file like `20250722_110221_NFS.mp4` would currently fail every one of those checks (`is_front` returns `False`) and get grouped under a wrong recording ID (`recording` wouldn't strip the trailing `S`). This predates this session's A/I work - it's a pre-existing gap the format spec just made visible, not something introduced by the recent changes.

**Deliberately not fixed yet** - Christer's explicit choice, to handle when any of this actually shows up in a real video listing rather than build ahead of what's been observed on real hardware.

## Idea: read recording segment length from config.ini to inform trip gap resolution (this session, no code change)

Christer: "ok, in the future i think we will have to check recording length in config.ini to adjust for trips gap resolution." Recorded for later - not acted on now.

**The idea:** BlackVue cameras record in fixed-length segments (commonly 1 minute, but configurable per camera/firmware) rather than one continuous file - `config.ini` should have a field for this somewhere (exact key not yet confirmed; Christer hasn't shared a real `config.ini` dump with this project yet - see the "get the complete file" exchange earlier this session for how to pull one). Trip-detection's gap logic (`TripBuilder`, `--max-gap`, the "fuzzy gap tolerance" and "duration-aware trip gap calculation" work from earlier in this project's history) currently reasons about gaps between consecutive recordings without reading this value from the camera's actual configuration. If a camera is set to a non-default segment length, the trip-gap heuristics might currently be tuned around an assumption that doesn't hold for that camera.

**Follow-up, still no code change:** Christer wondered whether the camera might write a per-recording config snapshot (e.g. a file literally named `20260801_095509_N_config.ini`) rather than one global file, given how much per-recording metadata already exists (`.gps`, `.3gf`, now `.thm`). Searched for this - found no evidence it exists. BlackVue's own documentation and `BlackVueClient.config()` (`core/blackvue_client.py`) both point at a single fixed path, `/Config/config.ini` - one file per camera, not one per recording. Usefully, changing settings via the BlackVue Viewer/App **reformats the SD card and wipes all recordings** (confirmed via BlackVue's own product manuals) - so there's no scenario where recordings currently on a card were made under a *different* segment-length setting than what's in the card's current `config.ini`. Reading the single global file is sufficient; no per-recording lookup is needed.

**The actual goal, restated by Christer:** "we need to know the recording length set in config.ini so we can adjust our max gap for trips" - i.e. `TripBuilder`'s `--max-gap` threshold should be informed by the camera's real configured segment length rather than assuming a fixed default, since a camera set to (say) 3-minute segments instead of 1-minute would have larger natural gaps between consecutive recording start-times, and the current gap heuristics don't know that.

**Not scoped or investigated yet** - would need a real `config.ini` (see the "get the complete file" exchange earlier this session for how to pull one) to confirm the actual field name/format for segment length, and a design decision on exactly how it should adjust `--max-gap` (e.g. read-and-use directly vs. only override the default when the configured value differs from what's currently assumed) before touching `TripBuilder` at all.

## RecordTime-derived --max-gap default: implemented (this session, direct follow-up)

Direct continuation of the "RecordTime found" entry above. Christer confirmed `RecordTime=1` means literally 1 minute, then asked the real design question: "how would you implement it, it needs to be recorded in a file that belongs to the recording or any previous recording if it hasnt changed."

**Design conversation, in order:**

1. **Whole config.ini vs just RecordTime.** Asked whether we'd ever need other fields later (future-proofing) vs. just the one value now. Christer shared his actual `config.ini` to settle it - it has `[Wifi]`/`[Cloud]` sections with real SSIDs in plaintext (`ap_ssid`, `sta_ssid`, `sta2_ssid`, `sta3_ssid`) and "encrypted" passwords of unverified strength (64 hex chars each - plausibly real AES output, but BlackVue's actual scheme was never confirmed, and the SSIDs alone are already sensitive regardless). Given this session started with a real camera-IP leak to GitHub, decided: **whitelist only** - parse `config.ini` with `configparser`, extract `RecordTime` and nothing else, never persist the raw file or response text anywhere. The pasted real file itself was never written to disk or used as test fixture data - all tests use fully synthetic values.

2. **The `--max-gap` formula.** Proposed `max_gap = max(5min-default, N × RecordTime)` for some tunable N (tolerate N dropped segments). Christer instead proposed the simpler `RecordTime + 10s` directly - checked the math: one fully-dropped segment leaves a gap of almost exactly one `RecordTime` between the recording before and after it (the "before" recording's own real duration is ~RecordTime, so `next.timestamp - (previous.timestamp + duration) ≈ RecordTime`), so `RecordTime + 10s` bridges exactly one dropped segment with a small margin, no arbitrary N needed. Flagged two real behavior changes this implies for his own footage (smaller than today's flat 5-minute default for his 3-minute camera; only tolerates one dropped segment, not two) - Christer: "No missing" (no floor, no extra headroom - accept both).

**Discovered mid-implementation: this was already half-built.** Before writing new code, found `archive/configuration.py` (`Configuration` class) and `Archive.configuration()` already existed from the very start of the project (`df05bec`/`c544231`/`a71e0e6`/`645a578`, long before this session) - `Configuration.maximum_gap` already computed exactly `record_time + TOLERANCE(10)`, and `Archive.configuration(recording)` already did the "most recent snapshot at or before this recording" lookup by `RecordingId` comparison. But `Archive._read_configurations()` was commented out/stubbed to `[]`, nothing ever wrote a snapshot, and - critically - the scaffold as originally written expected a full raw `<recording_id>.config.ini` copy on disk (`Configuration.__init__` parsed a whole file with `configparser` when given a path). Finishing it as originally scaffolded would have copied Christer's Wi-Fi/cloud credentials into the archive on every download - exactly what the whitelist decision above was meant to prevent. Nothing had leaked (never wired up), but reported this to Christer before touching it further.

**What was actually built**, keeping the pre-existing math/lookup and changing only what gets persisted:

- `archive/configuration.py`: added `RECORD_TIME_SUFFIX = ".record_time.txt"`, `parse_record_time_seconds(text)` (the only function allowed to see raw config.ini text - `ConfigParser(interpolation=None)`, extracts `[Tab1]/RecordTime` only, raises `ConfigurationError` if missing/invalid; `interpolation=None` so a stray `%` in an unrelated field like a Wi-Fi password can never break parsing), `write_record_time_snapshot()`/`read_record_time_snapshot()` (plain `"<seconds>\n"` text file, same format `.duration.txt` already uses). `Configuration.__init__`'s raw-path branch now calls `parse_record_time_seconds()` instead of inlining the parse (kept for API completeness, though the archive-side flow below never actually uses it - it always passes `record_time=` directly). `Configuration.recording_id` now strips `RECORD_TIME_SUFFIX` instead of the old `.config.ini`.
- `archive/archive.py`: `_read_configurations()` un-stubbed - globs `*.record_time.txt`, skips any that fail to parse (one corrupt snapshot can't break lookups for the rest), builds each via `Configuration(path, record_time=<int>)` (never the raw-text-parsing path), sorted by `recording_id`.
- `cli/bv_download.py`: new `_capture_record_time()`, called once per run (skipped on `--dry-run` or an empty recording list) right after the confirm/abort check. Fetches `client.config()`, extracts RecordTime, compares to the archive's most recent existing snapshot (a plain glob + sort, not a full `Archive()` construction - avoids reading every recording just for this check), writes a new one only if it differs. Anchored to `recordings[0].id` (the earliest recording this run is considering, chronologically first per `parse_vod()`'s own ordering) - correct provenance because changing a setting on the camera reformats/wipes the SD card, so every recording still present when `config.ini` is fetched was necessarily made under that same RecordTime. Best-effort: any exception (endpoint missing on older firmware, transient network failure, unparseable response) is caught broadly, reported via `-v` only, and never fails the download run - this only ever informs `bv-export`'s own default.
- `cli/bv_export.py`: new `_default_max_gap(archive, recordings, interval)`, used when `--max-gap` isn't given explicitly (unchanged: an explicit `--max-gap` always wins outright). For a bounded range (`--from`/`--until`/`--timestamp`), uses whichever configuration was active for the *earliest* recording actually touching the interval (`Archive.configuration()`'s existing lookup). For a full-archive export (no range at all), deliberately uses the *latest* known configuration instead - "what the camera is set to now" is more useful than whatever the very first recording in the archive's history happened to be made under. Falls back to the existing `DEFAULT_MAX_GAP` (5 min) if nothing in `recordings` touches the interval, or if the archive has no snapshots yet (the pre-existing `Archive.configuration()` fallback already returns exactly 300s with its own one-time printed warning in the no-snapshots-at-all case, so only the "nothing touches the interval" case needed a separate check here). Deliberately uses `configuration.record_time` alone, not `configuration.maximum_gap` - `TripBuilder` already adds its own `gap_tolerance` (default 10s, same value as `Configuration.TOLERANCE`) on top of `max_gap`, so using `maximum_gap` here would have double-counted that 10s margin.

**Verified directly** (no pytest in this sandbox, same limitation as all prior sessions) - `parse_record_time_seconds` against a synthetic config.ini and several malformed ones; write/read snapshot round-trip and confirmed the raw config text never appears in the written file; `Archive._read_configurations()`/`Archive.configuration()` against a synthetic two-era archive (3-minute recordings before a point, 1-minute after), confirming correct era lookup and the no-snapshot-yet fallback; `_capture_record_time` against a fake client covering first-write, unchanged-noop, changed-rewrite, broken-config, and raised-exception cases, and confirmed a Wi-Fi-credential-bearing fake config never leaves any trace on disk; `_default_max_gap` against the same synthetic two-era archive for a bounded range in each era, the full-archive-uses-latest case, and both fallback cases; and an actual end-to-end `bv_export()` run (real ffmpeg-generated video files, no `--max-gap` passed) proving a 90-second gap splits into two trips when the archive's RecordTime snapshot says 1 minute, but stays one trip when it says 3 minutes - confirming the derived default genuinely reaches `TripBuilder`, not just correct in isolation.

**Tests:** new `tests/blackvue/archive/test_configuration.py` and `tests/blackvue/archive/test_archive.py` (neither existed before), extended `tests/blackvue/cli/test_bv_download.py` (`_capture_record_time`) and `tests/blackvue/cli/test_bv_export.py` (`_default_max_gap`, plus the end-to-end split/no-split case). All test fixtures use synthetic config.ini content only - no real Wi-Fi/cloud values anywhere in the repo.

**Docs:** `docs/man/bv-download.md` (new paragraph on the RecordTime snapshot capture, best-effort framing) and `docs/man/bv-export.md` (`--max-gap` row updated to describe the derived default and 5-minute fallback).

**Pre-existing rough edge, not introduced by this work, not fixed:** `Archive.configuration()`'s missing-configuration warning ("archive contains no configuration snapshot") prints even when the archive *does* have snapshots but none apply yet (a recording predating every snapshot) - technically misleading wording for that specific case, harmless, left as-is since it predates this session and wasn't part of what was asked.

## scan_blackvue_endpoints.py: redact config.ini credentials in the preview (this session, direct follow-up)

Christer, after the RecordTime work above: "Will this change our scan_blackvue_endpoints.py script" - no, that script shares no code with what was just built, but checking it to answer surfaced a real, separate gap: it already probes `/Config/config.ini` and prints a 300-byte preview of the raw response with no special-casing, and this script's whole purpose is contributors pasting its output into a public GitHub issue. For Christer's own file `[Tab1]` alone runs past 300 bytes, so the preview happens to cut off before reaching `[Wifi]`/`[Cloud]`, but that's incidental to one file's field layout, not a guarantee for other models. Flagged it; Christer: "yes, filter out wifi passwords or say secret."

**Fixed:** new `redact_config_ini(text)` in `scripts/scan_blackvue_endpoints.py` - a regex (`_SECRET_KEY_LINE`) matching any `key=value` line whose key contains "pw", "pass"/"password", "secret", or "token" (case-insensitive), replacing the value with `[secret]` while keeping the key name visible. Matches by key *name*, not by value shape, so it isn't tied to Christer's own `ap_pw`/`sta_pw`/`sta2_pw`/`sta3_pw` field names specifically - should generalize to other models/firmware that name the field differently. Deliberately broad on purpose - an occasional false-positive redaction of some harmless field is the safe failure mode here, not the other way round. Network *names* (`ap_ssid`, `sta_ssid`, etc.) are left visible - only credential-looking values are redacted, matching exactly what Christer asked for.

Wired in at the `main()` print loop: only for the `/Config/config.ini` path, the raw body is decoded, redacted, and re-encoded *before* `preview()` ever sees it - not filtered after truncation/binary-detection, so there's no path where a credential could slip through some other branch of `preview()`'s own logic. Every other endpoint's preview is unchanged.

Extended the module's own docstring privacy note (which already covered `blackvue_vod.cgi`'s recording-timestamp privacy angle) to mention this.

**Verification:** direct unit checks of `redact_config_ini()` against synthetic config.ini text (all four real field names, generic alternate naming like `WifiPassword`/`PASSWORD`/`SecretToken`, a value truncated mid-string to simulate the script's own `READ_BYTES` cutoff, and confirming SSIDs remain visible while only password-shaped values are redacted) - all passed. Then a full end-to-end run: spun up a local `http.server` on `127.0.0.1` serving synthetic (never real) config.ini content including fake Wi-Fi/cloud passwords, ran the actual `scan_blackvue_endpoints.py` script as a subprocess against it, and confirmed the real passwords never appear anywhere in stdout while `[secret]` and the SSIDs do. No real camera reachable from this sandbox to test against.

## bv-gps: add --host to skip bv-config for a raw IP (this session, direct follow-up)

Christer, after asking how to loop `scan_blackvue_endpoints.py` over a list of IPs, then asked how to run `bv-gps` on the same list. It couldn't - `bv-gps <id>` only ever looked up a `bv-config`'d camera's `.cfg` file (tried endpoint by endpoint), with no way to hand it a bare IP the way the scan script already can. Confirmed and offered to add `--host`; Christer: "yes."

**Fixed:** `id` and `--host` are now a required, mutually exclusive pair in `cli/bv_gps.py`'s argparse setup (`id` given `nargs="?"` so it can share a `mutually_exclusive_group(required=True)` with `--host` - verified this actually works as intended: `id` alone, `--host` alone, neither, and both all produce the expected argparse behavior/exit codes). `--host HOST[:PORT]` builds a single synthetic `Endpoint(name=host, address=host)` and calls the existing `connect()` with just that one candidate - skips `config_path`/`load_camera_config` entirely, so no `--config-dir` lookup happens at all on that path.

**Self-caught bug, fixed before committing:** the existing "no GPS fix" message referenced `config.name` - a variable that only exists on the `id`-based path (the `--host` path never builds a `config` object at all). A `--host` run hitting a zero-fix reading would have raised a bare `NameError` instead of printing a clean message. Fixed by using `endpoint.name` instead (defined on both paths regardless of which one was taken - resolves to the configured endpoint's own name on the `id` path, or the bare host string on the `--host` path). Caught by writing out the "no fix" scenario as a test case, not by inspection alone.

**Tests:** extended `tests/blackvue/cli/test_bv_gps.py` - `parse_args` coverage for `--host` alone, `host:port`, and both required/mutually-exclusive error cases; `_run()` coverage confirming `--host` never touches `load_camera_config`/`config_path` (a monkeypatch that raises `AssertionError` if either is called), builds exactly one synthetic `Endpoint` with the raw host as both name and address, reports `CameraUnreachableError` cleanly, and - explicitly regression-testing the bug just caught - the no-fix path with `--host` prints cleanly instead of raising.

**Docs:** `docs/man/bv-gps.md` - synopsis, description, ARGUMENTS/OPTIONS tables, and two new EXAMPLES (`--host` alone, and looping it over a file of IPs) all updated.

**Verification:** `ast.parse()` on both changed files. No pytest in this sandbox - ran `parse_args()` directly against all four `id`/`--host` combinations (confirmed the exact expected argparse error text and exit codes), and exercised `_run()` directly with a stubbed `connect()` for the success, unreachable, and no-fix-with-`--host` cases (the last one specifically to confirm the `NameError` bug was actually fixed, not just theoretically).

Christer ran `scan_blackvue_endpoints.py` against his own Elite 10 for the first time (previously this project only had one Elite 10 firmware image analyzed offline, never a live camera) and pasted the output.
