## scan_blackvue_endpoints.py: also probe blackvue_live.cgi's direction=I and direction=O

Christer: "our script scan_blackvue_endpoints.py should also test direction I and 0" - the script only ever probed `blackvue_live.cgi?direction=F`/`direction=R`, missing two plausible variants: `I` (the interior-camera letter this project already recognizes elsewhere - `RecordingId`/`Recording`, thumbnails, task #314), and a fourth value for a channel beyond F/R/I.

**Fixed**, `scripts/scan_blackvue_endpoints.py`: added both as new `CANDIDATE_ENDPOINTS` entries and `STREAMING_PATHS` members (same bounded-read handling as the existing F/R live-view entries - these are continuous MJPEG streams too, if the camera answers at all). Placed immediately after `direction=F`/`direction=R` rather than down with the rest of the unconfirmed/Elite-10-only group the module's own ordering comment otherwise follows - documented as a deliberate exception right there, since keeping every direction of the same endpoint together for easy comparison matters more here than the confirmed/unconfirmed ordering convention.

Follow-up correction: the fourth value was first implemented as the digit `direction=0` (a guess at how a single-lens camera might address its own live view). Christer: "Not `?direction=0` it should be `?direction=O`" - the letter O, not zero. Fixed throughout (`CANDIDATE_ENDPOINTS`, `STREAMING_PATHS`, the ordering-exception comment).

Christer then ran the updated script against his own camera and reported something more important than the typo: F, R, I, and O *all* came back `HTTP 200` with the exact same `Content-Type` (`multipart/x-mixed-replace; boundary=--ptaboundary`) - "Strangely the scan says... only F and R are valid for that camera," i.e. he knows from the hardware itself that it's a 2-channel camera, yet the scan's Found/Valid columns marked all four as equally good. Conclusion: this firmware's `blackvue_live.cgi` doesn't validate the `direction` value at all - it streams *something* regardless of what's passed, so a `Valid` HTTP 200 here only proves the path answered, not that the channel is real. Four identical-looking 200s for F/R/I/O is itself the signal the parameter is being ignored, not four confirmed channels. Documented this directly in the script: a caveat comment above `CANDIDATE_ENDPOINTS` explaining the finding, plus a pointer from each of the I/O entries' own descriptions back to it, and a note that telling real channels apart needs actually watching each stream's content (this script only reads/discards a short prefix, per its own safety docstring), not just the HTTP status.

**Verification:** no camera available to actually probe from this sandbox (same as every prior change to this script - see task #311/329-337's own entries) - Christer's own real scan above is what caught both the O-vs-0 typo and the direction-ignored finding. Confirmed via direct import that `/blackvue_live.cgi?direction=O` (not `=0`) appears in both `CANDIDATE_ENDPOINTS` and `STREAMING_PATHS`, and that `--help`/`py_compile` still run cleanly. No existing test file covers this script (it's a standalone contributor diagnostic tool against real hardware, not exercised by the test suite).

## scan_blackvue_endpoints.py: make Valid mean genuinely streaming, not just HTTP 200

Follow-up to the direction=I/O finding above. Christer, after confirming the theory by actually trying to watch the streams himself: "I never get a stream to watch for I and O." Asked whether the script should be made accurate about this instead of just documenting it as a caveat - "yes, we want the test to be accurate."

**Fixed**, `scripts/scan_blackvue_endpoints.py`: `probe()` now, for any `path in STREAMING_PATHS` that got a valid HTTP status, calls a new `_confirm_live_stream()` after the initial bounded read - it extracts the multipart boundary token from the Content-Type header (new `_extract_boundary()`, handling BlackVue's own boundary value already carrying a leading `--`) and keeps reading (still bounded - new `STREAM_VERIFY_MAX_BYTES = 65536`, and still subject to the same per-request `--timeout`) until either that boundary token appears a *second* time in the body (proof the server sent a second frame - genuinely live) or the byte/time budget runs out (unconfirmed). A single boundary proves nothing on its own - a dead/placeholder response can carry one too - only a second one appearing is real evidence the server is still pushing.

New `is_valid_result(path, status, stream_confirmed)` replaces `is_valid_status()` at every call site that renders a path's Valid-ness (the summary table, the per-endpoint detail section, the final valid-count line): unchanged (pure HTTP<400) for ordinary endpoints, but for a `STREAMING_PATHS` member it also requires `stream_confirmed`. `probe()`'s return shape grew a 5th element (`stream_confirmed: bool | None` - None whenever it wasn't applicable/attempted, never a silent False standing in for "didn't check"), so `results` tuples and every place that unpacks them (`print_summary_table()`, the main loop, the two summary counts) were updated to match. The per-endpoint detail section for a streaming path now prints an explicit "confirmed live" / "no second frame arrived - looks like a dead/placeholder response" line instead of the old blanket HTTP-status-only Valid message. The summary table's detail column gets the same "stream confirmed"/"no second frame seen" annotation, deliberately placed right after the HTTP status and before Content-Type - Content-Type alone (`multipart/x-mixed-replace; boundary=--ptaboundary`) is long enough that `_shorten()`'s 60-char cap would otherwise have silently cut the new annotation off before it was ever visible (caught by testing this, not by inspection).

**Verification:** no pytest/real camera in this sandbox, and this script has no existing test file (see its own entry above). Verified instead with a small throwaway local `http.server` fake at `127.0.0.1` simulating exactly the real-world shape Christer described: `direction=F`/`direction=R` genuinely send four distinct multipart frames in a row; `direction=I`/`direction=O` send one single large frame (deliberately >2048 bytes, since a synthetic short-then-hang response turned out to just time out the *initial* bounded read before ever reaching the new logic - not realistic given the real camera answers 200 within the normal timeout) and then go silent without closing. Ran the real script against it end to end: F/R came back `Valid: yes (confirmed live - a second frame arrived)`, I/O came back `Valid: no (HTTP 200, but no second frame arrived...)` - exactly matching Christer's real-world report - and the summary table's Found/Valid columns and detail annotation matched too. `py_compile` passes; fake server and its throwaway script deleted after verification, nothing left in the repo from it.

### Follow-up bug: naive boundary counting false-positived on Christer's real camera

Christer ran the fixed script against his actual camera and reported it was "Still wrong" - all four of F/R/I/O came back `stream confirmed`, even though he'd already confirmed "I never get a stream to watch for I and O." The fake-server verification above hadn't caught this because that fake server, for I/O, just went silent after one frame with no proper MIME closing - not what a real camera most likely does.

**Root cause:** a standards-conformant multipart response, even one carrying just a single static frame, ends with a *closing* delimiter line (`boundary + "--"`), which itself contains the plain boundary token as a substring. The original `data.count(boundary) >= 2` therefore counted 2 for a genuinely single, dead frame - one opening delimiter, one closing one - and wrongly called it confirmed-live. The real camera's I/O responses most likely close their single frame properly rather than just trailing off; the fake server didn't reproduce that shape, so the bug sailed through the first round of verification.

**Fixed:** new `_count_part_delimiters(data, boundary)` counts only occurrences of the boundary token *not* immediately followed by another `-` - i.e. genuine "start of a new part" delimiters, excluding the closing `boundary + "--"` terminator. `_confirm_live_stream()` now calls this instead of a raw `.count()`. Re-verified with the same fake-server harness, this time with I/O sending a single frame *followed by a proper closing delimiter* (`boundary + "--\r\n"`) - the exact shape the bug depended on: F/R still correctly `stream confirmed`, I/O now correctly `no second frame seen`. Also unit-verified `_count_part_delimiters()` directly against three byte-string cases (single terminated frame -> 1, two real frames -> 2, two real frames plus a trailing terminator -> 2, not 3) before rerunning the full script.

Caveat worth being upfront about: this fix is based on a hypothesis about how the real firmware closes a dead direction's response (a proper MIME terminator), inferred from Christer's bug report rather than a byte-level capture of the actual camera traffic. It's the most standards-conformant explanation and the fake-server repro matches his exact report, but without a packet capture or another real-camera scan to confirm, there's some chance the real cause is subtly different and this fix is correct for the wrong reason. Flagged rather than presented as fully closed.

### Second follow-up: the delimiter-exclusion fix overcorrected - abandoned boundary parsing entirely

Christer ran it again: this time F/R/I/O *all four* came back `no second frame seen` - including F/R, which he can genuinely watch. The delimiter-exclusion fix above had overcorrected.

**Likely root cause:** the fix assumed this camera's firmware only ever appends `--` to a *closing* delimiter (standard MIME convention). Real embedded/IP-camera MJPEG implementations are notoriously inconsistent about this - a plausible alternative is that *every* per-frame delimiter on this firmware carries a trailing `--`, not just the final one, which would make the "exclude anything followed by `-`" check wrongly exclude every genuine frame boundary too, not just the true closing one. Two rounds of real-camera failures against two different assumptions about the exact wire format was a strong enough signal that reverse-engineering this camera's specific MIME framing from bug reports alone wasn't a reliable path forward.

**Redesigned rather than patched again:** dropped boundary/MIME parsing entirely. New `_confirm_live_stream(sock, resp, *, window_seconds)` doesn't look at the stream's framing at all - it just asks whether new bytes keep arriving well after the connection opened. It reads for up to `window_seconds` (tied to the probe's own `--timeout`, so a wider `--timeout` gets a proportionally longer observation window) and marks the stream confirmed only if data is still arriving in the *second half* of that window - proof the server is still actively pushing, not just answering once and holding the connection open. A single burst that arrives entirely in the first half and then goes silent (the I/O case) is unconfirmed; frames that keep landing throughout the whole window (F/R) are confirmed - true regardless of whatever delimiter convention, terminator style, or vendor quirk that particular firmware uses. New `STREAM_VERIFY_POLL_TIMEOUT = 0.25` (short per-read timeout so the polling loop stays responsive to the overall deadline) and `STREAM_VERIFY_MAX_BYTES` raised to 262144 (memory safety cap only now, not part of the confirmation logic itself).

**A real bug caught along the way:** the first working version of this crashed with `AttributeError: 'NoneType' object has no attribute 'gettimeout'` on the very first streaming path. Root cause: `probe()` sends `Connection: close`, and `http.client.HTTPConnection.getresponse()` reacts to a will-close response by calling its own `self.close()` immediately - which sets `connection.sock` to `None` - transferring real ownership of the socket to `resp.fp` instead. `_confirm_live_stream()` was trying to read `conn.sock.gettimeout()` after that had already happened. Fixed by capturing `sock = conn.sock` right after `conn.request()`, before `getresponse()` ever runs, and passing that saved reference through instead of reaching into `conn` later.

**Verification:** unit-verified the crash fix and design shift with the same fake-server harness, now covering four shapes in one run: F (standard framing, no trailing `--`), R (nonstandard - every delimiter carries a trailing `--`, the shape suspected of breaking the previous fix), I (single frame, never terminated, then silence), and O (single frame, properly MIME-terminated, then silence). All four now report correctly: F/R confirmed live, I/O not - the R case in particular proves the new approach doesn't care about delimiter style at all, unlike either of the two previous attempts. `py_compile` passes. Same caveat as before still applies: verified against a fake server built from Christer's bug reports, not a packet capture of the real camera - but this design is structurally immune to the specific failure mode both earlier versions hit (guessing a vendor's exact MIME framing), so a third framing-related surprise is much less likely than the previous two were.

### Third follow-up: the time-based version *also* failed on the real camera - actual root cause found and fixed

Christer ran it again: F/R/I/O all four came back `no second frame seen` again - including F/R. Three attempts in a row had now passed every local fake-server test and then failed on the real camera, which was reason enough to stop guessing a fourth heuristic blind and instead reproduce the failure locally with a fake server that more closely matched real network conditions (the previous fake servers all wrote their whole response over loopback near-instantly - nothing had yet tested data arriving *slower* than the poll loop could catch it).

**Reproduced and found the actual root cause:** a fake server trickling small chunks (200 bytes every 0.3s - well under `READ_BYTES`/`STREAM_VERIFY_POLL_TIMEOUT`'s implied rate) reproduced "no second frame seen" even for a stream that was genuinely, continuously live. Tracing it down: CPython's `socket.SocketIO.readinto()` sets a `self._timeout_occurred` flag the first time a `recv()` call times out - and once set, *every* read after that on the same socket-file-object wrapper immediately raises `OSError("cannot read from timed out object")`, forever, regardless of whether data has since arrived. It never resets. The previous design's poll loop (`while ...: try: resp.read(...) except timeout: continue`) is fundamentally incompatible with this: the very first poll that doesn't catch data in time - which is essentially guaranteed for any real, non-instant stream, since frame arrival almost never lines up perfectly inside one 0.25s window - permanently kills the ability to read anything else from that connection. That's why *every* direction reported dead: not a framing problem at all, a Python stdlib footgun in the retry-after-timeout pattern itself.

**Fixed with a two-phase, non-retrying design**, replacing `_confirm_live_stream()` entirely:

- Phase 1 (drain): reads (discarding) with a short per-read timeout until the *first* timeout or EOF - deliberately spending the one read this socket-file-object gets before the poisoning above kicks in, since this reader isn't touched again afterward anyway. If this drain alone spans past half the observation window (capped explicitly, since a genuinely fast live stream could otherwise keep succeeding forever and never hit a timeout at all - a second real bug caught during testing, see below), that alone is proof of a live stream and phase 2 is skipped.
- Phase 2 (wait and check): sleeps out the rest of the window, then does exactly one read - directly on the raw socket via `sock.recv()`, not through `resp`, since `resp`'s reader is already poisoned from phase 1 and the poisoning lives on that specific file-object wrapper, not on the underlying OS socket itself. One successful read is proof of new data; a timeout or closed-socket error is not.

Also fixed an intermediate false positive found while building this: a naive "sleep then one read via `resp`" version (without phase 1's drain) returned a false "confirmed" for a *dead* endpoint whose one-time response was bigger than `READ_BYTES` (2048) - `probe()`'s initial read only consumes the first 2048 bytes, and the rest sits already-delivered and waiting; the "one more read after sleeping" then returned those stale leftover bytes instantly, misread as fresh data. A real camera's first MJPEG frame is easily bigger than 2048 bytes, so this would have misfired on real hardware too - phase 1's explicit drain step exists specifically to rule this out before phase 2 ever runs.

**Verification:** three fake-server scenarios, each exercising a case a previous attempt got wrong: a dead endpoint whose single response exceeds 2048 bytes (would have false-positived the sleep-then-read version above); a genuinely live stream trickling slower than one read's worth per poll interval (the real repro of this whole bug); and a genuinely live stream sending continuously and indefinitely, never closing (would have infinite-looped phase 1 without the explicit half-window cap - caught by testing, not inspection). All three now report correctly (`confirmed=False`, `True`, `True`) via direct calls to `probe()`, and a full end-to-end run of `main()` against the slow-trickle fake camera produces the expected `Valid: yes (confirmed live...)` output with a readable phase-by-phase trace. `_confirm_live_stream()`'s trace is now also printed unconditionally for every streaming path (not just on a "no" result) - this check has been wrong three times in a row against real hardware despite passing local tests each time, so Christer's next real-camera run will show the actual phase 1/phase 2 timeline directly rather than one more unverifiable yes/no.

### Fourth follow-up: `stream_confirmed` isn't proof of a real distinct channel either - documentation-only, no code change

Christer scanned a different (3-channel) camera: this time F/R/I/O *all four* reported `stream confirmed` - a clean pass by the check's own logic - but "there is no video on /blackvue_live.cgi?direction=O" when he actually looked. Not a bug in the fixed check above: it correctly proved bytes keep arriving continuously for that URL, which is all it was ever designed to prove. The gap is in what "confirmed" gets read as - proof of a genuine, distinct camera channel - versus what it actually is - proof the endpoint isn't a dead/static placeholder. A camera that ignores an unrecognized `direction` value and just keeps streaming *something* (most likely aliasing one of its real feeds) passes the liveness check without being a real channel.

Asked Christer whether to (a) just document this more clearly, (b) build actual content-comparison across directions to detect aliasing, or (c) leave it - chose (a): documentation only, no logic change. Updated three places to say this plainly rather than implying "confirmed" settles the question: the `CANDIDATE_ENDPOINTS` caveat comment (now explicitly notes this survives the stream-confirmation logic, not just the earlier HTTP-status-only caveat), the I/O endpoint descriptions themselves, `is_valid_result()`'s docstring, and the per-endpoint `Valid: yes (confirmed live...)` message in `main()`, which now adds an explicit "not proof this is a distinct real channel" note inline. Telling real channels apart would need actually comparing frame content across directions - noted as a possible future enhancement, not built.

## bv-live: add Interior button alongside Front/Rear

Christer: "Time to add an 'I' button for bv-live. Should it be named Internal or Inside?" Neither - went with **Interior**, matching this project's own already-established term for the third camera direction (`Recording.interior`/`is_interior` in `domain/recording.py`, and the existing 'I' direction letter used throughout - recording filenames, thumbnails, `scan_blackvue_endpoints.py`'s own `direction=I` candidate). Introducing a third synonym for the same thing would have fragmented terminology across the codebase for no benefit.

Also asked (separately) whether `/blackvue_livedata.cgi` carries any audio - it doesn't; per `parser/livedata.py`, that endpoint only ever streams two kinds of JSON objects, `"GPS"` and `"3G"` (g-sensor) - no audio field exists in it at all.

**Implemented**, `src/blackvue/live/app.py`: `stream_camera()`'s `Query` pattern widened from `^[FR]$` to `^[FRI]$`; a third `<button id="btn-interior">` added next to Front/Rear in `_PAGE_HTML`; `setDirection()`'s JS updated to toggle all three buttons' `active` class instead of just two. Noted inline (route docstring + `docs/man/bv-live.md`) that a camera without a genuine interior channel may still answer `direction=I` with something live-looking rather than a clean error - see the `scan_blackvue_endpoints.py` caveat entries above about aliased directions - so the button deliberately doesn't try to hide itself for that case; there's no reliable way to distinguish "no interior channel" from "interior channel, nothing to see" from bv-live's side alone.

No dedicated test file exists for `live/app.py` (per its own earlier entries, most bv-live testing covers the underlying helper modules, not the FastAPI routes/HTML directly) - verified via `py_compile` and a read-through only.

## bv-download: sidecar probing was running for the whole matching range before the confirmation prompt

Christer: "bv-download ... takes a long time and nothing is happening, then i run it with --verbose and get a lot of messages like ... found ... (not listed by the camera's own recording listing) ... Looks like it scans through all records and print this. This should only be shown during download and i havent been asked yet if i want to download it."

**Root cause:** `_run()` had a loop right after building `recordings` (the full date-range-filtered list) that called `camera.probe_missing_sidecars()` for *every* one of them - unconditionally, before the interactive `confirm()` prompt, and even under `--dry-run`. On a camera/firmware combination whose listing doesn't already include `.gps`/`.3gf`/`.thm` (see probe_missing_sidecars()'s own docstring - this is apparently every camera confirmed so far), that's up to 5 extra HTTP round-trips per recording (2 sidecar suffixes + up to 3 per-direction thumbnails), run sequentially for the whole range before the user had said yes to anything - exactly the "long time, nothing happening" Christer described, and the `--verbose` "found ..." lines were printing before the "Proceed with download?" prompt even appeared, misleadingly suggesting a download was already underway.

**Fixed:** removed that eager pre-confirmation loop entirely. The same `probe_missing_sidecars()` call (and its `--verbose` "found ..." print) now happens inside the existing per-recording loop further down `_run()` - the one that already runs once per `(recording, want_video)` in `selection`, right before that recording is either listed (`--dry-run --files`, which needs entries populated to describe them) or actually downloaded. For a real run this loop only executes after the user has confirmed (or passed `--yes`); for `--dry-run` it runs at the same point as before (dry-run never hits the interactive prompt anyway), so `--dry-run --files`'s accuracy is unchanged. The set of recordings probed is identical to before - only the timing moved, from "the whole range, up front" to "one recording at a time, right when it's needed."

**Verification:** `run_tests.py` against `tests/blackvue/cli/test_bv_download.py` (39 passed) and `tests/blackvue/core/test_blackvue_camera.py` (11 passed, including all the `probe_missing_sidecars` cases from its earlier entry) - no regressions; none of the existing tests asserted on the old eager-loop's timing, so nothing needed updating. `docs/man/bv-download.md` updated to note the per-recording timing explicitly.

### Follow-up: `direction=O` confirmed as "Optional" - BlackVue's own camera-letter naming

Christer, unprompted, gave the full BlackVue direction-letter naming: F=Front (Främre), R=Rear (Bakre), I=Interior (Inre IR-/kupékamera), O=Optional (Extra/valfri extern eller intern kamera). This resolves `scan_blackvue_endpoints.py`'s own "unconfirmed candidate for how a camera might address a channel beyond F/R/I" wording for `direction=O` - it isn't a guess, it's BlackVue's real naming for an optional extra camera some models support (not every camera has one).

**Updated**, `scripts/scan_blackvue_endpoints.py`: the `direction=O` entry in `CANDIDATE_ENDPOINTS` now describes it as the confirmed "Optional" camera letter instead of "unconfirmed candidate ... beyond F/R/I", while keeping the existing caveat that a Valid/confirmed result there still isn't proof of a genuine channel (see the two entries above - that's a separate, still-open finding about aliasing, not about what the letter itself means). Documentation-only, no logic change.

Also relevant to bv-live's Interior-button entry above: this doesn't change anything there since I=Interior was already correctly named.

(Also flagged separately, not yet acted on: after confirming a download, Christer got a bare `bv-download: timed out` - `run_cli()`'s generic `OSError` catch-all, which doesn't say which recording or which step (RecordTime capture, sidecar probe, or a specific file download) actually failed. Could be the same benign WiFi flakiness as his very first message in this project's history, or worth making more granular/resilient - asked which, no answer yet, not pursued further.)

### Follow-up: fixed the bare "timed out" - one recording's network failure no longer aborts the whole batch

Asking Christer which of (a) no fix, (b) more granular error messages, or (c) skip-and-continue resilience he wanted went unanswered (the AskUserQuestion call itself failed to send, and his next messages moved on to other things), so went with the combination that needed no further input: both (b) and (c) together, matching the skip-and-continue precedent already established for corrupted sources during concat (see the mode-A/I-direction entry above referencing task #304).

**Root cause recap:** `_capture_record_time()` already caught its own failures internally (best-effort, `config.ini` fetch failures reported under `--verbose` and otherwise silently ignored - see its own docstring), but the per-recording loop's two other network calls - `camera.probe_missing_sidecars()` and `camera.download()` - had no try/except of their own. Any `OSError`/`TimeoutError` from either one (both go through `urllib.request.urlopen(..., timeout=...)` in `BlackVueClient`, which raises `OSError` subclasses on the network failures that matter here) propagated all the way up to `run_cli()`'s generic catch-all, which prints one bare `bv-download: timed out` with no indication of which recording or step failed, and gives up on every recording still left in the batch - even ones a moment's retry would have fetched fine. Exactly what Christer hit after confirming a 10-recording range: one line, nothing downloaded, no clue which of the 10 it was.

**Fixed**, `src/blackvue/cli/bv_download.py`'s `_run()`: both calls inside the per-recording loop are now individually wrapped in `try`/`except OSError`. A failure prints `bv-download: <recording id>: couldn't check for sidecar files (<error>) - skipping this recording` or `bv-download: <recording id>: download failed (<error>) - skipping to the next recording` to stderr (unconditionally, not gated behind `--verbose` - this is a real failure, not routine progress detail) and `continue`s to the next recording instead of raising. Failed ids are collected; if any occurred, a summary line (`N of M recording(s) failed and were skipped: <ids>`) prints at the end and `_run()` returns a new `EXIT_PARTIAL_FAILURE = 4` instead of `EXIT_OK` - lets a script or cron job tell "some but not all downloaded" apart from a clean run without having to scrape stderr.

**Verification:** added three new tests to `tests/blackvue/cli/test_bv_download.py` - a fake `BlackVueCamera` stand-in whose `download()`/`probe_missing_sidecars()` raise `OSError` for one chosen recording id, exercised through a real call to `_run()` (with `connect()`/`BlackVueCamera` monkeypatched) rather than just the extracted helper functions, since this bug was specifically about the loop's own control flow: confirms the failing recording is skipped, its neighbours on either side still download, the exit code is `EXIT_PARTIAL_FAILURE`, and the right id/message land on stderr; a third test confirms a fully-successful run still returns `EXIT_OK` with no failure summary. Full `run_tests.py` pass on `test_bv_download.py`: 42 passed, 0 failed (was 39 before these three). `docs/man/bv-download.md` updated: a new paragraph describing the skip-and-continue behavior, and exit code 4 added to the EXIT STATUS table.

### Follow-up: shortened the --verbose "found ..." sidecar line to kind-level labels

Christer, after the sidecar-probing timing fix above, pointed out `--verbose`'s per-recording line was still noisy once a recording actually needed several probed files - e.g. `20260803_143738_N: found 20260803_143738_N.gps, 20260803_143738_N.3gf, 20260803_143738_NF.thm, 20260803_143738_NI.thm, 20260803_143738_NR.thm (not listed by the camera's own recording listing)` - and asked for something closer to `20260803_143738_N: Found gps, 3gf and thumbnails for downloading.`

**Implemented**, `src/blackvue/cli/bv_download.py`: new `_summarize_found_kinds(found)` collapses `probe_missing_sidecars()`'s returned entries into up to three fixed-order labels - `"gps"`, `"3gf"`, `"thumbnails"` (the last one covers however many per-direction `.thm` files were found, F/R/I alike, as a single word rather than naming each one) - joined as `"gps, 3gf and thumbnails"` (no Oxford comma, matching Christer's own phrasing). The per-recording `--verbose` print now reads `bv-download: <id>: found <summary> for downloading`, dropping both the individual filenames and the "(not listed by the camera's own recording listing)" trailer entirely, per what he asked for. `VodEntry` is now imported into `bv_download.py` for this function's type hint.

**Verification:** five new tests in `tests/blackvue/cli/test_bv_download.py` - `_summarize_found_kinds()` unit tests for zero/one/two/three-kind inputs (including that multiple thumbnail files still collapse to one "thumbnails" label), plus an end-to-end `_run()` test (monkeypatched camera, `--verbose`) confirming the new short line appears and neither an individual `.thm` filename nor the old trailer text leak back into stdout. Full `run_tests.py` pass on `test_bv_download.py`: 47 passed, 0 failed (was 42 before these five).

## bv-export: detect and trim an Event/Manual recording's pre-record buffer

Christer: "I believe it's only E and M mode videos that might have a prebuffer of 6 - 7 seconds added at the beginning. My question is it possible via audio, gps or 3gx to find out how much is a prebuffer if you compare with the previous recordingid and then trim it away when generating trips. A trip that starts with an E or M mode should not be trimmed." Follow-up guidance: a visible jump/glitch at the trim point would be nice to avoid but is acceptable if unavoidable, and prebuffer trimming should run *before* front/rear duration alignment (which cuts at the *end* of a video) rather than after.

**Feasibility research, validated on real data before any code was written:** GPS fixes carry real wall-clock timestamps (NMEA `$GPRMC`), immune to the recording-relative-offset problem, but a BlackVue's GPS fix rate is far too sparse (~1Hz) to pin down a multi-second overlap precisely. Audio would work in principle but adds real decode cost for no accuracy benefit over g-sensor. Settled on g-sensor (`.3gf`) cross-correlation: Christer uploaded a real consecutive N→M pair from his own archive (`20260802_103513_N.3gf` / `20260802_103545_M.3gf`, confirmed by him to be exactly the E/M-follows-N shape needed) to validate against. A first prototype's cross-correlation was flawed - it tied the comparison window's length to the candidate offset itself, so different candidates weren't comparable (score jumped from 0.591 to 0.986 between adjacent candidates two hundredths of a second apart). Fixed by using a *fixed*-length comparison window across every candidate offset, which produced a single, sharp, isolated correlation peak at ~5.1s (score ~0.98) - stable whether the window itself was tried at 1.5s, 2s, 3s, or 4s, with everything else sitting in a noise floor around ±0.15-0.2. Independently corroborated by N's own recording duration running ~5s longer than its nominal ID-timestamp gap to M would suggest.

**Implemented**, new `src/blackvue/export/prebuffer.py`, pure Python (no numpy - confirmed via `pyproject.toml` that numpy isn't a base dependency, so this doesn't introduce one just for this feature). `detect_prebuffer_seconds(preceding, following, *, window_seconds=3.0, max_seconds=12.0, grid_seconds=0.02, min_score=0.75)` slides a fixed-length window across the *preceding* recording's tail (from `window_seconds` up to `min(max_seconds, preceding's own length)`), z-scoring each axis (x/y/z demeaned to unit variance, concatenated into one vector) and comparing against `following`'s fixed head window via dot-product correlation; returns the best-scoring offset only if it clears `min_score`, else `None` - refuses to guess on an ambiguous or unrelated pair rather than picking whatever happened to score highest. Verified this reproduces the exact 5.1s hand-validated result against the real fixture pair.

Two supporting primitives added: `trim_media_head()` in `src/blackvue/export/media.py` (stream-copy `ffmpeg -ss <offset> -i <source> -c copy`, documented to only be able to land on a real keyframe - snaps to the nearest one *before* the requested offset, the safer direction per Christer's own "if it can't be avoided its ok": risks leaving a small duplicated sliver rather than ever cutting real content) and `trim_gsensor_head()` in `src/blackvue/telemetry/gsensor_reader.py` (drops samples before the cutoff, rebases the remainder so the new head starts at 0 - a sample exactly at the cutoff is kept).

**Wired into `trip_export.py`** via new `_trim_prebuffers(trip, work_dir, warnings, log)`, called from `export_trip()` before `_align_front_rear_durations()` (matching Christer's ordering requirement), satisfying "a trip that starts with an E or M mode should not be trimmed" by starting its scan at index 1 - a trip's own first recording is never compared against anything outside the trip and is therefore never trimmed regardless of its kind. For each Event/Manual recording with a predecessor in the trip, both `.3gf` tracks are read and run through `detect_prebuffer_seconds()`; on a confident hit, `trim_media_head()` runs against that recording's FRONT/REAR/AUDIO into a temp work directory (paths collected into a `media_overrides` dict keyed by `(RecordingId, Asset)`) and `trim_gsensor_head()` rewrites its g-sensor samples in memory (collected into a `gsensor_overrides` dict keyed by `RecordingId` - no redundant `.3gf` written to disk). A warning naming the recording, its predecessor, the detected offset, and which assets were trimmed is added either way something's actually trimmed.

These two override dicts compose onto the *existing* alignment machinery rather than duplicating it: `_align_front_rear_durations()` gained a `source_overrides` parameter (checked before falling back to the recording's real FRONT/REAR path, so alignment measures and trims the *already-prebuffer-trimmed* file, not the original), and `_merge_gsensor()` gained a `gsensor_overrides` parameter (checked before falling back to reading the recording's real `.3gf` from disk). `export_trip()`'s tempdir block now runs `_trim_prebuffers()` first, merges its `media_overrides` into `_align_front_rear_durations()`'s own result to form one `duration_overrides` dict fed to `_recording_video_offsets()`/the front/rear/audio concatenation calls, and passes `gsensor_overrides` through to `_merge_gsensor()`.

**Incidental fix found while wiring this in:** `_concatenate_asset()`'s call for `Asset.AUDIO` inside `export_trip()` was never passing `duration_overrides` at all, even before this feature - meaning a front/rear alignment trim was never actually reflected in the exported audio, silently drifting out of sync with the (correctly trimmed) video. Now fixed as a side effect of wiring prebuffer trimming through the same dict, so audio benefits from both alignment and prebuffer trimming and stays in sync with picture.

**Verification:** `tests/fixtures/gsensor/` now holds the real N/M `.3gf` pair Christer uploaded, as a first-class test fixture. New `tests/blackvue/export/test_prebuffer.py` (8 tests): the real fixture pair resolves to 5.0-5.2s; unrelated-random, flat/zero-variance, too-short-preceding, too-short-following, and too-few-samples tracks all correctly return `None`; a synthetic distinctive (non-random) pattern with a known copied overlap is detected within the expected range; `DEFAULT_MIN_SCORE` is regression-guarded to stay between the confirmed noise floor and true-positive score. New tests added to `test_export_media.py` (`trim_media_head` - a real ffmpeg stream-copy trim, plus a missing-source error case) and `test_gsensor_reader.py` (`trim_gsensor_head` - drops-and-rebases, keeps-a-sample-exactly-at-cutoff, can-drop-everything). Discovered along the way: a default lavfi `testsrc` test clip only gets one keyframe at t=0 under libx264's default GOP settings, which would make any `-ss`-based head-trim test silently pass by returning the untrimmed file - fixed by a dedicated `_make_video_with_frequent_keyframes()` helper (`-g 10 -force_key_frames`) used everywhere a real trim needs to be provable.

8 new tests added to `test_trip_export.py` using a purpose-built N→M trip fixture (`_n_to_m_prebuffer_trip()`, built from the real `.3gf` pair plus synthetic FRONT/REAR/AUDIO): confirms `_trim_prebuffers()` trims exactly the M recording's FRONT/REAR/AUDIO/g-sensor and leaves the N recording untouched; confirms an E/M recording that starts the trip is never trimmed; confirms a normal-kind recording is never even checked for overlap regardless of its g-sensor content; confirms missing g-sensor data and a low-confidence/unrelated pair both correctly skip rather than trim; confirms `_align_front_rear_durations()` measures against a passed-in `source_overrides` path rather than the recording's real file; confirms `_merge_gsensor()` returns passed-in `gsensor_overrides` samples rather than reading from disk. Full regression pass: `test_prebuffer.py` 8/8, `test_export_media.py` 23/23, `test_gsensor_reader.py` 9/9, and the complete `test_trip_export.py` suite (102 tests, run in three range-batches to fit the sandbox's 45s-per-command cap) 102/102 - no regressions from the `source_overrides`/`gsensor_overrides` signature changes on any of the ~94 pre-existing tests that don't pass them explicitly. `docs/man/bv-export.md` updated with a new "Pre-record buffer trimming" section, positioned ahead of "Front/rear duration alignment" to match the real execution order.

### Follow-up: prebuffer trim left map.mp4's overlay lagging the trimmed video by the trimmed amount

Christer, after actually watching a real export: "I got a little little glitch which i wouldnt have noticed unless i was checking it very closely" at the prebuffer trim point. Investigated by extracting the 3-frame `.mp4` clip he sent frame-by-frame (`ffprobe`/`ffmpeg` in the sandbox) and diffing them - no detectable lateral pixel shift in the actual front/mirror footage between frames (a small-window cross-correlation search across ±10px found the best alignment at essentially 0px offset, well inside normal frame-to-frame noise). But the map panel burned into that same stitch export told a different story: its own on-screen date/time readout stayed frozen at `2026-08-02 10:35:45` - recording M's plain ID timestamp - while the camera's own burned-in timestamp on the same frame already read `2026-08-02 10:35:50`, a 5-second gap that lines up almost exactly with the ~5.1s prebuffer offset trimmed from that recording just above.

**Root cause, found by re-reading `_video_position_breakpoints()`:** it anchors a recording's video-position-0 to `recording.id.timestamp` unconditionally - correct for an untrimmed recording (frame 0 really was recorded at that instant), but wrong for one whose head just got cut by `_trim_prebuffers()`. A trimmed recording's *new* frame 0 is whatever used to be `offset_seconds` into the original file - meaning it was actually recorded `offset_seconds` *after* the ID timestamp, not at it. `map_video.py`'s renderer (fed these breakpoints to convert a video-elapsed position back to a wall-clock instant, in turn used to look up the right GPS position for that frame) had no way to know this, so it consistently read `offset_seconds` too early - map.mp4 for that stretch of video showed wherever the car had been ~5 seconds before the frame actually being shown, not a full teleport, but exactly the kind of thing that reads as "a little glitch" without being obviously broken. The same staleness would apply to `--stitch-subtitles`' burn-in timing for any trimmed recording, since it's driven by the same breakpoints.

**Fixed:** `_trim_prebuffers()` now also returns `prebuffer_offsets` (`{recording id: detected offset_seconds}`, only present for a recording actually trimmed) as a third element of its return tuple. `_video_position_breakpoints()` gained a matching optional `prebuffer_offsets` parameter: when building a recording's `(video_position, wallclock_start)` breakpoint, it now adds `timedelta(seconds=prebuffer_offsets.get(recording.id, 0.0))` on top of `recording.id.timestamp` - a recording absent from the dict (the overwhelming majority) is completely unaffected, same as before this parameter existed. `export_trip()`'s tempdir block was updated to unpack and thread the third value through to the one `_video_position_breakpoints()` call site.

**Verification:** two new tests in `test_trip_export.py` - `test_video_position_breakpoints_shifts_a_trimmed_recordings_wallclock_start` (confirms the offset lands correctly on a trimmed recording's breakpoint) and `test_video_position_breakpoints_leaves_an_untrimmed_recording_alone` (confirms an empty/missing `prebuffer_offsets` entry doesn't change anything); the existing `test_trim_prebuffers_trims_front_rear_audio_and_gsensor` extended to also assert the real fixture pair's ~5.1s offset shows up correctly in the new `prebuffer_offsets` return value. All six other `_trim_prebuffers()` call sites across the test file updated for the new 3-tuple return shape. Full regression pass: complete `test_trip_export.py` suite, now 104 tests (102 plus these 2 new ones), run in range-batches - 104/104, no regressions. `docs/man/bv-export.md`'s "Pre-record buffer trimming" section extended with a paragraph on the map/subtitle timing correction.

Christer: "What does it take to do a public release now?" Found mostly good shape already: GPL-3.0 `LICENSE`, a solid `README.md`, `CONTRIBUTING.md`, `AUTHORS.md`/`COPYRIGHT.md`/`NOTICE`, an honestly-labeled `Development Status :: 2 - Pre-Alpha` classifier, optional dependencies correctly split so a plain install stays light, no hardcoded secrets anywhere (the HF diarization token is env-var-only), and no leftover `TODO`/`FIXME` markers in `src/`. Extensive `docs/` - architecture, deploy, pipeline, testing, man pages for 8 of 9 commands (`bv-web` is the one gap, covered instead by `docs/WEB_ARCHITECTURE.md`).

Two items surfaced that needed a decision from Christer specifically, since they're privacy/content calls rather than mechanical fixes: a real-looking GPS coordinate (`59.334591,18.06324`, Stockholm, sub-meter precision) hardcoded across several test files as expected output - asked whether it was sensitive; he confirmed it's fine to leave, not a real/sensitive location. Also asked, alongside three purely mechanical items, whether to fix them now - all four approved.

**Fixed, this pass:**

- **Escaped-markdown rendering bug**: `AUTHORS.md`, `COPYRIGHT.md`, and `CHANGELOG.md` had literal backslash-escaped headers (`\# AUTHORS`, `\## Founder`, `\- Initial project architecture.`) plus doubled blank lines throughout - almost certainly an artifact of whatever tool originally generated them. On GitHub this renders as visibly broken text (literal backslashes) instead of real headers/bullets - the first thing a visitor to a brand-new public repo sees. Rewritten as plain, correctly-formatted markdown with the same content.
- **~31MB of dead weight removed from `images/`**: six AI-generated (Kling) "No_Parking" video clips, left over from the `--parking-transition-clip` feature that was fully removed earlier this project (see the "Simplify `--include-parking`" entries above) - confirmed via `git grep`/source search that nothing in `src/`, `docs/`, or `pyproject.toml` references them anymore. `git rm`'d; the small PNG icons in the same folder (`mirror.png`, `red_car.png`, etc.) are still genuinely used as design references and were left alone.
- **No CI existed at all** (`.github/workflows/` was empty) despite `CONTRIBUTING.md` already inviting outside camera owners to send PRs, and `pytest`/`ruff`/`mypy` already sitting in `requirements-dev.txt` unused. Added `.github/workflows/ci.yml`: installs ffmpeg explicitly (a real runtime dependency for most of the export/generate test suite, not just assumed present on the runner image), installs the package with all three optional-dependency groups plus the dev tools, then runs `pytest` (blocking - the real regression gate) and `ruff`/`mypy` (`continue-on-error: true` - the codebase has never been run through either tool before, so a first pass is far more likely to surface a real backlog than genuine new regressions; left visible-but-non-blocking until that backlog's been triaged, at which point removing `continue-on-error` tightens it for real). Couldn't verify the workflow executes cleanly end-to-end from this sandbox (no outbound network to actually dispatch a GitHub Actions run) - worth Christer confirming with a real push once this lands.
- **`.gitignore` gap**: `camera_gps.txt` (real personal location data), `check_mp4_recoverability.py`, and `inspect_mp4_boxes.py` had been sitting untracked at the repo root through real development/debugging sessions - fine as long as nobody ever ran a blanket `git add -A`/`git add .`, but that's a thin safety margin for a file with real location data in it once the repo goes public. Added explicit root-anchored entries (`/camera_gps.txt` etc.) as a real safety net; confirmed with `git check-ignore -v` that all three are now actually ignored.

**Not changed, flagged for Christer's own judgment rather than acted on unilaterally:** `CHANGELOG.md` is still a placeholder ("Nothing yet") despite 263 real commits worth of shipped features - left as-is, since backfilling it is an editorial decision (write it from scratch at the release point vs. reconstruct history) rather than a mechanical fix. `WORKING_CONTEXT.md` itself (this file) is a ~900KB, extremely granular real-time development diary that will ship in full once the repo is public - not a blocker, since nothing in it is more sensitive than what's already been individually reviewed above, but worth Christer consciously deciding that's the level of transparency he wants rather than it just happening as a byproduct of this project's own working convention.

### Follow-up: purged the No_Parking clips from git history, not just HEAD

Christer, on a double-check pass after the cleanup above: asked whether the deleted clips were actually gone or just no longer in the current tree. They were only gone from HEAD - `git rm` never touches earlier commits, so all 6 files (~31MB) were still sitting in the object database, which is why `.git` was still ~51-64MB despite the working tree cleanup. Asked whether to purge them for real (a real history rewrite - every commit hash from the point they were introduced onward changes, requiring a force-push, riskier than anything else in this pass) - Christer chose to purge.

**Tooling constraint:** `git-filter-repo` (the modern, recommended tool for this) isn't installed and this sandbox has no outbound network to install it. `git filter-branch` (built into git, officially discouraged for being slow) is available, but at ~2.8 commits/sec against 264 commits it needs ~95 seconds - over this sandbox's hard 45-second-per-command cap, and `filter-branch` can't be resumed mid-run from a later command (confirmed: killed it mid-way, `HEAD`/refs were untouched - safe - but restarting needs `--force`, which discards prior progress rather than resuming it).

**Used a `fast-export`/`fast-import` pipeline instead** - the same underlying technique `git-filter-repo` itself is built on, and fast enough to fit the time budget: `git fast-export --all` dumps every ref's full history as a single text/binary stream (3s, 156MB); a small Python script reads that stream and drops just the `M`/`D` lines referencing the target paths, correctly treating `data <length>` blocks as opaque binary payloads (not text lines) so blob content/commit messages can never be misparsed as stream commands; `git fast-import --force` replays the filtered stream back into the same repository, rewriting every affected commit and updating `refs/heads/main`/`refs/remotes/origin/main`/`refs/remotes/origin/HEAD` in place. Total runtime for the actual rewrite: under 5 seconds.

**Caught a second copy on the first double-check pass:** the initial purge only targeted `images/No_Parking*.mp4` (where they'd been sitting most recently). `git rev-list --objects --all` afterward showed the *same* six blob hashes still reachable under a second, earlier path - `src/blackvue/export/assets/no_parking_1.mp4` through `_6.mp4` - from when these clips were originally bundled as package-data (see "Bundle Christer's 6 Kling clips..." above) before being deleted in the later "Drop Parking-mode recordings entirely..." commit. Re-ran the same fast-export/filter/fast-import cycle with that second path list; confirmed with `git rev-list --objects --all | grep -i no_parking` returning nothing at all afterward - fully gone from every ref, not just the one path that happened to get double-checked.

**Verification, each step confirmed before moving to the next:** a full-repo `git bundle create --all` backup taken before touching anything (`/tmp/beyond-video-before-purge.bundle`, 34MB - a safety net in case anything went wrong, not committed anywhere). After each fast-import: `git diff <pre-purge HEAD> <new ref> --stat` produced zero output both times, confirming the working tree content is byte-for-byte identical to before the rewrite - only history shrank, nothing visible changed. `git log --oneline | wc -l` still 264 (no commits silently dropped - `--prune-empty` was deliberately *not* used this time, unlike the abandoned `filter-branch` attempt, since none of the target commits would have become empty anyway and there was no reason to risk it). `git fsck --full --unreachable` came back completely clean (no dangling/corrupt objects). Commit metadata (author, date, message) spot-checked on the three most recent commits - all preserved exactly. `git reset --hard` to point the working tree at the new history, then `git reflog expire --expire=now --all && git gc --prune=now --aggressive` to actually reclaim the disk space rather than leaving the old objects reachable via reflog: `.git` went from 64MB to 2.1MB. Re-ran a handful of the prebuffer feature's own tests afterward as an unrelated-functionality sanity check (6/6 passed) - nothing about the rewrite touches test behavior, but cheap to confirm.

**What Christer needs to do next:** this rewrite only happened in this sandbox's checkout - `origin/main` on GitHub still has the old history (this sandbox can't reach GitHub to push). Pushing the rewritten history requires `git push --force origin main` (a plain push will be rejected - the history no longer has the old commits as ancestors). Since nobody else is known to have cloned this repo yet, that's a normal, low-risk force-push for this specific case - but is exactly the kind of one-way door that's the user's call to actually execute, not something to do unilaterally even if it were technically reachable from here.

**Update:** Christer force-pushed (`--force-with-lease`, one retry needed after a `git fetch` to clear a stale local tracking ref - not an actual remote conflict) and tagged `v0.1.0` once he'd confirmed the push landed. `beyond-video` is now a real, public, tagged release.

## Public-release follow-up: issue intake for bug reports/feature requests, and a real "new camera" workflow

Christer, now that the repo is actually public: "How do we handle requests? and new camera from public." The camera-compatibility path was already solid (`CONTRIBUTING.md` + the "Camera endpoint scan" issue template, the same process that got the Elite 10 confirmed without owning one) - but there was no intake for anything else, and the camera workflow itself stopped at "I'll take it from there" without saying what that actually means once a report lands.

Asked two things rather than assuming: what level of formality for general bug/feature intake (chose two lightweight issue templates, matching the existing camera-scan template's style), and what the real "new camera" process should be (chose: document the Elite-10 precedent explicitly - endpoint variants get added from the scan output alone, landing the model in README's "confirmed via scan, not full pipeline" bucket, rather than either blindly trusting an untested report or making every reporter iterate on test patches Christer can't personally validate either way).

**Added**, `.github/ISSUE_TEMPLATE/bug-report.yml` and `feature-request.yml` (new, alongside the existing `camera-endpoint-scan.yml`): same structured-fields style, `labels: ["bug"]`/`["enhancement"]` respectively (GitHub's own default label set, no new labels to create). Bug report asks for the exact command run, expected vs. actual behavior, camera model (optional - not every bug is camera-specific), and OS/Python version. Feature request asks for the underlying problem before a proposed solution, and points anyone planning a PR back to opening the issue first - ties directly into `CONTRIBUTING.md`'s existing "discuss before you code" guidance rather than duplicating it.

**Updated `CONTRIBUTING.md`:** new "What happens after your report lands" paragraph spelling out the actual camera-support process (matches the Elite 10 precedent, explains *why* - Christer can't run the full pipeline against hardware he doesn't own, so a scan-verified subset of support is the honest ceiling rather than an all-or-nothing gate); the "Code contributions" section now names the two new templates explicitly and clarifies CI's real current gate (`pytest` blocking, `ruff`/`mypy` informational-only - matching the `continue-on-error` design from the CI-workflow entry above, not overclaiming enforcement that doesn't exist yet); new "Response time" section sets expectations plainly (single maintainer, day job, no SLA) rather than leaving that unsaid.

**Verification:** all three issue templates (`camera-endpoint-scan.yml` plus the two new ones) parse as valid YAML (`yaml.safe_load()`); `README.md`'s existing "Tested"/"Likely to work, untested" compatibility-table wording already matched the terminology used in the new CONTRIBUTING.md paragraph, so no changes needed there. No source code touched this pass - docs/templates only.
