### Follow-up: the real bottleneck - `read_recording()`'s `glob()` still lists the whole archive directory

Christer reported "still very slow" for both thumbnails and video after `ArchiveRecordingCache` shipped. Before writing more speculative code, asked him to check whether a *single* thumbnail or video, loaded in isolation with nothing else competing for the server, was also slow - if yes, that rules out request-queuing/concurrency theories and points at genuine per-lookup cost; if no (only the whole grid was slow), it would point at either concurrency or bandwidth instead. He confirmed: slow even alone. That single answer eliminated two plausible theories at once (server-side request serialization from `async def` routes doing blocking I/O on the shared event loop, and raw network bandwidth, since a single `.thm` thumbnail is tiny) and left one: something in resolving *one* recording, on its own, was genuinely expensive - and neither of the two caches added so far could touch that, since a cache only helps on a *second* lookup of the same recording, and a thumbnail grid asks for a different recording every time.

Root cause, found by reading `archive/archive_reader.py`'s `read_recording()` closely: its docstring claimed it was "targeted" and didn't "scandir()/stat() every file in the archive," implemented as `self._path.glob(f"{recording_id.value}*")`. That's not actually true of `Path.glob()` - CPython's implementation still calls `os.scandir()` on the parent directory and filters every entry's name against the pattern; it only *saves* the per-entry `stat()` calls for non-matches, not the directory listing itself. So every single call to `read_recording()` - one thumbnail, one detail page, one video range request - was paying a cost proportional to the *total number of files in the whole archive directory*, not to anything about the one recording being looked up. Christer's archive has years of unpruned recordings sitting in one flat directory (a dashcam in Normal mode produces a new file every 1-3 minutes, so years of driving is a very large flat directory) - on that kind of directory, sitting on whatever storage his NAS's `/data/archive` mount actually is, that per-lookup listing cost is plausible as the real, dominant "still very slow" cause, and explains why it showed up even for a single isolated request: the cost was never about concurrency or caching, it was paid fresh on every call regardless.

Fixed by rewriting `read_recording()` to never list the directory at all: instead of a glob pattern, it now builds the small, fixed set of exact filenames a recording could have (one per `ASSETS` entry - `F.mp4`, `.gps`, `.thm` variants, generated-asset suffixes, etc. - about a dozen) by appending each known suffix directly to `recording_id.value`, and probes each with a plain `Path.is_file()`/`.stat()`. An exact-name lookup goes through the filesystem's own directory index (hash/B-tree, depending on filesystem) rather than a linear scan of every entry, so this is now a fixed number of stat() calls regardless of how large the archive directory has grown - the performance `read_recording()`'s docstring always claimed to have, actually delivered this time. Behavior is unchanged (same `Recording`/`AssetFile` results, same handling of a missing archive directory or unknown id returning `None`) - all 14 pre-existing tests in `tests/blackvue/archive/test_archive_reader.py` pass unmodified, confirming this was a pure performance fix, not a behavior change.

Added `test_read_recording_never_lists_the_directory`, which monkeypatches `os.scandir`, `Path.glob`, and `Path.iterdir` to raise if called at all, then asserts `read_recording()` still returns the right result - proving the method genuinely never lists the directory rather than just asserting on its return value (which the old glob-based version would also have passed, despite having exactly the bug this exists to catch and prevent from regressing).

**Verification**: 15 tests in `tests/blackvue/archive/test_archive_reader.py` (14 pre-existing + 1 new) and all 34 tests in `tests/blackvue/web/test_archive_browser.py` pass via the hand-built harness (no real pytest in this sandbox) - the browser-level tests matter here too since `find_recording()` calls straight through to `read_recording()`. `archive_reader.py` also checked with `ast.parse()`. This is a genuine root-cause fix rather than another cache layer, so it should actually move the needle where the two prior rounds didn't - worth Christer confirming on the real NAS, and if it's *still* slow after this, the next thing to check would be whether `/data/archive`'s underlying storage itself (disk type, whether it's local vs. a further network mount inside the NAS) is the bottleneck, since at that point the application-level cost would be down to a small constant number of syscalls.

### Follow-up: 7 seconds is acceptable - explaining the remaining cost, then closing the last redundant read

Christer confirmed the `read_recording()` fix worked - "faster, takes about 7 second before player are ready to play, thats acceptable" - and asked what bv-web is actually doing to explain that number, with his own guess (list `*F.thm` once, one call per thumbnail, then range-request the video's start and end atoms for playback). Walked through what's really happening: the thumbnail grid does one full `ArchiveReader.read()` pass (every filename, not just thumbnails, since the page needs full recording info - timestamps, kind, `has_video` for the red-cross overlay), not a `*F.thm`-only listing; each thumbnail is then its own HTTP request resolving one recording (matching his "1 call per file" guess, now cheap after the `read_recording()` fix); and the ~7s for video is very plausibly the MP4 `moov` atom sitting at the *end* of BlackVue's raw camera files rather than the front ("faststart") - a camera that writes continuously while recording generally can't know its own final index until the clip ends, so the player has to reach toward the tail of a large raw file before it can start decoding at all. That's a real, physical amount of data crossing the network before playback starts, inherent to the untouched raw file the archive browser deliberately serves as-is (unlike the trip player, which only ever plays `bv-export`'s own re-muxed/re-encoded output). No code change from this part - explanation only, and correctly identified as not really fixable without re-muxing the raw archive file, which isn't something the archive browser should start doing.

Christer then asked specifically what config file was being read per request, and once shown it was his camera's own `.cfg` (the same file pasted earlier in this engagement) being opened and TOML-parsed fresh on every single archive-browser request just to re-derive `CameraConfig.target`, asked "why not read it only once per page" - the honest answer being that HTTP requests are stateless: the browser fires off N independent requests for N `<img>` tags, and the server has no built-in memory tying them together into "one page load," so the real fix has to be the same short-TTL caching pattern already used twice this session, not a literal "once per page."

Added `CameraConfigCache` to `core/camera_config.py` (not `web/app.py`, unlike where it was first drafted) - same short-TTL wrapper pattern as `web/trips.py`'s `TripCache` and `web/archive_browser.py`'s `ArchiveRecordingCache`, keyed by camera id, wrapping `load_camera_config()`. Moved out of `app.py` specifically for testability: this sandbox has neither `fastapi` nor (being on Python 3.10, below this project's own `requires-python = ">=3.13"`) `tomllib` installed, but `TripCache`/`ArchiveRecordingCache` were both written to live in modules that don't import `fastapi`, precisely so they could be exercised with the hand-built harness this whole engagement has relied on - keeping the new cache in `app.py` would have made it untestable here despite being trivially testable in real CI. `core/camera_config.py` is shared with every CLI tool (bv-config, bv-gps, ...), which keep calling `load_camera_config()` directly and are entirely unaffected - a one-shot CLI invocation should always see a config fresh from disk, and nothing forces it through this cache; it's purely opt-in by whichever caller (bv-web) wants it. A `CameraConfigError` (missing/corrupt `.cfg`) is never cached, matching the "don't cache a miss" rule the other two caches already follow - it isn't caught inside `get()`, so it propagates straight to `_find_camera_archive()`'s existing 404 handling.

Wired into `app.py`: `app.state.camera_config_cache = CameraConfigCache()` created once in `create_app()`; `_find_camera_archive()` now takes the cache as an explicit parameter and calls `cache.get(default_config_dir(), camera_id)` instead of `load_camera_config(config_path(...))` directly; `_find_archive_recording()` now takes both `recording_cache` and `camera_config_cache` (it calls `_find_camera_archive()` internally) and passes both through; all four call sites (`archive_recording_list()`, `archive_recording_detail()`, `archive_recording_thumbnail()`, `archive_recording_file()`) updated. `_camera_options()` (the job-trigger forms' camera pick-list) deliberately left alone - it's a once-per-form-load, O(number of cameras) operation, not part of the per-thumbnail/per-range-request hot path this cache targets.

**Verification**: since this sandbox can't import `tomllib` (Python 3.10 vs. the project's `>=3.13`) or `fastapi`, verified `core/camera_config.py` and `app.py` with `ast.parse()` for syntax, then built a throwaway local `tomllib`/`pytest` stub (minimal `tomllib.load()` matching `save_camera_config()`'s own simple output shape, plus a `pytest.raises`/`pytest.mark.parametrize` shim) purely to exercise the real test file end-to-end in this sandbox - not committed anywhere, just a verification aid. Added four new tests to `tests/blackvue/core/test_camera_config.py` (`test_camera_config_cache_reuses_result_within_ttl`, `test_camera_config_cache_reloads_once_ttl_expires`, `test_camera_config_cache_does_not_cache_a_load_failure`, `test_camera_config_cache_keys_are_per_camera_id`), same `monkeypatch.setattr(camera_config_module.time, "monotonic", fake_clock)` pattern as the other two caches' tests. All 19 non-parametrized tests in the file pass through the stub harness (15 pre-existing + 4 new); the file's 3 parametrized tests (`test_validate_id_rejects` etc.) aren't runnable through this particular stub and were skipped, unrelated to this change. Also re-ran the full `test_archive_reader.py` (15), `test_archive_browser.py` (34), and `test_trips.py` (15) suites as a final regression check - all pass. This is the third and (for now) last layer of the "why is the archive browser slow" investigation Christer raised: `read_recording()`'s directory-scan bug was the dominant cost, this config-cache is a smaller but real remaining redundancy, and the ~7s video-start time is explained but not something bv-web itself can shorten further.

### Follow-up: lazy-load thumbnails instead of a zip bundle

Christer confirmed the previous fix worked ("Faster now playback in 3 to 7 seconds") and asked whether all 9260 of his archive's thumbnails (~400MB total) could be fetched in a single call - a zip bundle, unpacked client-side. Talked through the tradeoffs before building anything: a zip would work, but it's solving the wrong layer - the archive page currently renders every recording it has on one page with no pagination at all, so a zip bundle is really just a different way to ship "load everything, always," and that payload only grows as his archive keeps accumulating (400MB today, more every month, forever). It would also add real new complexity this server-rendered, zero-client-JS project doesn't have yet: server-side zip building (with its own caching/invalidation problem, since the raw build cost for 9260 files isn't free either) and a client-side JavaScript unzip dependency. Offered three options via `AskUserQuestion`: lazy-load images only, lazy-load plus defaulting the page to a recent window (e.g. last 30 days, using the filter bar's existing From/Until), or building the zip approach as described. Christer picked lazy-load only.

Added `loading="lazy" decoding="async"` to the thumbnail `<img>` tag in `archive_recording_list.html`. `loading="lazy"` tells the browser to defer fetching each thumbnail until it's near the viewport (browsers use their own lookahead distance, not literally "only when visible," so scrolling still feels smooth) - so a page with 9260 recordings now only actually issues thumbnail requests for the handful near what's currently on screen, not all 9260 at once on load. `decoding="async"` is a small additional hint that image decoding shouldn't block rendering. Zero new dependencies, no server-side change, and it keeps scaling fine as the archive keeps growing - the opposite of the zip approach's problem.

**Verification**: no existing template-rendering tests in this project (server-rendered Jinja2, previously reviewed by eye per earlier entries in this file, no headless browser available in this sandbox). This sandbox does have `jinja2` itself installed, though, so rendered `archive_recording_list.html` directly via `jinja2.Environment(loader=jinja2.FileSystemLoader(...))` with a fake `Recording`-shaped object standing in for the real `ArchiveRecording`, and asserted `loading="lazy"` and `decoding="async"` are present in the output HTML - a genuine render, not just a source-file grep. Worth Christer confirming the archive page feels snappier to first paint now, especially scrolled to a day far down the list.

### Follow-up: front/rear "both ready" explained, and underscore/hyphen allowed in camera ids

Christer confirmed the lazy-load fix ("Feels much bitter for thumbnails" - i.e. better), then asked two things.

**Why did rear look ready as soon as front was?** No code change - explanation only. Both `archive_recording_detail.html` and `trip_detail.html` only ever render a single `<video>` element (playing the first/primary video); rear and interior only ever appear as plain download links, never as a second embedded player, so there's no simultaneous video-element preloading happening. What's really going on: `ArchiveReader.read_recording()` discovers every asset file belonging to a recording - front, rear, interior, thumbnails, gps, everything - in one pass, so the `ArchiveRecording` object handed back already knows about all of them together. Clicking the rear link after the front one doesn't trigger a fresh "does this recording have a rear video" scan; it's already known, and (per the `ArchiveRecordingCache` TTL) very likely still cached from the same request that resolved the front video too. So "both ready together" is a real, correct observation - just not because of anything video-player-specific.

**Underscore/hyphen in camera ids**: Christer wants to split his archive into per-year camera ids (`Kirby_2019` .. `Kirby_2026`, each with its own `.cfg` and `target` pointing at that year's own subfolder) - a manual, much more direct fix for "one huge archive page" than lazy-loading alone, since it turns one 9260-recording page into up to eight much smaller ones. `validate_id()` (`core/camera_config.py`, used only by the `bv-config` wizard) previously allowed pure ASCII alphanumeric only - confirmed by its own existing test suite, which explicitly listed `"has-dash"` as a *rejected* case. Relaxed it to accept `_` and `-` too (`all(c.isalnum() or c in "_-" for c in id_)` in place of the old `id_.isalnum()`), while still rejecting anything else non-alphanumeric (space, `/`, `\`, non-ASCII) - the id doubles as both a filename (`config_path()`'s `f"{id_}.cfg"`) and a raw URL path segment in bv-web's `/archive/{camera_id}/...` routes, so it still needs to stay filesystem- and URL-safe without escaping. This is a self-contained validation-only change: nothing else in the codebase restricts camera id characters beyond bv-web's own separate `/`, `\`, `..` guard in `_find_camera_archive()`/`_find_trip()` (untouched, still correct), and the per-camera-id caches added this session (`ArchiveRecordingCache`, `CameraConfigCache`) key on the id as a plain string, so `Kirby_2019` and `Kirby_2020` simply become distinct cache keys with no special handling needed. `docs/man/bv-config.md` updated (the `ID` argument description and its exit-code-1 explanation both said "ASCII alphanumeric").

Splitting the physical archive files into year-based subfolders on the NAS and creating the new `.cfg` files is Christer's own work to do (via `bv-config` or by hand) - not something built or automated here.

### Follow-up: back-link now preserves filters instead of resetting them

Christer's PC-native `bv-config` command worked ("now it works ok on the pc"), then he asked whether there's a way to back out of video playback other than the browser's own Back button. Both `archive_recording_detail.html` and `trip_detail.html` already had a back-link at the top of the page (`&larr; {camera_id} archive` / `&larr; All trips`), so the real gap wasn't "no link exists" - it's that `archive_recording_detail.html`'s link pointed at the bare `/archive/{{ camera_id }}` with no query string, resetting any Mode/Date/"only with videos" filters he'd set on the list page, while the browser's native Back button preserves them exactly. That's the more likely reason he'd reach for Back instead of the in-page link.

Fixed by threading the current filter query string through both hops, with no server-side code change: `archive_recording_list.html`'s thumbnail-card links now append `{% if request.url.query %}?{{ request.url.query }}{% endif %}` (the list page's own incoming query string) onto each `/archive/{camera_id}/{recording_id}` link, and `archive_recording_detail.html`'s back-link does the same trick in reverse, appending whatever query string it itself received (which is exactly what the list page just forwarded) onto its `/archive/{camera_id}` href. `request` is available in both templates without any context-dict change - FastAPI/Starlette's `templates.TemplateResponse(request, name, context)` signature (already used at every call site in `app.py`) auto-injects `request` into the Jinja2 context. `trip_detail.html`'s own back-link is untouched - the trip list page has no filters to lose in the first place.

**Verification**: rendered both templates directly via `jinja2.Environment(loader=jinja2.FileSystemLoader(...), autoescape=select_autoescape(["html"]))` (matching Starlette's own autoescape behavior, which a first draft of this check missed and had to correct) with a fake `request.url.query` and a fake `Recording`-shaped object: confirmed a filtered list page (`mode=E&videos_only=true`) produces `/archive/Kirby/<id>?mode=E&amp;videos_only=true` thumbnail links, that the detail page's back-link round-trips the same query string back to `/archive/Kirby?mode=E&amp;videos_only=true`, and that with no filters set both links render exactly as before (`/archive/Kirby/<id>` and `/archive/Kirby`, no trailing `?`) - the change is additive/backward-compatible, not a behavior change for the unfiltered case. No Python/route code touched, so no existing test suite is affected. Worth Christer confirming on the real archive that clicking the back-link after applying filters now returns to the same filtered view.

### Follow-up: archive detail page can show a recording's start location

Christer asked for a way to get a recording's first valid GPS coordinate (when its `.gps` file exists) and show the location "at the start" - in the same format `bv-gps` already prints (`Coordinates: lat,lon` / `Google Maps: <link>` / `Address: <reverse-geocoded>`, from `cli/bv_gps.py`'s live-query output).

Added `ArchiveRecording.gps_path` (`web/archive_browser.py`) resolving `Asset.GPS` to a `Path | None`, and a new `first_valid_gps_fix(gps_path)` function that scans a `.gps` sidecar via the existing `telemetry.gps_reader.read_gps()` and returns the first fix with a real position (`fix.valid` and both lat/lon parsed) - `None` if the file exists but never got a fix (a cold start with no sky view is common for the very first recording after the car's been parked somewhere). Wired into a new route, `GET /archive/{camera_id}/{recording_id}/location` (`web/app.py`), rendered by a new template `archive_recording_location.html`. Three outcomes: no `.gps` file at all ("This recording has no GPS log."), a `.gps` file with no valid fix ("No valid GPS fix found... ### Follow-up: fixed "Internal Server Error" on the start-location page

Christer hit an Internal Server Error clicking the new "Show start location" link on `Kirby_2023/20231231_181926_E` on the NAS. Traced two real, related bugs, both in GPS-reading code, neither exercised until this new per-recording route made someone actually call it on an older/imperfect recording:

1. **`app.py`'s new route didn't guard `MediaToolError`.** `first_valid_gps_fix()` calls `read_gps()`, which raises `MediaToolError` if the `.gps` file can't be read (permissions, a truncated file, etc.) - `trip_export.py`'s own `_merge_gps()` already guards this exact same `read_gps()` call (`try/except MediaToolError: continue`), but the new route only wrapped the *geocoding* call in a `try/except MediaToolError`, not the GPS-read call itself. Fixed by wrapping `first_valid_gps_fix()` too, rendering "could not read this recording's GPS log: ..." instead of 500ing.

2. **The real root cause, in `telemetry/gps_reader.py`'s `_parse_rmc()`**: its own docstring already claimed it returns `None` for "too malformed to use" sentences, but the implementation only checked the field *count* (`len(fields) != 13`) - a field that's present but doesn't parse as the number it's supposed to be (a coordinate with no decimal point, a non-numeric speed/course - exactly the kind of corruption an abrupt power loss mid-write can produce, the same class of real-world file corruption this project has hit before) raised a raw, uncaught `ValueError` straight out of `read_gps()`. Since every existing caller (`_merge_gps()` included) only ever guards `MediaToolError`, this was a latent bug that could in principle have crashed a `bv-export` run too, not just this new web route - it just never got exercised on a bad-enough file until now. Fixed by wrapping the field-parsing block in `try/except ValueError: return None`, so a single corrupted sentence is now skipped exactly like a non-matching line already was, matching what the docstring always claimed.

**Verification**: two new tests in `tests/blackvue/telemetry/test_gps_reader.py` (`test_read_gps_skips_a_sentence_with_a_malformed_coordinate`, `test_read_gps_skips_a_sentence_with_a_non_numeric_speed`) - both would have raised `ValueError` before this fix, now correctly skip the bad sentence (and keep any other well-formed ones in the same file). All 12 tests in the file pass (10 pre-existing + 2 new), and all 38 tests in `test_archive_browser.py` still pass (nothing there changed behaviorally). `app.py`'s route fix verified via `ast.parse()` and manual review only, same limitation as every other app.py route in this project (no fastapi in this sandbox, no `test_app.py` exists for any route). Christer's specific `.gps` file wasn't available to inspect directly, so which of the two bugs actually fired for `20231231_181926_E` is unconfirmed - both are real, both are now fixed, and either one alone would have caused exactly the symptom reported. Worth Christer retrying that same recording's link once this is deployed to confirm it now shows a real result (or a friendly message) instead of a 500.

### Follow-up: fixed real 500 on the NAS - geocode cache tried to write to a read-only mount

Christer hit another Internal Server Error on the archive start-location page, this time with the real traceback (`docker-compose logs bv-web`), which made this one exact rather than guesswork: `OSError: [Errno 30] Read-only file system: '/data/archive/2022/.osm_cache'`, from `load_or_reverse_geocode()`'s `cache_dir.mkdir(...)`.

Root cause: the route cached reverse-geocoded addresses under `<camera's archive path>/.osm_cache`, copying `trip_export.py`'s own `destination.parent / ".osm_cache"` convention for `trip_info.txt`. That convention is only safe for `bv-cli`'s container, which mounts `/data/archive` read-write (`docker-compose.yml`'s `bv-cli` service). `bv-web`'s own container mounts the *same host path* read-only (`- ./data/archive:/data/archive:ro`) - the archive browser was always meant to only ever read recordings, never write into that folder - so the very first reverse-geocode lookup from bv-web crashed the moment it tried to create a cache directory there. This didn't show up in this sandbox's verification (no real filesystem-permission simulation, and `ast.parse()`/manual review can't catch a deployment-topology mismatch like which mount is read-only in which container), which is exactly why Christer's real NAS + the real traceback mattered here.

Fixed by pointing the geocode cache at `default_config_dir() / ".osm_cache"` instead - the same directory `CameraConfigCache` and the job runner already read/write freely (`BEYOND_VIDEO_CONFIG_DIR=/data/camera-config` in `docker-compose.yml`, mounted read-write for `bv-web`), rather than anywhere under the archive. One shared cache across every camera (keyed by rounded lat/lon regardless of which camera/recording it came from) rather than per-camera-archive, which is arguably more correct anyway - the same coordinate geocoded from two different cameras' recordings now shares one cache hit instead of two. This also removed a redundant `_find_camera_archive()` call the old code only needed to compute the (wrong) cache path.

Christer asked for the dark theme back too, on top of the light theme just shipped. Asked how it should be selectable (manual toggle / auto-follow system / both) - he picked manual toggle.

Added `THEME_COOKIE_NAME = "bv_theme"` to `web/auth.py` alongside the existing `SESSION_COOKIE_NAME` (a plain preference cookie, not session/login state - read directly via `request.cookies`, not through `get_current_user()`/`require_login`). ## bv-web job runner: bv-generate and bv-export triggerable from the browser (increment 2)

Christer: "start on putting bv-generate and bv-export on the web to[o]" - the two commands increment 1's own job runner (bv-config/bv-gps) was explicitly built with in mind but never wired up. Asked how much of bv-export's own much larger CLI surface the web form should expose, since bv-config/bv-gps had deliberately exposed only a curated subset (no `--config-dir`/`--host`). Christer's answer: "Full parity but grouped by required, default and the rest" - every flag gets a field, organized into the same Required/Defaults/Optional groups the earlier "grouped form fields" follow-up established.

**bv-generate, the smaller of the two, done first.** `bv_generate.py` refactored to the same injectable `say`/`warn` pattern `bv_config.py`/`bv_gps.py` already use - not just the top-level `_run()`, but every internal helper it calls (`_report`, `_should_write`/`_should_write_for`, all five `_do_*` per-recording action functions), since `bv-generate`'s own existing test suite calls several of those helpers directly without passing `say`/`warn` and needed real-`print` defaults preserved exactly. `JobRunner.start_bv_generate()` builds a real argv list from its own ~17 keyword parameters and runs it through `bv_generate.parse_args()` - full flag parity, per Christer's answer, with the same cross-field validation (`--diarize`/`--srt`/`--lrc` need `--transcribe`/`--translate`; at least one action selected) re-checked in `app.py`'s route *before* calling the job runner, so a bad web form re-renders with a friendly error instead of `parse_args()` raising `SystemExit(2)` inside a route. New `GET`/`POST /jobs/bv-generate` routes, `job_new_bv_generate.html` (camera + action checkboxes + translate language required; model size/language-hint defaulted; everything else optional), a nav tab. All 62 existing `test_bv_generate.py` tests pass with a single one-line change (`bv_generate.run(args)` -> `bv_generate._run(args)` in one test, since `run()` was renamed to match every other bv-* command's own `_run()` shape).

**bv-export was a bigger undertaking, for three real reasons found along the way, not just "more flags."** First, `bv_export()` (the function the CLI has always called) genuinely raises `SystemExit` itself in two places - an empty `--duration-heal-archive` request, a bad `LexicalTimeParser` value - and `test_bv_export.py` has a real `pytest.raises(SystemExit)` around one of them, making that a tested public contract that couldn't just become a `warn()`+return like an ordinary error. Solved by adding `say`/`warn` to `bv_export()` itself (needed anyway, since a real export can run for many minutes and the browser needs live progress) while leaving its two `raise SystemExit(...)` sites completely untouched, then wrapping a *new* `_run()` function around it (used by both `main()` and the job runner) that catches `SystemExit` at exactly that one call site and converts it to `warn(str(exc)) + return 1` - careful here not to double up one raise site's message, which already bakes its own `"bv-export: "` prefix into the text itself. Second, `bv_export.py` turned out to have no standalone `parse_args()` function at all - unlike every other bv-* command, its argument parser was built inline inside `main()`, so there was no reusable way to turn a web form's own argv into parsed `args`. Pulled the parser-building code out into its own `bv_export.parse_args(argv)`, the identical split every other command already has; purely mechanical, confirmed by the existing 109-test suite passing completely unchanged. Third, `bv-export` has dozens of `type=`/mutually-exclusive-group argparse validators (numeric ranges, `--stitch-resolution`'s `WIDTHxHEIGHT` shape, `--stitch-gsensor-pos`/`--stitch-gsensor-xy` being mutually exclusive) - far too many to hand-replicate as `app.py` pre-checks the way bv-generate's own 3-condition check does. Solved with a new `BvExportArgError` exception: `start_bv_export()` runs its own `parse_args(argv)` call under a synchronous, single-call-scoped `contextlib.redirect_stderr()`, and any `SystemExit` from a rejected value gets re-raised as `BvExportArgError` carrying argparse's own message text; `app.py`'s route catches it and re-renders the form, same friendly-error pattern as bv-generate's. This one narrow redirect doesn't conflict with `jobs.py`'s own module docstring warning against redirecting stdout/stderr for a running job - it wraps one plain synchronous function call entirely before any `Job` exists or any thread is spawned, so no concurrently-running job's output could ever be affected by it.

`start_bv_export()` takes ~49 keyword parameters - every one of `bv-export`'s ~44 CLI flags plus `camera_id`/`archive_path`/`target`/`username` - with one deliberate, documented exception to "full parity": `--target` is never a web form field. It's always `app.state.target`, the exact directory the Trips tab already scans, so a web-triggered export shows up there immediately and the form can never be pointed at an arbitrary filesystem path - the same "curated, not an arbitrary-target escape hatch" reasoning bv-gps's own omitted `--host` already established, applied to the one bv-export flag where full parity would have been a real security regression rather than just more form fields. `JobRunner._spawn()`'s completion handler also now catches `SystemExit` alongside the usual `Exception` as defense in depth - `SystemExit` subclasses `BaseException`, not `Exception`, so the old bare `except Exception` would have silently missed one and left a job stuck showing `running` forever; not a substitute for handling it at the source (bv-export's own new `_run()` already does), just a backstop that benefits every job type.

New `GET`/`POST /jobs/bv-export` routes and `job_new_bv_export.html` - the full Required (camera)/Defaults (`--stitch-layout` and every `--stitch-mirror-*`/`--stitch-gsensor-size` flag that ships with a real argparse default)/Optional (everything else: time filters, gap tuning, map/g-sensor/graph rendering toggles, every `--stitch-*` panel flag, `--overwrite`/`--dry-run`/`--debug`) grouping Christer asked for, plus a nav tab ("Export trips"). `app.py`'s stale module docstring ("bv-download/bv-generate/bv-export aren't wired in yet") corrected to name only `bv-download` as still outstanding.

**Verification**: `bv_generate.py`/`bv_export.py`/`jobs.py`/`app.py` all `ast.parse()`-clean. `job_new_bv_generate.html`/`job_new_bv_export.html` rendered directly via `jinja2.Environment(..., autoescape=select_autoescape(["html"]))` across normal/error/no-cameras-yet states, and `base.html`'s nav confirmed to mark the right tab active for both new routes - genuine template checks, same limitation as every other `app.py`-adjacent template in this project (no fastapi in this sandbox, so the routes themselves can't run, only their templates and the `jobs.py` logic underneath them). All 62 `test_bv_generate.py` and all 109 `test_bv_export.py` tests re-run and pass after their respective refactors. `tests/blackvue/web/test_jobs.py` grew from 28 to 39 tests: `start_bv_generate()` covered for say/warn wiring, flag-to-parsed-args fidelity, and a failing exit code; `start_bv_export()` covered for say/warn/command_line wiring, its own defaults and flags reaching `parse_args()` correctly, confirming `target` stays keyword-only and is never taken from anywhere but the one `Path` given, `BvExportArgError` raised (and no phantom `Job` left behind) for both a bad scalar value (`--stitch-resolution garbage`) and a rejected mutually-exclusive combination (`--stitch-gsensor-pos` + `--stitch-gsensor-xy` together), and a failing exit code. This sandbox's Python (3.10) can't import `tomllib` at all (the project needs 3.11+, and `bv_config`/`camera_config` are imported transitively by `test_jobs.py`) - worked around with a throwaway local `tomllib` shim module (`load`/`loads`/`TOMLDecodeError` stubs, never actually exercised since every test here monkeypatches the target `_run()` before anything would call them) placed first on `PYTHONPATH`, not part of the repo. All 39 tests pass through it. `docs/WEB_ARCHITECTURE.md` updated throughout (increment framing, the Job runner section's `SystemExit`-handling/`parse_args()`-extraction/`BvExportArgError` design notes, the curated-subset-vs-full-parity design decision, the structure/template listing).

## bv-web full-app background image (light/dark matched pair, blur + tint overlay)

Christer shared two AI-generated background mockups - an aerial city render with a red car, one styled for each theme - and asked for design feedback. Flagged that the two didn't read as a matched pair (different rendering styles) and that both were too busy for a full-bleed page background without some treatment. Christer's response: derive the dark-theme image *from* the light-theme one specifically, rather than treating them as two independent images, so they'd actually match. No image-generation tool exists in this environment (confirmed via `ToolSearch`), so this was done as a deterministic pixel transform instead: `matplotlib.colors.rgb_to_hsv`/`hsv_to_rgb` remap the light source's Value channel only (`V_new = shadow_v + (highlight_v - shadow_v) * V_original`, `shadow_v=0.045`, a small saturation boost `S_new = clip(S_original * 1.12, 0, 1)`), leaving Hue untouched everywhere - a uniform brightness curve applied to every pixel regardless of original saturation, so both saturated content (the red car, pink roofs) and desaturated content (pavement) darken together instead of the saturated areas staying bright while everything else goes dark (a real problem in an earlier RGB-duotone attempt). First result (`highlight_v=0.20`) came back from Christer as "a little to dark"; raised to `highlight_v=0.27` (~35% brighter) and that version was accepted outright: "Yes we go with that for now, we can always change it if it feels wrong."

Asked where the accepted pair should actually apply and how to keep text legible over it - Christer picked "Full app background, every page" and "Blur + dark gradient overlay."

**Implementation.** The two accepted images were downscaled from their original PNGs (2720x1536, up to 8.24MB) to 1920px-wide JPEGs (~255-575KB) and placed at `src/blackvue/web/static/backgrounds/bg-light.jpg`/`bg-dark.jpg` - full-resolution PNGs would have been a heavy, pointless page-weight cost for what's ultimately a blurred backdrop, and JPEG's compression artifacts are invisible once blurred. Added a `static/backgrounds/*.jpg` entry to `pyproject.toml`'s `[tool.setuptools.package-data]` `"blackvue.web"` block (same lesson that file's comments already document twice over for templates and the bundled font/mirror-icon - a real install silently drops anything not listed there) and a `StaticFiles` mount (`app.mount("/static", StaticFiles(directory=STATIC_DIR), ...)`) in `app.py` - the first static-file serving this app has needed, since trip/archive files were always served through their own authenticated allow-list routes rather than a blanket mount. This one's deliberately unauthenticated: it's two cosmetic images, not trip data, and the login page itself wants the same background.

`base.html` gained `--bg-image`/`--bg-rgb` custom properties (light values in `:root`, dark overrides in the existing `html[data-theme="dark"]` block - the same per-theme mechanism every other color in this file already uses) and two new fixed, full-viewport layers inserted right after `<body>`: `.page-bg` (the theme's image, `background-size: cover`, `filter: blur(18px)`, scaled 1.1x to hide the blur's own edge fringe) at `z-index: 0`, and `.page-tint` (a `linear-gradient` wash of `rgba(var(--bg-rgb), 0.82-0.9)` - `--bg-rgb` exists purely because CSS can't add alpha to a bare hex custom property directly) at `z-index: 1` on top of it - this tint layer is what Christer's "dark gradient overlay" choice maps to, and is what actually keeps everything legible; the blur alone wasn't enough over the busier parts of the source photo. All of the old page content, previously styled directly on `<body>` (`max-width: 960px`, centered, padded), now lives in a `.page-shell` div at `z-index: 2` wrapping everything between `<body>` and `</body>` - `body` itself keeps only a plain `background: var(--bg)` as a same-color fallback if the image never loads, `margin: 0`, and `color: var(--text)`. Every existing panel/table/form component (`.panel`-style backgrounds, `pre.job-output`, `.command-help`, thumbnail cards, etc.) already had its own solid `var(--panel-bg)` and needed no changes - only the page's own margins/chrome (header, tab bar, empty space around content) now show the blurred/tinted photo instead of a flat color.

**Verification**: `app.py` and `base.html` both changed cleanly - `ast.parse()` on `app.py`; `base.html` rendered directly via `jinja2.Environment(..., autoescape=select_autoescape(["html"]))` across dark/light cookie states and both a logged-in (`trip_list.html`) and logged-out (`login.html`, no `user`) context, confirming `.page-bg`/`.page-tint`/`.page-shell` all render, `data-theme` still resolves correctly per cookie, and the background layers render even on the login page (no toggle control shown there, matching the existing `{% if user %}` gating, but the image/tint still apply). Ran the rendered HTML through Python's `html.parser` to walk the full tag stack and confirm it balances to empty at the end - catches any mismatched/unclosed div from wrapping the old body content in the new `.page-shell`, which a plain visual read-through of the diff could easily miss. Confirmed both JPEGs actually exist on disk at their expected sizes and that `pyproject.toml`'s package-data entry matches the real path. Same sandbox limitation as every other `app.py`/template change this engagement: no fastapi here, so the `StaticFiles` mount itself and the real HTTP `/static/...` response can't be exercised directly - worth Christer confirming on the real deployment that both images actually load (not just that the CSS referencing them is well-formed) and that the blur/tint strength reads right on a real monitor, not just in isolated crops.

## bv-web job runner: bv-download triggerable from the browser (increment 3, completing pipeline coverage)

Christer: "wire bv-download into bv-web's job runner, same pattern as bv-generate/bv-export" - the last of the five `bv-*` pipeline commands (`bv-config`/`bv-gps` in increment 1, `bv-generate`/`bv-export` in increment 2) to get a browser trigger, completing full pipeline coverage from the web UI.

Unlike `bv-export`, `bv_download.py` already had a clean standalone `parse_args()`/`main()` split - no bug to fix first. The refactor to injectable `say`/`warn` was purely mechanical: a new `_default_warn()` matching the other commands' own, both `_run()` and `_capture_record_time()` gaining `say=print, warn=_default_warn` keyword params, every internal `print()`/`print(..., file=sys.stderr)` call converted to `say(...)`/`warn(...)`. All 47 pre-existing `test_bv_download.py` tests pass unchanged, confirming the refactor is behavior-preserving.

**The one real design question: `confirm()`'s interactive prompt.** `bv-download` has exactly one interactive moment - a plain `input()` call gated behind `sys.stdin.isatty() and sys.stdout.isatty()` - never built around `ask()` the way `bv-config`'s wizard is, because it reads real process stdin directly, which the job runner's queue-based `ask()`/`Job.submit_answer()` mechanism has no way to intercept. A stray real-stdin block here would hang a job forever with no way for the browser to unblock it. Solved the same way the tty gate itself would likely already handle it in a backgrounded server process, but made it unconditional rather than incidental: `start_bv_download()` always appends `--yes` to the argv it builds, so `confirm()` is never reached from a job regardless of the host process's actual tty state. Documented in both `_run()`'s own docstring and `start_bv_download()`'s.

`bv-download`'s positional CLI argument is already the camera id itself (unlike `bv-generate`/`bv-export`, whose positional argument is a bare archive path needing `app.py`'s `_find_camera_archive()` resolution), so `start_bv_download()` follows `start_bv_gps()`'s simpler shape - just the id, no path lookup - and lets `bv_download._run()` do its own config lookup exactly as a real terminal invocation would.

`bv-download` sits between the two "curated subset" (`bv-config`/`bv-gps`) and "full parity" (`bv-generate`/`bv-export`) precedents: full parity for its actual download-tuning flags (`--mode`, `--from`/`--until`/`--timestamp`, `--dry-run`, `--files`, `--verbose`, `--trace`), but `--host`/`--target`/`--config-dir`/`--yes` are deliberately never form fields - the first three for the same curated-id-only reasoning `bv-gps`'s omitted `--host` already established, `--yes` because it's always forced on internally instead of exposed. `--files` requires `--dry-run` is bv-download's only cross-field rule, handled with the same plain `app.py` pre-check `bv-generate`'s own small-condition-count approach uses.

New `GET`/`POST /jobs/bv-download` routes, `job_new_bv_download.html`, and a nav tab ("Download recordings"). The form introduces a new `Time range` `.option-group` (From/Until/Timestamp laid out side by side via the existing `.field-row` CSS) placed right after `Required` rather than buried in `Optional`, and groups the recording-kind checkboxes plus the dry-run/files/verbose/trace toggles into `.checkbox-row`s - both conventions established in the immediately-prior session's form-grouping work, applied here for the first time to a brand-new form rather than retrofitted onto an existing one. `--trace`'s progress dots stay on raw `print()`, not `say()` - a partial-line, no-trailing-newline stream has no sensible representation in `Job.output`'s list-of-complete-lines shape, so a `--trace` job's dots land in bv-web's own process console/log instead of the job's browser-visible output, called out explicitly in the trace checkbox's own label text so the owner isn't left wondering where they went. `app.py`'s module docstring updated from "bv-download isn't wired in yet" to "every bv-* pipeline command now has a browser trigger."

**Verification**: `bv_download.py`/`jobs.py`/`app.py` all `ast.parse()`-clean. `job_new_bv_download.html` rendered directly via `jinja2.Environment(..., autoescape=select_autoescape(["html"]))` across normal/error/no-cameras-yet states and checked for balanced tags via `html.parser`; `base.html`'s nav confirmed to mark the new tab active for `/jobs/bv-download`. Field names in the template cross-checked by regex against `app.py`'s `Form(...)` parameter names to rule out a silent mismatch. All 47 `test_bv_download.py` tests re-run and pass after the refactor. `tests/blackvue/web/test_jobs.py` grew from 39 to 47 tests: `start_bv_download()` covered for say/warn wiring and the forced `--yes`, defaults/modes/time-range/dry-run+files/verbose+trace all reaching `parse_args()` correctly, `--host`/`--target` confirmed absent from the method's own signature via `inspect.signature()`, and a failing exit code. Same sandbox limitations as every other increment in this series (Python 3.10, no real fastapi/pytest - verified via the same `ast.parse()`/shim-harness/Jinja2-render approach) - worth Christer confirming on the real deployment that a submitted job actually runs to completion and that `--trace` output shows up in the container's own logs as expected, not in the job page. `docs/WEB_ARCHITECTURE.md` updated throughout (job runner's target-module list, the new `confirm()`/forced-`--yes` design paragraph, the camera-id-not-archive-path note, routes list, curated-subset-vs-full-parity's bv-download paragraph, structure/template listing, and the Form layout paragraph's new `Time range` group).

## bv-web welcome landing page (Trips moved off GET /)

Christer, after a genuine "pat yourself on the back" for the bv-download increment: "I don't think we should start with trips after login, yes trips are the end goal, but not the starting. Maybe we should have a Big 'WELCOME to BEYOND VIDEO' as start page, with a short summary, we could also make the background totally untinted for this page."

**Routing.** `GET /` used to be the trip list directly (`trip_list()`). Moved the trip list to its own `GET /trips` (same `require_login` gating, same `trips.py`/`scan_trips()` underneath, unchanged otherwise), and gave `GET /` a new `welcome()` handler rendering a new `welcome.html` template - a short "Welcome to Beyond Video, {username}" heading and summary, plus a `Home`/`Trips`/`Browse archive` quick-link grid available to any logged-in user, and a second owner-only grid linking every job-trigger route (`bv-config`/`bv-gps`/`bv-download`/`bv-generate`/`bv-export`). `POST /login`'s own redirect (`next or "/"`) needed no change - it already defaulted to `/`, which now happens to be the welcome page instead of the trip list, exactly the behavior Christer asked for. Every internal link that used to point at bare `/` expecting the trip list (`base.html`'s "Trips" nav tab, `trip_detail.html`'s "All trips" back-link, `forbidden.html`'s "Back to trips" link) was repointed at `/trips`; `base.html`'s header title link and a new "Home" nav tab now own `/` instead. Verified nothing else in the templates directory still assumed `/` meant trips (grepped every `href="/"` after the change).

**Untinted background.** `base.html`'s `.page-tint` div previously had no per-page override - every page got the same fixed dark wash over the blurred background photo (see the earlier full-app-background entry above). Added a `{% block page_tint_class %}{% endblock %}` to the tint `<div>`'s own class attribute (empty by default, so every existing template renders identically to before) and a `.page-tint--none { opacity: 0; }` rule; `welcome.html` is the only template that fills the block, turning the tint off completely so the background photo shows through at full strength - a deliberate one-page opt-out rather than a reusable opacity variable, since there was only one real request for it. Paired with new `.welcome-hero`/`.quick-links`/`.quick-link-card` CSS - the hero heading/summary text gets a subtle text-shadow so it stays readable directly over the now-untinted photo, and the quick-link cards keep their own solid `--panel-bg` background so they read clearly regardless.

**Verification**: `app.py` `ast.parse()`-clean. All five affected/new templates (`welcome.html` for both an owner and a viewer, `trip_list.html`, `trip_detail.html`, `forbidden.html`, `login.html`) rendered directly via `jinja2.Environment(..., autoescape=select_autoescape(["html"]))` and checked for balanced tags via `html.parser` - confirmed the tint-override class only appears on `welcome.html`'s render, that a viewer's welcome page never contains any `/jobs/*` link while an owner's does, and that the `Home`/`Trips` nav tabs each get `active` on the correct path (`/` vs. `/trips`) and not the other. No route-level tests exist for `app.py` anywhere in this project (this sandbox has no real fastapi, and no prior increment added any - `app.py` changes have always been verified this same template-rendering-plus-`ast.parse()` way), so this is the same depth of verification every other `app.py` change in this engagement has had - worth Christer confirming on the real deployment that the welcome page actually renders end-to-end and that the untinted background reads well against the real photo, not just that the CSS class wiring is correct in isolation.

## bv-web welcome page: also remove the blur, not just the tint (follow-up)

Christer, after seeing the welcome page: "It look tinted to me." Walked through it together - checked the rendered page source live, confirmed `class="page-tint page-tint--none"` was actually present and the `opacity: 0` rule was correctly wired (both verified against the exact commit that shipped in the entry above). A screenshot then made the real cause obvious: the dark wash genuinely was off, but `.page-bg`'s existing `filter: blur(18px)` alone was enough to make the photo read as flat and gray - a heavily blurred image looks desaturated/washed out even with zero color overlay on top of it, and the tint this page used to show was already down to a subtle 0.09-0.18 opacity (see the earlier tuning history), so removing it made less visual difference than expected against that same blur.

Added the same override mechanism `.page-tint`/`.page-tint--none` already established, mirrored for `.page-bg`: a `{% block page_bg_class %}{% endblock %}` on the `.page-bg` div (empty by default, so no other page is affected) and a `.page-bg--sharp { filter: none; transform: none; }` modifier - `transform: scale(1.1)` only ever existed to hide blur's own edge fringe, so it goes too once there's no blur to hide. `welcome.html` now fills both blocks (`page_bg_class` -> `page-bg--sharp`, `page_tint_class` -> `page-tint--none`), the only template that opts into either.

Removing the blur meant the hero heading/summary now sits directly over a much busier, higher-contrast photo than any blurred backdrop - strengthened `.welcome-hero`'s text-shadow (a tight dark shadow for edge contrast plus a wider, softer one) rather than adding a background chip/box behind the text, which would have reintroduced exactly the kind of solid wash Christer asked to remove from this page in the first place.

**Verification**: same Jinja2-render-plus-tag-balance approach as the entry above, re-run after this change - confirmed `welcome.html` renders `class="page-bg page-bg--sharp"` and `class="page-tint page-tint--none"` together, and that `trip_list.html` (and by extension every other unmodified template) still renders plain `class="page-bg"`/`class="page-tint"` with neither modifier, so this change is scoped to the one page it's meant for. `app.py` untouched this round (`ast.parse()`-clean regardless). This bug only turned up because Christer looked at a real screenshot and shared the live page source on request - worth remembering for future CSS-only changes in this project that the sandbox's static verification (rendering + tag-balance checks) can confirm markup/CSS *correctness* but can't catch a design choice that looks different than intended once actually seen.

## bv-web login page also gets the untinted background

Christer, right after confirming the header/nav fix: "i think the login page should also have an untinted background." A natural follow-on - `login.html` is the other single-purpose "entry" page in the app (no table/panel-dense content to protect, same as welcome.html), so it gets the identical treatment rather than a bespoke third option.

`login.html` now fills the same `page_bg_class`/`page_tint_class` blocks `welcome.html` introduced (`page-bg--sharp`/`page-tint--none`) - no new CSS needed for the photo itself. The header title renders on the login page too (logged-out `base.html` still shows "Beyond Video", just without the nav tabs/account bar, which are gated behind `{% if user %}`), so it already picks up the header text-shadow fix from the entry above for free via the same `.page-tint--none ~ .page-shell header` selector. The one genuinely new gap: `login.html`'s own field labels ("Username", "Password") and its error message sit as plain text directly on the page with no panel behind them, same problem the welcome page's hero copy had - extended the existing shadow selector to include `.login-box label` and `.error`, scoped by the same sibling combinator, so this only ever applies on a page with the tint off.

**Verification**: rendered `login.html` via Jinja2 for both a logged-out anonymous request and an error state ("Invalid username or password."), confirmed `class="page-bg page-bg--sharp"`/`class="page-tint page-tint--none"` both present, the new selector text appears in the served `<style>` block, and both renders stay tag-balanced. `app.py` untouched this round.

## bv-web untinted pages: text-shadow gives way to frosted-glass panels

Christer, after the header/nav shadow fix from the entry above: sent a fresh screenshot, essentially unchanged from the one that started that entry - "Not readable in light mode." Two rounds of text-shadow (first the hero copy alone, then extended/strengthened to cover the header and nav too) both came back the same way. The real problem: this particular background photo (dense aerial rooftops/streets, detail everywhere) has no flat stretch of color a shadow's small blur radius can reliably darken against - a shadow wins locally, against whatever's directly behind one letter, not against every possible pixel color text might land on across a whole heading or nav bar.

Replaced the shadow rules entirely with small frosted-glass panels: `background: rgba(var(--bg-rgb), 0.78)` plus `backdrop-filter: blur(14px)` (`-webkit-backdrop-filter` alongside for broader support) on the header, `.tabs`, `.login-box`, and `welcome.html`'s own `.welcome-hero` card, with a smaller matching chip style for `.quick-links-group-label`. This is a real solid surface, not a shadow trick, so it doesn't depend on what's behind it at all - guaranteed contrast regardless of photo content. Deliberately framed as different from the `.page-tint` Christer originally asked to remove: the tint covered the *entire* photo at all times; these panels cover only the handful of small regions that actually hold text - a toolbar strip, a couple of cards - leaving the rest of the photo, which is most of the visible page, fully exposed. Still gated through the exact same `.page-tint--none ~ .page-shell` sibling-combinator scoping the shadow rules used, so only `welcome.html`/`login.html` are affected; every other page's header/nav is untouched.

Mechanically: `header`/`.tabs`/`.login-box` share one base rule (background/blur/border-radius/`box-sizing: border-box`) with per-element padding/margin tweaks layered on (`.tabs` drops its usual `border-bottom` since the panel itself now provides the visual separation). `.welcome-hero` became a centered, max-width card (was previously unconstrained full-width text) with padding instead of a bare heading/paragraph. `.quick-links-group-label` gained `display: inline-block` so its own chip background only wraps the label text rather than spanning the full row.

**Verification**: same Jinja2-render-plus-tag-balance approach as every prior round in this feature - `welcome.html` (confirmed `backdrop-filter: blur(14px)` and all four new selector blocks present in the served `<style>`), `login.html`, and `trip_list.html` (to confirm zero effect on an untinted-off page) all render cleanly and stay tag-balanced. `app.py` untouched. `backdrop-filter` is well-supported in Chromium/Safari/current Firefox, so no fallback beyond the semi-opaque `background` itself (which alone, without the blur, still provides adequate contrast - the blur is a visual nicety, not load-bearing for legibility) - worth Christer confirming the frosted look reads well on the real deployment, since this sandbox can't render actual CSS, only verify the markup/rule text is correct and well-formed.

## Easter egg: a submarine glimpse in the welcome page's water

"Now Crazy Christer think it would be fun so se a glimps/shadow of an underwater u-boat with periscope up at the water to the left" - a pure fun request, no functional motivation, made possible by the untinted/unblurred welcome-page background from the entries above: with the photo now shown at full clarity, the wide dark-navy water area on the left of both `bg-light.jpg`/`bg-dark.jpg` was an obvious place to hide something.

Composited directly into the two background image files themselves (not a CSS overlay) - a submarine sighted at this angle/distance should scale and crop together with the rest of the photo exactly like everything else in it, which only works if it's baked into the same pixels rather than positioned separately by CSS coordinates that would drift out of alignment at different viewport sizes. Built with Pillow: a supersampled (4x), rotated, Gaussian-blurred dark ellipse (hull) plus a smaller, slightly-more-opaque ellipse (sail/conning tower) for the submerged shadow - the blur is what makes it read as *underwater* rather than a flat black cutout, since a shadow beneath the surface should have soft, uncertain edges. On top of that, unblurred and fully opaque: a thin periscope tube rising above the sail with a small head-cap and a single-pixel lens glint, plus a few faint concentric ripple rings at the waterline - the one part of the submarine that's actually above the water gets to look sharp and real, everything submerged stays soft and shadowy.

Placed in the deep-water region on the left (roughly 10% in from the edge, well clear of the coastline curve and the marina in the bottom-left corner), oriented at a slight diagonal as if mid-transit. Sampled the water's own base color at that spot in each image (light theme: `~(4, 16, 31)`; dark theme: `~(1, 8, 18)`, confirming the dark theme's water is close to pure black) and tuned the hull's fill/alpha separately per theme - the same near-black hull that reads as a subtle shadow against the light theme's slightly-lighter navy was nearly invisible against the dark theme's near-black water, so the dark-theme version uses a marginally lighter, bluer fill and higher alpha to stay a "glimpse" rather than disappearing entirely.

## Submarine invisible: browser cache, not the image

Christer, after the easter egg shipped: "I cant see it even when i am searchin." My own verification (Pillow renders, cropped and full-page) clearly showed the submarine in both theme images, so the image itself wasn't in question - something between the updated JPEG on disk and what actually reached the browser was.

Root cause: `bg-light.jpg`/`bg-dark.jpg` are served through a plain `StaticFiles` mount, which sends `Last-Modified`/`ETag` but no explicit `Cache-Control`. Without an explicit directive, browsers fall back to heuristic freshness (roughly Chromium's "10% of the file's age" rule), and since these files have sat unchanged at the same URL for a while, a plain reload can be satisfied straight from the browser's disk cache without even asking the server whether the file changed - only a hard reload (or a genuinely new URL) is guaranteed to see the new bytes. Overwriting the JPEGs in place, same filename, was exactly the case this bites: the HTML re-fetches fresh every request, but the referenced background image doesn't.

Fix: cache-bust with a manual version query string on both `--bg-image` URLs in `base.html` (`bg-light.jpg?v=2` / `bg-dark.jpg?v=2`), bumped from whatever implicit "v1" the original unversioned URLs were. A query-string change is a different URL as far as the browser cache is concerned, so it forces a real fetch regardless of heuristic freshness - no server-side cache-control changes needed. Documented directly in `base.html`'s own comment above `--bg-image` that the `?v=` number must be bumped by hand whenever either JPEG is overwritten again, since nothing computes it automatically (no build step in this project, deliberately, so a manual bump matches how everything else here already works).

**Verification**: rendered `welcome.html` via the same `jinja2.Environment(..., autoescape=select_autoescape(["html"]))` approach as every other template check this session, confirmed both `--bg-image` URLs render as `bg-light.jpg?v=2` / `bg-dark.jpg?v=2` in the served `<style>` block. This is a browser-caching behavior fix, unverifiable by static rendering alone (the sandbox has no real browser or HTTP cache to exercise) - the real test is Christer doing one more normal (non-hard) reload against the live server and finally seeing the submarine, which the bumped query string should now guarantee even without a hard refresh.

## Submarine still invisible after the cache-bust fix: real root cause was contrast, not caching

Christer, after the cache-bust commit: "No, not even in another browser." With both of those eliminated, went back to first principles and actually measured pixel values instead of trusting a visual "looks fine" read from a Pillow render: sampled the hull's own drawn pixels against the surrounding open water in both images. Light theme: hull `(2, 10, 21)` vs. water `(5, 17, 33)` - a delta of single digits per channel. Dark theme: hull `(9, 21, 37)` vs. water `(1, 8, 18)` - similarly small. The original tuning (near-black hull fill blended at 145-175/255 alpha onto water that's *already* near-black) produced almost no measurable contrast at all - the "shadow" was real in the sense that the pixels were genuinely drawn, but indistinguishable from the water around it to an actual eye. Every earlier "verification" in this thread only ever confirmed the ripple rings and periscope tip (which do have real contrast) were present and correctly shaped, never that the hull shadow itself - the main body of the submarine - was visible. Dark theme, where the water is already close to true black and can't be darkened further, goes the other way - a distinctly lighter steel-blue `(30,55,85)` at alpha 225 (was a barely-lighter near-black at 175), producing a ~25-60 delta. Periscope line/cap widened slightly and ripple-ring alpha raised too, same direction as the hull fix - more contrast, not more subtlety.

Also fixed the underlying reason contrast couldn't be verified through the actual serving path: `base.html`'s `--bg-image` URLs already had a `?v=` cache-buster from the previous round, bumped `v=2` -> `v=3` here since the image bytes changed again - unrelated to why the sub was invisible this time, but still needed so this round's fix actually reaches a browser without relying on a hard refresh.

Re-saved at quality=85 (light 606KB, dark 283KB, same size class as every prior version). ## Submarine visibility: light too subtle, dark too bold - per-theme rebalance

Christer, after the contrast-fix commit: "I see some rings on the water but not much more than that in light mode, in dark mode its too obvious." Confirms the contrast diagnosis from the entry above was the right direction (both themes now genuinely visible, unlike the totally-invisible original), but the two themes needed opposite corrections rather than one shared tweak.

Light theme: the hull's Gaussian blur (radius 5, on top of an already-modest 230x52px shape) was spreading the black fill thin enough that only the ripple rings and periscope - the crisp, unblurred elements - registered; the hull itself stayed under the eye's contrast threshold even at alpha 235. Fixed by going bigger and sharper rather than just darker: hull/sail alpha to full 255, blur radius cut from 5 to 3 (less diffusion, denser core), and the ellipse itself enlarged (length 190->230, half-width 20->26) so there's more area for the eye to catch even softened at the edges.

Dark theme: the opposite problem - hull alpha 225 at a distinctly lighter steel-blue fill against near-black water made the shape read as a solid, obvious blob rather than a glimpse. Pulled back hard: hull/sail alpha 225/245 -> 150/175, hull fill darkened from `(30,55,85)` to `(16,30,48)` (still lighter than the water, just less aggressively so), ripple alpha roughly halved. Kept the same blur radius (5) and size as the very first attempt here, since dark theme's problem was never diffusion - it was too much raw contrast, not too little.

Bumped `?v=4` on both `--bg-image` URLs in `base.html`, same cache-bust mechanism as the previous two rounds.

## bv-web job page: pause auto-refresh instead of losing scroll position

Christer, after confirming the submarine easter egg was settled ("Hard to see, but a very good easter-egg. Nice."): "Now to the refreshable job output, i tried to see what the log said, but it kept refreshing and go back to the top. Should we have some pause button or can it be solved in a different way."

`job_detail.html`'s `<meta http-equiv="refresh" content="2">` is a full page reload, not a partial update - fine for a short job, but reading anywhere above the very bottom of a long-running job's output means getting yanked back to the top every two seconds. Considered a JS-polled partial update (fetch the output, patch just the `<pre>`, preserve scroll) but this app has stayed deliberately JS-free everywhere else (server-rendered Jinja2, plain forms for Cancel/Answer/filters), so introducing the first script just to fix a scroll position felt like the wrong tool. Went with what Christer suggested instead: a pause button.

`GET /jobs/{job_id}` now reads a `?paused=1` query param and passes it into the template. The `<meta refresh>` (and the "Running... this page refreshes automatically." note) are suppressed whenever `paused` is true, and a small `.refresh-toggle` line above the output offers "Pause auto-refresh" (links to the same URL with `?paused=1`) or, once paused, "Auto-refresh paused - output frozen as of this load. Resume auto-refresh" (links back to the plain URL). No JavaScript, no new state on the `Job` itself - `paused` lives entirely in the URL, the same server-rendered-link pattern the archive browser's own filters already use. Pausing freezes the page on whatever snapshot it already loaded; resuming is just an ordinary reload that happens to go back to auto-refreshing.

**Verification**: rendered `job_detail.html` across `status in {running, waiting_for_input, succeeded}` crossed with `paused in {True, False}` via the usual `jinja2.Environment(..., autoescape=select_autoescape(["html"]))` approach - confirmed the `<meta refresh>` tag is present only for `running` + not paused, the Pause/Resume links appear on exactly the states that make sense, and every combination stays tag-balanced via the `html.parser`-based checker. `app.py` `ast.parse()`-clean.

## bv-ls joins the job runner - the first bv-* command, wired in last

Same message as the pause-button request: "We have also forgotten to include the first bv- command created." `bv-ls` (`git log --diff-filter=A` confirms it was genuinely the very first `bv-*` CLI command this project ever had, in the commit literally titled "Add archive library and initial bv-ls command") had never gotten a browser trigger across every earlier round of wiring bv-config/bv-gps/bv-download/bv-generate/bv-export into `bv-web` - an oversight nobody had noticed until now, despite `app.py`'s own module docstring having claimed "every bv-* pipeline command now has a browser trigger" since the bv-download round.

**Refactor first.** `bv_ls.py` was pure `print()` throughout, with no injectable output at all - unlike every other bv-* CLI, which already went through this same refactor in an earlier round. Threaded a `say=print` parameter through `print_trips()` and `bv_ls()`, and split `main()`'s inline argparse setup into a standalone `parse_args()` plus a new `_run(args, *, say=print)` wrapper - the same `parse_args()`/`_run()`/`main()` shape every other bv-* CLI already has. `bv-ls` has no warnings or prompts of its own, so unlike `bv_gps.py`'s `_run()` there's no `ask`/`warn` to thread through, just `say`.

One real wrinkle the refactor had to solve: the grouped (non-`--trips`) table built each header/data row across several `print(..., end=...)` calls rather than one call per line - relying on `end="  "`/`end=" "` to build up one continuous line across calls, finished off by a bare `print()` for the trailing newline. A `say` that appends one complete `Job.output` entry per call (as the job runner supplies) has no way to represent a still-open partial line - the same problem `--trace`'s progress dots hit in the bv-download round, solved there by leaving `--trace` on raw `print()` since there was no other option. Here there was a better option: each row is now built up as a single string first (`group_header`, `asset_header`, and each per-group `row`) and handed to `say` once, complete. Verified byte-for-byte equivalence directly - ran `bv_ls()` once with real stdout captured via `contextlib.redirect_stdout` and once with `say=list.append` joined back into a string, for the grouped table, `--trips`, and `--all` paths, and confirmed identical output (aside from one unrelated pre-existing warning line printed by a different module entirely).

**Job runner + routes.** `JobRunner.start_bv_ls()` mirrors `start_bv_generate()`/`start_bv_export()`'s shape (full flag parity, `archive_path` resolved by the caller via `_find_camera_archive()`) rather than the curated-id-only shape `bv-config`/`bv-gps` use - there's no destructive operation or arbitrary-target escape hatch to guard against here, so there was no reason to curate a subset. `GET`/`POST /jobs/bv-ls` follow the same pattern as `bv-generate`'s own routes; the two numeric fields (`--max-gap`/`--gap-tolerance`, both genuinely optional - blank means "use bv-ls's own default", not zero) are cleaned to `int` or `None` directly in the route with a friendly re-render on `ValueError`, rather than reaching for `BvExportArgError`'s `parse_args()`-`SystemExit`-catching machinery, which would be overkill for two unconstrained integers with no cross-field rules. `job_new_bv_ls.html` follows `job_new_bv_download.html`'s `Required`/`Time range`/`Optional` grouping (no `Defaults` group - bv-ls has no fields that ship with a non-empty default worth calling out separately). Added a `List recordings` nav tab (owner-only, same gating as every other job tab) and a quick-link card on the welcome page's "Run a pipeline step" grid.

**Verification**: `bv_ls.py`/`jobs.py`/`app.py` all `ast.parse()`-clean. Manually re-ran every scenario `tests/blackvue/cli/test_bv_ls.py` already covers (asset-group-span logic, missing/non-directory path errors, every `--trips` gap/movement/duration/tolerance case) directly against the refactored module via `PYTHONPATH=src` (no pytest available in this sandbox, same constraint as every other increment) - all pass unchanged. `JobRunner.start_bv_ls()` exercised end-to-end for real (a real temp archive, real background thread, no mocking) - confirmed it reaches `SUCCEEDED` and produces the expected trip table in `Job.output`. `job_new_bv_ls.html` and the updated `welcome.html`/`base.html` rendered via the usual Jinja2-render-plus-tag-balance approach across owner/viewer and with/without an error, confirming the new quick-link only shows for an owner and the nav tab activates only on `/jobs/bv-ls`. `trip_list.html` re-rendered to confirm the `base.html` nav change caused zero regression elsewhere. Added 6 new tests to `tests/blackvue/web/test_jobs.py` for `start_bv_ls()` (say-wiring, `--all`, the `--trips` flag group, the `duration=True`-omits-`--no-duration` default, and a failing exit code) - not run through pytest for the same sandbox-limitation reason as everything else here, but structured identically to the existing `start_bv_generate()`/`start_bv_gps()` tests they sit beside. Worth Christer confirming on the real deployment that the new job page and nav tab render and submit correctly end-to-end.

Christer, after using the new bv-ls job page: "Your hint talks about lexical dates like yesterday, when did we support that?" It never did. `lexicaltimeparser.py`'s `LexicalTimeParser`/`TimeInterval` only do digit-prefix expansion - `20260715` pads out to a full `YYYYMMDD_HHMMSS` interval, `2026` pads out to cover the whole year - there is no keyword parsing anywhere in the codebase, no "today"/"yesterday"/"tomorrow", nothing natural-language at all. The four job-form tooltips (`From` field on `job_new_bv_ls.html`, `job_new_bv_download.html`, `job_new_bv_generate.html`, and the equivalent line on `job_new_bv_export.html`) all claimed "or a lexical time like 'yesterday'" regardless. Replaced the false claim on all four with an accurate description of what the prefix expansion actually does: "or a shorter prefix - 2026 matches the whole year, 20260715 matches just that day."

**Verification**: `grep -rn "yesterday" src/blackvue/web/templates/` now returns nothing. ## Real "Beyond Video" wordmark - header, favicon, welcome hero

## Job page showed stale output after browser Back - bfcache, not the job runner

Christer, after confirming background jobs survive navigating away: "I noticed it wasnt enough to go back to the job, you also needed to refresh the page." The job runner itself was never the problem - each job really does keep running server-side in its own thread regardless of what page the browser is on (see "Job runner" in `docs/WEB_ARCHITECTURE.md`). The bug was purely a browser caching behavior: hitting Back after navigating away from a running job's `/jobs/{job_id}` page restores the browser's back/forward cache (bfcache) snapshot of that page exactly as it looked when Christer left, instead of making a fresh request - so the `<meta http-equiv="refresh">` never gets a chance to fire again (no new page load happens on a bfcache restore) and the output/status just sit frozen until a manual reload forces a real request.

Fixed by adding `Cache-Control: no-store` to the `GET /jobs/{job_id}` response (`app.py`'s `job_detail` route) - this tells the browser the page can never be served from any cache, bfcache included, so Back now always triggers a fresh request and shows current status/output exactly like a manual reload would. No JS needed, consistent with the rest of this app; it's a one-line header addition on the response object `templates.TemplateResponse()` already returns.

**Verification**: `ast.parse()`-clean on `app.py`. Couldn't exercise this against a real browser or `fastapi.testclient.TestClient` in this sandbox (no `fastapi`/`starlette` installed, no network to install them - the same constraint every increment in this session has worked around), so this rests on the header being both necessary and sufficient by HTTP spec (`Cache-Control: no-store` is explicitly defined to disable bfcache in every major browser) rather than an end-to-end test here. Worth Christer confirming on the real deployment: start a job, navigate to another job-trigger page, hit Back, and check the output/status are current without a manual reload.

## NAS: bv-generate through bv-web's own UI hit read-only archive + missing ffmpeg

Christer, running bv-generate from bv-web's job page on the NAS:

```
bv-generate: 20260806_070217_N: ffprobe not found on PATH
20260806_070217_N: 31s
Error: [Errno 30] Read-only file system: '/data/archive/20260806_070217_N.duration.txt'
```

Two separate problems, both traceable to the same root cause: bv-web's job runner grew triggers for bv-download/bv-generate/bv-export (see the earlier job-runner entries in this file), but the Docker deployment around it was never updated to match - it was still built entirely around the original "bv-web only browses, never writes" assumption from before that feature existed.

1. **`ffprobe not found`**: `Dockerfile` installed only the `web` extra (fastapi/uvicorn/jinja2) - no ffmpeg at all. The pure-Python MP4-box fallback (see the earlier "Pure-Python MP4 box parser fallback" entry) covered duration lookup well enough to still print "31s", masking how broken this was - a real `--transcribe`/`--diarize` job would have failed outright, not just warned, since there's no fallback for those.
2. **`Read-only file system`**: `docker-compose.yml` mounted bv-web's `/data/archive` (and `/data/trips`) `:ro` - correct for a pure archive browser, wrong the moment that same container's own job runner needs to write `.duration.txt`/`.aac`/exported trip folders into those same paths.

Asked Christer which way to fix it: make bv-web's container capable of running these jobs for real (heavier image, read-write mounts), or keep it light and steer NAS users back to `bv-cli`/the PC path for anything beyond browsing. He picked the former.

**Fix**: `Dockerfile` now installs `ffmpeg` via `apt-get` and `.[web,speech,translate]` instead of `.[web]` alone - the same toolchain `Dockerfile.cli` already carries (torch and its build time included; same trade-off, already accepted there). `docker-compose.yml` drops `:ro` from both of bv-web's `./data/archive` and `./data/trips` mounts. `pyproject.toml`'s `web` extras group itself is untouched (still just fastapi/uvicorn/jinja2) so `bv-live` - which shares that group and has no need for the heavy stuff - and any future truly-read-only bv-web deployment can still install `.[web]` alone; the Dockerfile just now asks for more groups explicitly. `docs/DEPLOY.md` updated throughout: "Two ways to run bv-generate/bv-export" is now "Three ways" (adds triggering from bv-web's own job pages), the directory-tree/mount comments no longer say read-only, the `docker-compose.override.yml` example for a differently-located archive folder drops its `:ro` suffix on bv-web's override too, and step 4's build command now warns the first `bv-web` build is slow/multi-GB, same warning `bv-cli`'s build already carries.

**Verification**: grepped `docker-compose.yml` for `:ro` - none remain. Read back the full `Dockerfile`, `docker-compose.yml`, and the touched sections of `docs/DEPLOY.md` to confirm every comment referencing the old read-only/lightweight assumptions was updated, not just the mounts themselves - stale comments claiming "read-only" next to a now-read-write mount would be worse than no comment.
